q: A buyer purchases a used forklift. Unknown to the buyer, a bank holds a security interest in it, and the seller says nothing. Breach of the title warranty?
o: Only if the seller is a forklift dealer.
Only after the bank repossesses the forklift.
Yes, because of the lien.
No; the buyer should have searched the public filings.
No; the warranty covers ownership, not liens.
oe: Every seller makes it.
Eviction isn't required.
Correct. Section 2-312(1)(b): goods must be delivered free of any security interest or lien the buyer didn't actually know of at contracting.
"Knowledge" means actual knowledge.
It expressly covers liens.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Undisclosed lien

q: A dentist sells her own used boat, knowing its hull has a hidden crack, and says nothing. Which is correct?
o: She is a merchant because she is a licensed professional.
No § 2-314 warranty, but she should have disclosed the crack.
She warrants merchantability because every sale of goods includes it.
Her silence creates an express warranty of seaworthiness.
She has no liability of any kind for silence.
oe: Merchant status is about the goods or practices, not one's profession.
Correct. A person making an isolated sale isn't a merchant for § 2-314, but good faith requires disclosing known material hidden defects (cmt. 3).
Only merchants in goods of the kind do.
Silence isn't an affirmation.
Comment 3 and fraud law cut against that.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — Isolated seller's hidden defect

q: In a hybrid transaction the services predominate. Which Article 2 rule would NOT apply?
o: The buyer's right to reject nonconforming goods.
The risk-of-loss rules.
The § 2-201 requirement of a signed record.
The implied warranty of merchantability.
The seller's right to cure a rejected tender.
oe: Applies. Acceptance and rejection relate to the goods.
Apply. Tender and risk of loss relate to the goods.
Correct. Provisions relating primarily to the transaction as a whole don't apply: § 2-201, formation (§§ 2-204 to 2-207), and § 2-209's no-consideration rule.
Applies. Warranties (§§ 2-312 to 2-318) relate to the goods.
Applies. Cure (§ 2-508) is listed in cmt. 5.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Goods don't predominate: what drops out

q: A buyer's signed email says, "Confirming our deal for 300 jackets." The oral deal was for 500. The seller sues for 500. Under § 2-201, the seller can enforce:
o: Nothing, because the seller never signed the email.
500 jackets, if it proves the oral deal by clear and convincing evidence.
500 jackets, because only the price must be stated accurately.
300 jackets at most, the quantity in the email.
Nothing, because a record that misstates the quantity is insufficient.
oe: Only the party to be charged (the buyer) must sign.
No standard of proof gets past the quantity limit.
Backwards. Price may be omitted or wrong; quantity limits enforcement.
Correct. The contract "is not enforceable under this paragraph beyond the quantity of goods shown" in the record.
A misstated term doesn't make the record insufficient; it caps enforcement at the quantity shown.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Quantity shown controls

q: When a contract is terminated under § 2-106(3), what survives?
o: Only claims for future lost profits.
Nothing; every right is extinguished.
Rights based on prior breach or performance.
Only the seller's rights.
All executory duties.
oe: Those are what termination cuts off.
Prior-breach rights survive.
Correct. All obligations still executory on both sides are discharged.
Both sides' rights from prior breach or performance survive.
Those are discharged.
topic: XIV · Termination & cancellation (§§ 2-106, 2-309) — Effect of termination

q: For a merchant seller under § 2-509(3), risk passes on the buyer's "receipt" of the goods. "Receipt" means:
o: acquiring title.
being told the goods are ready.
receiving the invoice.
paying for the goods.
None of the above.
oe: Not the test.
That's notice, part of tender.
Not receipt of goods.
Payment is irrelevant.
Correct. None of these. "Receipt" means taking physical possession of the goods (§ 2-103(1)(c)). A merchant seller keeps the risk until then.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Meaning of receipt

q: A five-year contract obligates a cabinet maker to buy 50,000 sq. ft. of particle board a year. Demand shifts to hardwood. Can the buyer cut to 20,000 without the seller's assent?
o: Yes, if it gives reasonable notice first.
Yes, because buyers may vary quantity in good faith.
Yes, because 20,000 isn't unreasonably disproportionate.
Yes, under § 2-615 impracticability.
No; with a fixed quantity, falling demand is its risk.
oe: Notice doesn't let one party rewrite a fixed quantity.
That's for requirements contracts.
The disproportion test applies to requirements terms.
A market shift doesn't excuse.

Correct. It's a fixed-quantity contract, not a requirements contract; the risk of falling demand is the buyer's. Cutting back needs a modification, or it's a breach. Excuse arguments are weak, since a market shift is the classic risk a fixed contract allocates.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Problem 4-1(a) fixed quantity

q: The windows were improperly crated. (1) The bad crating causes the damage. (2) Instead, a carrier's crash causes it. Who bears each loss?
o: They split both losses.
(1) Buyer; (2) Buyer.
(1) Buyer; (2) Seller.
(1) Seller; (2) Seller.
(1) Seller; (2) Buyer.
oe: No splitting.
Loss caused by the seller's improper shipment stays with the seller.
Reversed.
The bad crating didn't cause the crash loss.

Correct. Problem 4-7(d). Improper crating is a failure to make a reasonable transport contract (§ 2-504(a)); where it causes loss, it's a ground for rejection, so § 2-510(1) keeps risk on the seller. Where the crash causes the loss, the crating caused no loss, so risk had passed (Windows v. Jordan Panel).
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Bad crating vs. carrier crash
pre: Custom windows are to be "shipped properly crated ... and delivered to" the buyer's New York construction site. Properly crated, they're destroyed in transit. Who bears the loss?

q: A buyer pays a lab $400 to test delivered fabric. The fabric fails, and the buyer rightfully rejects it. Who bears the $400?
o: The buyer, unless the contract says otherwise.
The seller, because the goods failed and were rejected.
They split it.
The buyer, in every case.
The seller, even if the fabric had passed.
oe: The statute shifts it here by default.
Correct. Section 2-513(2): the buyer bears inspection expenses, but may recover them if the goods don't conform and are rejected.
No splitting rule.
It can recover them here.
Only if nonconforming and rejected.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Who pays for inspection

q: Under § 1-304 and § 1-201(b)(20), good faith means:
o: honesty in fact plus reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing.
honesty in fact, and nothing more.
a fiduciary's duty of loyalty and candor.
the care a reasonable merchant would use in performing, judged objectively.
fair dealing, judged by the party's own standards of what is commercially fair.
oe: Correct. A subjective prong (honesty, motive) and an objective one (fair dealing). Section 1-304 imposes it on the performance and enforcement of every contract or duty under the UCC.
That was old Article 1's subjective-only definition.
Market Street: good faith is well short of a fiduciary duty.
Good faith isn't a negligence standard.
The objective prong uses reasonable commercial standards.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Definition of good faith

q: When can a repudiating party NO LONGER retract?
o: After the aggrieved party materially relies on it.
Only if the aggrieved party has sued.
Only after the repudiating party's next performance comes due.
Immediately; repudiation is irrevocable.
Never; retraction is always available.
oe: Correct. Section 2-611(1): retraction is allowed until the next performance is due unless the aggrieved party has canceled, materially changed position, or otherwise indicated it considers the repudiation final. Retraction reinstates the contract with allowance for delay.
Suing usually shows it considers the repudiation final, but the listed rule is broader.
That's the outer limit, not the cutoff here.
It can be retracted.
It's cut off by those events.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Retraction cutoff

q: Which statement about § 2-313 is correct?
o: It requires the buyer to prove the seller knew the statement was false.
It keeps the common-law line between representations and warranties intact.
It applies only to statements in the written contract itself.
It rejects caveat emptor and makes affirmations of fact warranties.
It codifies caveat emptor for sales between merchants.
oe: Warranty liability doesn't depend on the seller's knowledge; that's fraud.
It blurs that line.
Oral statements, samples and models count too.
Correct. The text calls it "staggering alchemy": it blurs the common-law line between a representation of fact (tort) and a warranty (contract).
It rejects caveat emptor.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — What § 2-313 changed

q: A signed writing states definitively the terms it covers but doesn't contain the whole deal. How is it classified?
o: A confirmation under § 2-201(2).
A complete and exclusive integration.
An unfinished draft outside the PER.
A final, partial integration.
A merger clause.
oe: That's a SOF concept.
That would contain the whole deal.
It's final as to what it covers.

Correct. Evidence can't contradict its terms, but consistent additional terms may come in. An unfinished draft is outside the rule; a complete and exclusive writing also bars consistent additional terms.
A merger clause is a term, not a classification.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Partial integration

q: Which loss is consequential under § 2-715(2)?
o: Profits lost in a foreseeable shutdown the buyer couldn't avoid by cover.
Profits lost from a use the seller had no reason to know about.
The cost of inspecting the goods.
The cost of storing rejected goods.
The contract-market price difference.
oe: Correct. Consequential damages cover losses from needs the seller had reason to know of at contracting that the buyer couldn't reasonably prevent, plus injury to person or property from breach of warranty.
Not foreseeable, so not recoverable.
Incidental.
Incidental.
Direct damages under § 2-713.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Consequential damages

q: Which statement about the Uniform Commercial Code is NOT correct?
o: A state may enact it with non-uniform changes, so you must check the enacted version.
Once the ALI and the ULC approve its text, it binds courts in every state.
Article 2's principal innovations include minimizing the relevance of title.
The proposed 2003 amendments to Article 2 were never enacted and were withdrawn in 2011.
Louisiana has never enacted Article 2 or Article 2A.
oe: True. States can and do vary the text, which is why the enacted version controls.
Correct. This is the false statement. The UCC is a model code drafted by the ULC and the ALI; it is not law anywhere until a state legislature enacts it.
True. The text names two: de-emphasizing title and new rules on how agreements are formed.
True. No state adopted them, and the sponsors withdrew them.
True. Every other state enacted the Code by 1968; Louisiana still hasn't adopted Articles 2 and 2A.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — What the UCC is

q: Under the 2022 definition of "sign," which is the weakest argument that an email was signed?
o: The sender attached an electronic symbol with intent to adopt the email.
The sender typed her name at the end.
An automatic signature block the sender set up appears at the bottom.
A scanned letter bearing the sender's handwritten signature was attached.
The sender's address appears only in the email's "From" line.
oe: Strong: that's the definition.
Strong: a typed name adopted with intent to authenticate is a signature.
Likely a signature, per the text.
Strong.
Correct. The text calls the bare "From" field debatable. A typed name is almost certainly a signature, and an automatically appended signature block likely is.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Weakest signature argument

q: A seller delivers goods that don't conform. Before the buyer decides whether to keep them, they're stolen from the buyer's loading dock. Who bears the loss?
o: They split it.
Whichever party is insured.
The buyer, because it hadn't rejected yet.
The buyer, because the goods were in its possession.
The seller, until cure or acceptance.
oe: No splitting.
Insurance matters under § 2-510(2)-(3), not (1).
The nonconformity keeps risk on the seller.
Possession doesn't move risk here.
Correct. Where a tender fails to conform so as to give a right of rejection, risk remains on the seller until cure or acceptance (§ 2-510(1)).
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Theft during inspection

q: Which pairing of a UCC Article with its subject is wrong?
o: Article 5: letters of credit.
Article 2A: leases of goods.
Article 7: investment securities.
Article 12: controllable electronic records, such as some crypto assets.
Article 9: secured transactions.
oe: Right pairing. Letters of credit are Article 5.
Right pairing. Article 2A (1987) governs leases of goods.
Correct. This pairing is wrong. Article 7 covers documents of title (warehouse receipts, bills of lading); investment securities are Article 8.
Right pairing. Article 12 was added by the 2022 amendments.
Right pairing. Security interests in personal property are Article 9.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — Map of the Articles

q: A college student sells her bike "as is." It turns out to have been stolen before she bought it. Has she breached the warranty of title?
o: No, because "as is" disclaims all warranties.
No; only merchants warrant title.
Yes; every seller warrants good title.
Only if she told the buyer it was hers.
No, because she didn't know it was stolen.
oe: It doesn't reach title.
All sellers do.
Correct. Every seller, merchant or not, warrants good title and rightful transfer, and "as is" doesn't disclaim title.
The warranty arises without any statement.
Knowledge is irrelevant.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Student sells a stolen bike

q: An oven that breaches a warranty starts a fire that damages the buyer's kitchen. How is the kitchen damage classified?
o: Consequential damages.
Liquidated damages.
Not recoverable in contract.
Incidental damages.
Direct value damages under § 2-714(2).
oe: Correct. Injury to person or property proximately resulting from a breach of warranty (§ 2-715(2)(b)).
Nothing was agreed in advance.
Recoverable.
Those are response costs.
That measures the oven's lost value.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Oven fire

q: Which statement about the § 1-304 duty of good faith is NOT correct?
o: It is a lens for interpreting the agreement, not a stand-alone claim.
It requires good faith while negotiating the contract.
It applies to every contract within the UCC.
It can't be used to contradict the express terms.
It can't be disclaimed, but parties may set standards that aren't manifestly unreasonable.
oe: True. A failure to perform a specific duty in good faith is a breach of that duty, not an independent cause of action.
Correct. This is false. Section 1-304 covers performance and enforcement, not negotiation or formation.
True.
True.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Limits of the duty of good faith

q: A seller ships "F.O.B. seller's city" under a negotiable bill of lading to its own order and demands payment against the bill while the goods are still en route. The contract says nothing about paying against documents. Which is correct?
o: The buyer may wait, and risk hasn't passed because the seller reserved title.
The buyer may wait to inspect, and risk passed at shipment anyway.
The buyer must pay now; reserving the bill requires payment against documents.
The seller breached by shipping, so the buyer may cancel.
The buyer must pay now, but may sue later for defects.
oe: Risk passes even under reservation.

Correct. Problem 4-8: payment is due where the buyer receives the goods, and the buyer may inspect after arrival before paying (§§ 2-310(a)-(b), 2-513(1)). Shipping under reservation (§ 2-505) doesn't stop risk from passing on delivery to the carrier (§ 2-509(1)(a)).
Merely using a bill of lading isn't an agreement to pay against documents.
Shipping under reservation isn't itself a breach unless the deal was on credit.
It needn't pay before inspecting.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Shipment under reservation

q: A party retracts its repudiation but ignores the other side's justified demand for assurance. Is the retraction effective?
o: No; it must include the justified assurance.
Only if the next performance isn't due yet.
Yes; any clear statement of intent to perform is enough.
Yes, if it's in writing.
Yes, because retraction can't be conditioned.
oe: Correct. A retraction may be by any method clearly indicating intent to perform, but must include any assurance justifiably demanded under § 2-609 (§ 2-611(2)).
It still needs the assurance.
It must include the justified assurance.
Writing doesn't replace the assurance.
It must include justified assurance.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Retraction without assurance

q: A "requirements" contract at $1 per sq. ft., with no estimate. Requirements ran 25,000, 32,500 and 35,000. In year four, with the market at $1.15, the buyer demands 60,000, its plant's full capacity. The seller's best arguments?
o: Lack of consideration.
Impracticability.
None; without an estimate there's no limit.
Disproportion to past requirements, and bad faith.
The statute of frauds, since no quantity is stated.
oe: Not the issue.
A market rise doesn't excuse.
Prior requirements serve as the benchmark.

Correct. With no estimate, compare normal prior requirements (60,000 is about 71% above 35,000), weigh the Orange & Rockland factors (market above contract price), and note that a demand set at plant capacity suggests opportunism.
A requirements term satisfies the quantity requirement.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Problem 4-1(b) plant capacity

q: Which statement contrasts express and implied warranties correctly?
o: Implied warranties apply only if stated in the contract.
Both require that the seller intend to make a warranty.
Implied warranties apply only when the buyer relies on the seller's skill.
Express ones are bargained for; implied ones are imposed by law.
Express warranties arise by law; implied ones are bargained for.
oe: They're implied by law without being stated.
Neither requires intent.
Only fitness has a reliance element.
Correct. A warranty is a promise that a fact is true, backed by an implied promise of indemnity if it's false.
Reversed.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Express vs. implied

q: Which contract term takes away the buyer's right to inspect BEFORE paying?
o: Sale on approval.
C.O.D.
F.O.B. seller's plant.
Payment within 30 days.
Delivery in a single lot.
oe: Trial use is the point of approval.
Correct. Section 2-513(3): no inspection before payment under C.O.D. or similar terms, or payment against documents of title (unless payment is due only after the goods are available for inspection).
A delivery term; the buyer still inspects after arrival before paying.
Credit doesn't remove inspection.
Irrelevant to inspection.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — No inspection before payment

q: Weighing predominance under § 2-102 cmt. 3, which statement is correct?
o: Manufacturing services count toward goods; design services usually don't.
Installation services always count toward the goods.
An agreed allocation of the price between goods and services is irrelevant.
Design services for specially manufactured goods count toward the goods.
Only the price split counts; the parties' purposes are irrelevant.
oe: Correct. Because goods include specially manufactured goods, services involved in making them are attributed to the goods side. Design services normally are not.
Wrong. Installation is a service; it doesn't automatically count as goods.
Wrong. The portion of the price attributable to the goods matters, and an agreed allocation is ordinarily binding.
Wrong. The comment treats design services differently from manufacturing services.
Wrong. The factors also include the agreement's language, the parties' purposes and the nature of their businesses.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Predominance factors in cmt. 3

q: Which statement about samples and models is correct?
o: Under § 2-317, a sample beats exact technical specifications if they conflict.
Neither creates a warranty unless the written contract mentions it.
A sample from the bulk is presumed to describe the goods; a model, less so.
A sample warrants only that the goods will be merchantable.
A model is drawn from the actual goods to be delivered.
oe: Reversed: exact or technical specifications displace an inconsistent sample or general description.
Either can create a warranty if part of the basis of the bargain.
Correct. Comment 6: a sample is drawn from the actual bulk; a model is offered when the goods aren't at hand, so the presumption that it describes them is weaker.
It warrants that the whole of the goods will conform to the sample.
That describes a sample.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Sample vs. model

q: A writing is final but NOT complete and exclusive. Which evidence is admissible?
o: A contemporaneous oral agreement contradicting a written term.
A prior oral promise that negates the written price.
A prior oral agreement contradicting a written term.
A consistent additional term from a prior oral agreement.
A prior written agreement contradicting a written term.
oe: Inadmissible.
Contradictory, so inadmissible.
Inadmissible.

Correct. The Problem 5-10 chart: consistent prior or contemporaneous terms come in against a partial integration; contradictory prior terms (oral or written) and contradictory contemporaneous oral terms don't.
Inadmissible.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Admissible against a partial integration

q: When is termination (not cancellation) most typical?
o: Whenever the parties mutually agree to end the deal early.
After the other party repudiates.
When a buyer rejects nonconforming goods.
After goods are destroyed before risk passes.
Indefinite supply deals, or a long lag before performance.
oe: That's rescission.
That's cancellation.
That's rejection and, possibly, cancellation.
That's § 2-613 avoidance.
Correct. E.g., monthly, requirements or output deals of indefinite length, or a contract for an airplane not yet designed. Termination may also occur at an agreed time or event.
topic: XIV · Termination & cancellation (§§ 2-106, 2-309) — Where termination is typical

q: A buyer orders 500 custom brackets by sending blueprints. No words in the contract describe the brackets. Has the seller made an express warranty?
o: Only if the seller signed the blueprints.
No. The buyer supplied the blueprints, so only fitness could apply.
Yes. A description needn't be in words.
No. Descriptions must be stated in words.
Only if the blueprints are attached to a signed contract.
oe: No signature requirement.
Buyer's specs tend to defeat fitness (no reliance), not express warranty by description.
Correct. Comment 5: technical specifications and blueprints can be descriptions, and past deliveries can set the description by course of dealing.
Not under cmt. 5.
No such requirement.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Blueprints as a description

q: The buyer's order said "Ship to Buyer, Council Bluffs." The seller's later invoice said "F.O.B. delivered $1.20 rate." The seller loaded the carrier's rail car and got a signed bill of lading; fire destroyed the car before the carrier moved it. Who likely bears the loss?
o: They split it.
The seller, because the buyer never signed the invoice.
The seller, because the carrier hadn't moved the car yet.
The seller, because "F.O.B. delivered" means a destination contract.
The buyer, because risk passed when the car was loaded.
oe: No splitting.
The invoice term isn't needed for the buyer to bear risk.
Delivery to the carrier, not movement, is the test.
The phrase, sent after formation, addresses freight.

Correct. Problem 4-9: the contract formed on the order (a shipment contract); the invoice came after formation (at most a § 2-207 proposal that would materially alter risk); and "F.O.B. delivered $1.20 rate" reads as a freight-price term. Risk passed when the goods were duly delivered to the carrier.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Later invoice term

q: Under § 1-103(b), principles of law and equity supplement the UCC unless a particular provision displaces them. Which common-law rule has Article 2 displaced?
o: The defense of mistake.
The law of principal and agent.
Estoppel, including reliance on the other party's conduct.
The mirror-image rule for acceptances.
The defense of duress.
oe: Not displaced. Mistake is listed in § 1-103(b).
Not displaced. Agency law is listed in § 1-103(b) and supplements the Code.
Not displaced. Estoppel is named in § 1-103(b) and is one of the four bases for barring a breach claim in Problem 3-5.
Correct. Section 2-207(1) displaces it: a definite and seasonable acceptance works even if it states additional or different terms.
Not displaced. Duress is one of the "validating or invalidating" causes § 1-103(b) expressly preserves.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — Common law displaced by Article 2

q: Which statement about the objective prong of good faith is correct?
o: In states that kept the old Article 1 definition, merchants face only honesty in fact.
It asks only what the party honestly believed was fair.
It concerns fair dealing, not carelessness.
It makes a party who performs carelessly guilty of bad faith.
It requires each party to disclose all material facts.
oe: Merchants in those states are still held to Article 2's objective standard.
That's the subjective prong.

Correct. Comment 20 to § 1-201: it's about fair dealing, not negligence. Some states kept a subjective-only Article 1 definition; there, merchants are still held to Article 2's "in the trade" standard (§ 2-103(1)(b)).
Negligence isn't the test.
No general duty of disclosure.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Objective prong

q: A seller produces a record signed by the buyer that satisfies § 2-201(1). What has the seller established?
o: That a contract exists on the terms stated in the record.
Only that the statute of frauds won't bar the claim.
That the buyer breached, unless the buyer proves otherwise.
That the buyer has no other defense, such as fraud or mistake.
That the contract is enforceable for any quantity the seller proves.
oe: The record removes the defense; it doesn't prove the terms.

Correct. Satisfying the SOF only opens the courthouse door; the seller must still prove a contract was made, its terms and breach. (Flowchart: SOF applies? Sufficient signed record? If not, an exception?)
The seller still bears its burden on breach.
Other defenses survive.
Enforcement can't exceed the quantity in the record.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — SOF only opens the door

q: A monthly supply arrangement has no end date. The buyer wants out. Which is correct?
o: It must show good cause.
It may end it any time, with reasonable notice.
It may end it without any notice.
It may never end it without the seller's consent.
It must perform for a reasonable time first.
oe: No reason is needed.

Correct. Section 2-309(2)-(3): a contract for successive performances of indefinite duration is valid for a reasonable time but may be terminated at any time by either party; except on an agreed event, reasonable notification (time to find substitutes) is required.
Reasonable notification is required.
Either party may terminate.
It may terminate at any time.
topic: XIV · Termination & cancellation (§§ 2-106, 2-309) — Ending an open-ended deal

q: A third party sues a buyer, claiming to own goods the buyer bought. The buyer wins after costly litigation. Has the seller breached the title warranty?
o: Only if the buyer lost possession.
No, because Article 2 no longer warrants quiet possession.
Only if the claimant won.
No, because title turned out to be good.
Yes, under most courts, if the claim was colorable.
oe: The warranty of quiet possession was abolished; disturbance is just one way to prove breach.
The abolished warranty doesn't mean colorable claims are harmless.
The claim must be colorable, not successful.
A colorable claim can breach.

Correct. Comment 1: the buyer should get a title good enough that it won't be exposed to a lawsuit. Most courts find breach from a colorable claim even if title proves good, and the buyer may recover its fees defending title as consequential damages (not fees suing the seller).
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Colorable claim

q: A seller fails to deliver, and the buyer cancels. Which is NOT among the buyer's remedies?
o: Incidental and consequential damages.
Cover price minus contract price (§ 2-712).
Recovering any part of the price it paid.
The seller's lost profit under § 2-708(2).
Market price minus contract price (§ 2-713).
oe: A buyer's remedy: § 2-715.
A buyer's remedy.
A buyer's remedy: § 2-711.
Correct. That is a SELLER's remedy against a breaching buyer.
A buyer's remedy.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Buyer's remedies for nondelivery

q: A writing is complete and exclusive. Which evidence is still admissible?
o: A consistent prior oral term.
A consistent contemporaneous oral term.
A contradictory prior oral term.
A consistent prior written term.
Usage of trade that supplements the written terms.
oe: Barred by full integration.
Barred.
Barred.
Barred.

Correct. Course of dealing, usage of trade and course of performance may supplement even a complete and exclusive record unless carefully negated (§ 2-202(a), cmt. 2). Consistent additional terms from prior or contemporaneous agreements are barred.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Admissible against a full integration

q: A buyer's requirements were 90,000, then 100,000. Which year-3 demand is proportionate to history but NOT in good faith?
o: 110,000, so it can resell some at the higher market price.
105,000, for normal growth.
400,000, ordered honestly after landing a huge customer.
100,000, to meet ordinary needs.
95,000, after a mild slowdown in the buyer's own customer orders.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-2(B): the quantity is in line, but it isn't an actual requirement occurring in good faith. Buying only 85,000 because it's secretly buying cheaper elsewhere would be another example.
Proportionate and in good faith.
Good faith but disproportionate.
Proportionate and in good faith.
Proportionate and in good faith.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Proportionate but bad faith

q: Which is NOT an implied warranty recognized on the Week 3 slides?
o: Merchantability.
Fitness for a particular purpose.
A warranty arising from course of dealing or usage of trade.
That the goods are the best available on the market.
Against infringement.
oe: Implied: § 2-315.
Implied: § 2-314(3), e.g., providing pedigree papers for a pedigreed dog (cmt. 12).
Correct. No warranty promises the best goods; merchantability requires minimal quality.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — List of implied warranties

q: A buyer rightfully revokes acceptance of a defective boat. Before the seller picks it up, a storm destroys it. The buyer's insurance covers half the loss. Who bears the other half?
o: The buyer, because revocation doesn't affect risk.
The buyer, because it had accepted the boat.
The seller, to the extent of the insurance gap.
The seller bears all of it; the buyer's insurance is irrelevant.
They split the uninsured half.
oe: Section 2-510(2) says it does.
Revocation lets it shift the uninsured part.
Correct. Section 2-510(2): a buyer who rightfully revokes may, to the extent of any deficiency in its effective insurance, treat the risk as resting on the seller from the beginning.
Only to the extent of the insurance deficiency.
No splitting.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — After revocation

q: Speedy Offset agrees to print and bind 500 copies of an art book that the author wrote and designed. The author sues over poor printing and binding. Does Article 2 apply?
o: Yes. Printing and binding are part of manufacturing the books.
No. Printing is a service, so services predominate.
Only to the binding claim, because binding produces a finished good.
No. The author's design work is the predominant part of the deal.
Only if the author is a merchant.
oe: Correct. Services involved in manufacturing goods count toward the goods, and the design was the author's own. Even if services predominated, both claims are about whether the goods conform, so the goods-related provisions would still apply.
Cmt. 3 attributes manufacturing services to the goods side.
Both claims concern the conformity of the books.
The design was the author's, not Speedy's, so it isn't part of what Speedy supplied.
Scope doesn't depend on merchant status.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Problem 1-2 art books

q: A buyer treats an ambiguous email as a repudiation and cancels. A court later finds there was no repudiation. Result?
o: The buyer may recover its costs of canceling.
The buyer is the one in breach.
The seller is in breach for writing an ambiguous email.
The contract is rescinded by mutual consent.
Nothing; canceling in good faith is always safe.
oe: No.
Correct. The "game of chicken": if you guess wrong about repudiation and suspend or cancel, you may be liable. Lawyers should first pin down each side's obligations.
Ambiguity isn't repudiation.
No mutual consent.
Good faith doesn't excuse a wrongful cancellation.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Game of chicken

q: The contract says goods will be inspected at the buyer's plant by a named lab. What is the effect?
o: It's presumed exclusive; delivery and risk don't move.
It makes the buyer's plant the place of delivery.
Risk stays with the seller until the lab reports.
It waives the buyer's right to reject.
It's void, because the inspection rules of § 2-513 can't be varied.
oe: Correct. Section 2-513(4). If compliance becomes impossible, the default rules apply unless the agreed method was an indispensable condition.
It doesn't shift the place of delivery.
It doesn't shift the passing of risk.
No.
They can be.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Agreed place of inspection

q: Which statement correctly contrasts the common law with Article 2?
o: The common law needs agreement on all material terms; Article 2 tolerates open terms.
Both require an acceptance that mirrors the offer.
Article 2 requires consideration for a firm offer, but the common law does not.
Article 2 is based on promise, the common law on bargain.
The common law allows any reasonable medium of acceptance; Article 2 presumes the offer's medium.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-204(3), a contract doesn't fail for indefiniteness if the parties intended to contract and there's a reasonably certain basis for a remedy.
Wrong. Section 2-207(1) abolished the mirror-image rule for sales of goods.
Reversed. The common law requires consideration (an option); § 2-205 does not.
Reversed. The common law is based on promise; Article 2 on bargain.
Reversed. The common law presumed the same medium; § 2-206(1)(a) allows any reasonable one.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Common law vs. Article 2 formation

q: At delivery, after the price is paid, a buyer asks, "Is this generator rated for 10 kW?" The seller says, "Yes." Can that be an express warranty?
o: Yes, as a modification that needs no consideration.
Only if the buyer and seller sign a new contract.
Only if the generator later fails within the first year.
No; the buyer gave no new consideration for it.
No; statements after the deal closes are never part of the bargain.
oe: Correct. Comment 7: timing is immaterial; language used after the deal closes becomes a modification under § 2-209 and needs no consideration.
No new contract is needed.
Failure goes to breach, not to whether a warranty exists.
Modifications need no consideration.
Comment 7 says otherwise.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Statement at delivery

q: Under "F.O.B. seller's packing house," the seller hands fresh strawberries to a carrier in an unrefrigerated truck, though refrigeration was plainly needed. The fruit spoils on the way. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer, unless the seller also failed to notify it of shipment.
The buyer, because risk passed when the carrier took the fruit.
They split it, since either could have insured.
The seller, because its unreasonable transport contract caused the loss.
The carrier alone, because it accepted the fruit.
oe: The bad transport contract alone is enough because it caused the loss.
Not when the seller's improper shipment caused the loss.
No splitting.

Correct. Section 2-504(a) requires a contract for transportation reasonable "having regard to the nature of the goods." Because material loss ensued, the buyer may reject, and § 2-510(1) keeps the risk on the seller.
As between the parties, the seller bears it; the seller may pursue the carrier.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Unrefrigerated truck

q: A buyer takes goods into its warehouse and pays the invoice that day, planning to inspect next week. Has it accepted the goods?
o: Yes, by taking possession.
Not yet; possession and payment aren't acceptance.
Yes, because it didn't object on arrival.
Yes, by paying.
Yes, because accepting goods works like accepting an offer.
oe: Possession isn't acceptance.
Correct. Possession isn't acceptance (the buyer may be inspecting), and payment isn't acceptance (§ 2-512(2)). Acceptance of goods differs from acceptance of an offer.
It has a reasonable opportunity to inspect first.
Payment doesn't constitute acceptance.
They are different concepts.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Possession and payment

q: How does "good faith" in § 2-403's good-faith purchaser rule differ from the § 1-304 duty?
o: It requires the purchaser to investigate the seller's title before paying.
It applies only to merchant purchasers.
It is the same concept applied to buyers.
It is purely objective.
It concerns third parties, not a duty owed to a contract partner.
oe: No duty to investigate is imposed.
Any purchaser can be a good-faith purchaser for value.
The text distinguishes them.
Not the point of the distinction.
Correct. The text notes that § 2-403 good faith concerns the purchaser's relationship to the rest of the commercial world.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Good-faith purchaser is different

q: A signed contract for 1,000 sacks of potatoes says the price is "to be agreed at delivery." The parties never agree. If they intended to be bound, the price is:
o: a reasonable price at the time for delivery.
whatever the seller demands, if in good faith.
nothing; the contract fails.
the average of the two sides' last offers.
the market price on the contract date.
oe: Correct. Section 2-305(1)(b). The same rule applies when nothing is said about price, or when an agreed market or third-party standard isn't set.
That's for prices to be fixed by one party.
Not if they intended to be bound.
No such rule.
The time for delivery controls.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Price to be agreed, not agreed

q: A supply contract says either party may terminate "immediately, without notice." Is that enforceable?
o: Only between merchants.
No; notice can never be waived.
Only if the contract has a fixed term.
Yes, always; it's freely variable.
Yes, unless its operation would be unconscionable.
oe: Not the test.
It can, subject to unconscionability.
It's for indefinite contracts.
Subject to unconscionability.
Correct. Section 2-309(3): an agreement dispensing with notification is invalid if its operation would be unconscionable.
topic: XIV · Termination & cancellation (§§ 2-106, 2-309) — Waiving termination notice

q: A sales contract and a separate side letter are signed at the same meeting. The side letter adds a term. Does § 2-202 bar it?
o: Yes, unless the side letter is notarized.
Yes; any agreement outside the main contract is barred.
No; a contemporaneous writing is read with the record.
Only if the main contract has no merger clause.
Yes; contemporaneous writings are treated like prior oral ones.
oe: No such rule.
Contemporaneous writings aren't barred.

Correct. Section 2-202 bars evidence of prior agreements and contemporaneous ORAL agreements. A contemporaneous writing is read together with the final record (and for a complete and exclusive record it is part of the record itself).
Not the test.
They aren't.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Side letter signed the same day

q: When can a buyer get specific performance?
o: Whenever the buyer can't afford to cover.
Whenever the seller fails to deliver.
Only if the contract says so.
Only in limited cases, such as unique goods.
Never under Article 2.
oe: Not the test.
Only in limited circumstances.
It's a statutory remedy.
Correct. Section 2-716 (and § 2-502 for identified goods); the buyer then pays the price.
Section 2-716 allows it.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Specific performance

q: The Week 3 slides list title among the "implied" warranties. What does the UCC itself say?
o: It's an implied warranty that "as is" excludes.
It arises only if title is mentioned in a writing.
It isn't called implied, so § 2-316 doesn't govern disclaiming it.
It arises only when the seller is a merchant dealing in goods of the kind.
It's a kind of express warranty.
oe: "As is" doesn't disclaim title.
It arises in every contract for sale.
Correct. Section 2-312 cmt. 6. The title warranty is disclaimed only by specific language or circumstances under § 2-312(2); "as is" doesn't work.
Every seller makes it.
It arises without any statement.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Is the title warranty "implied"?

q: A buyer repudiates a contract for 50 identified, conforming crates of olive oil still in the seller's warehouse. A week later a fire destroys them. The seller's insurance covers 60%. Who bears the uninsured 40%?
o: The buyer, however long after the repudiation the fire occurs.
The buyer, if a week is within a commercially reasonable time.
The seller's insurer pays all of it.
The seller, because risk hadn't passed.
They split it.
oe: Only for a commercially reasonable time.

Correct. Section 2-510(3): when the buyer repudiates as to conforming goods already identified, before risk passes, the seller may treat the risk as on the buyer for a commercially reasonable time, to the extent of any deficiency in the seller's insurance.
Only 60% was insured.
The buyer's breach shifts it.
No splitting.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Buyer repudiates, then fire

q: Two weeks before the first of six valve installments, Ace emails: it will be late on the first, "we expect you will cover the extra expenses," and it will catch up by the second. The buyer, who now needs only half the valves, wants out. Best advice?
o: Do nothing until the second installment is due.
Don't cancel yet; send a § 2-609 demand and reserve rights.
Pay the extra expenses to avoid a dispute.
Reject the first installment and cut the order in half.
Cancel now; any late installment ends the whole contract.
oe: Better to demand assurance now.

Correct. Problem 6-5: Ace has repudiated installment 1, but the cost demand isn't a repudiation unless performance is conditioned on it, and canceling the whole requires substantial impairment of the whole (§§ 2-610, 2-612). Overestimating needs isn't a valid reason. If Ace insists on extra pay or gives no adequate assurance, cancel, recover the 25% advance and cover.
The contract price is fixed.
Not a valid basis.
Only substantial impairment of the whole does.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Ace valves advice

q: Which statement about § 2-201's $500 threshold is correct?
o: It is adjusted for inflation every five years by the Permanent Editorial Board.
It looks to the goods' market value at delivery, not the contract price.
The 2022 amendments raised it to $5,000.
It hasn't changed in decades; the withdrawn 2003 amendments proposed $5,000.
It was eliminated for contracts formed by electronic records in 2022.
oe: No adjustment mechanism exists.
It looks to "the price."
The 2022 amendments changed "writing" to "record"; the threshold stayed $500.
Correct. The text also doubts the SOF's justifications (preventing perjured claims, encouraging memorialization).
Electronic records satisfy it; they didn't eliminate it.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — The $500 threshold

q: For limitations purposes, when does breach of the warranty of title occur?
o: When the buyer discovers the defect.
When the true owner first asserts a claim.
At tender of delivery.
When the buyer loses possession.
Four years after tender.
oe: That's for warranties explicitly extending to future performance.
Breach occurs at tender.
Correct. Comment 2: it doesn't extend to future performance. Notice rules apply but are read liberally if the seller acted in bad faith.
Not the trigger.
That's when the limitations period would end.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — When title breach occurs

q: Which of the following is NOT a reason the UCC is rarely the only law that governs a sale of goods?
o: Federal law, such as Magnuson-Moss or the CISG, may supplement or preempt it.
State statutes such as lemon laws or consumer-protection acts may supplement or displace it.
Parties can make their own "law" by agreement, course of dealing and usage of trade.
Common law and equity supplement it unless a particular provision displaces them.
Article 1 governs any commercial transaction on its own, even one no other Article covers.
oe: A real reason. The CISG is a treaty with the force of federal law.
A real reason: § 2-102(3)(b) says Article 2 doesn't impair statutes regulating sales to consumers, farmers and similar buyers.
A real reason: §§ 1-302 and 1-303.
A real reason: § 1-103(b).
Correct. This is false. Under § 1-102, Article 1's general provisions apply only when another Article governs the transaction.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — Why the UCC is never the only law

q: Which excuse doctrine concerns circumstances existing when the contract was FORMED, rather than later events?
o: Intervening illegality.
Impracticability.
Mistake.
Frustration of purpose.
Death of a party.
oe: A later event.
A later event.

Correct. Formation-time doctrines: incapacity, fraud, mistake, duress, illegality, unconscionability, statute of frauds. Later events: death, impracticability, frustration, intervening illegality, failure of a condition.
A later event.
A later event.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Formation-time doctrine

q: In Market Street Associates v. Frey, Judge Posner placed the contractual duty of good faith:
o: at the negligence standard of a reasonable merchant in the same trade.
halfway between a fiduciary duty and merely avoiding fraud.
nowhere, because good faith doesn't apply to a land lease.
at a fiduciary's duty of candor.
at the duty merely to refrain from active fraud.
oe: Not a negligence standard.
Correct. It isn't a duty of candor or altruism, but it forbids deliberately exploiting a partner's oversight during performance.
The case applied the common-law duty, used as the model for the UCC concept.
Too high; parties needn't be each other's keepers.
Too low; opportunism after contracting violates good faith.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Market Street standard

q: A supply contract lets the seller set the price at each delivery. What limits the seller?
o: A jury's view of a reasonable price, regardless of good faith.
It must charge the market price on the contract date.
The buyer's approval of each price.
Nothing; the buyer agreed to let the seller decide.
It must fix the price in good faith.
oe: The test is good faith.
Not required.
Then the price would be "to be agreed."
Good faith limits the discretion.
Correct. Section 2-305(2). It must also fix it within a reasonable time (§ 2-309).
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Price set by one party

q: Which of the following does § 1-103(a) list as a purpose the UCC must be liberally construed to promote?
o: Simplifying, clarifying and modernizing the law of commercial transactions.
Permitting continued expansion of commercial practices through custom, usage and agreement.
Making the law uniform among the jurisdictions.
Protecting buyers who lack bargaining power.
A, B and C, but not D.
oe: A listed purpose, but not the only one listed here.
A listed purpose, but not the only one listed here.
A listed purpose, but not the only one listed here.
Not listed. Consumer protection comes from other law (and doctrines like unconscionability), not § 1-103(a).
Correct. Section 1-103(a) lists exactly three purposes: simplify, clarify and modernize; permit expansion through custom, usage and agreement; and make the law uniform.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — Purposes in § 1-103(a)

q: A buyer has (1) typed notes of an oral boat deal that the seller never signed and (2) a software license both signed that never mentions the boat. Can the two be read together to satisfy § 2-201?
o: No. They neither refer to each other nor connect without parol testimony.
Yes, if the buyer testifies that both papers concern the same deal.
Yes, because the license bears the seller's signature.
No, because a software license can never be part of a sale-of-goods record.
Yes. Papers involving the same parties may always be combined.
oe: Correct. That's Casazza v. Kiser: the signed license didn't refer to a boat sale, so combining the papers would "eviscerate the statute of frauds."
Connection must appear without parol testimony.
The signed paper must connect to the terms of the sale.
Any record can count if it's connected; this one wasn't.
Common parties aren't enough.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Reading papers together

q: A seller loads wheat into its own truck to deliver it. On the way, the truck catches fire and the wheat is destroyed. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer, because the wheat was delivered to a carrier.
The buyer, if it paid in advance.
They split it.
The buyer, if the seller isn't a merchant, because tender had begun.
The seller, merchant or not.
oe: The seller's own truck isn't a carrier.
Payment doesn't matter.
No splitting.
Risk passes at the completion of tender, not the start.

Correct. Problem 4-6(a): the seller's own truck isn't a "carrier," so § 2-509(3) applies. A merchant keeps risk until receipt; a non-merchant until tender is completed, which never happened. Fungible wheat must be re-tendered.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Seller's own truck

q: Which statement about course of dealing and usage of trade under § 2-202 is correct?
o: Any merger clause excludes them.
They can always override express terms.
They can supplement even a full integration.
They come in only if the writing is ambiguous.
They're barred whenever the writing is final.
oe: A merger clause doesn't carefully negate a usage.
Express terms prevail if irreconcilable.

Correct. They're assumed to be taken for granted when the document was phrased. No finding of ambiguity is needed to admit them (cmt. 1(c)). If they can't be reconciled with express terms, § 1-303(e) makes the express terms control.
No ambiguity threshold for course and usage.
They can explain or supplement final writings.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Course and usage under the PER

q: A buyer accepts a machine that turns out to be defective. Its basic damages are:
o: the full purchase price.
lost profits only.
value as warranted minus value as accepted.
contract price minus market price.
cover price minus contract price.
oe: It keeps the machine.
Lost profits may be consequential, but the basic measure is § 2-714(2).
Correct. Section 2-714(2), measured at the time and place of acceptance, plus incidental and consequential damages. A buyer who rightfully rejects is instead treated like a buyer facing nondelivery.
That's § 2-713, for nondelivery or rejection.
That's § 2-712, after rejection.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Accepted defective machine

q: Which statement about varying the UCC by agreement is NOT correct?
o: Parties may disclaim the duty of good faith if the disclaimer is conspicuous.
Parties may set standards for measuring good faith that aren't manifestly unreasonable.
The effect of most UCC provisions may be varied by agreement.
"Unless otherwise agreed" in some sections doesn't mean other sections can't be varied.
Where the Code calls for a "reasonable time," parties may fix a specific time that isn't manifestly unreasonable.
oe: Correct. This is false. The obligations of good faith, diligence, reasonableness and care can't be disclaimed (§ 1-302(b)), however conspicuously.
topic: X · Variation by agreement (§ 1-302) — What § 1-302 allows

q: How do "agreement" and "contract" differ under § 1-201?
o: The agreement excludes course of dealing and usage of trade, but the contract includes them.
They mean the same thing in Article 2.
An agreement must be written; a contract may be oral.
The agreement is the bargain in fact; the contract is the resulting legal obligation.
The contract is the bargain in fact; the agreement is what the Code adds.
oe: Wrong. The "agreement" expressly includes course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade.
They are defined separately in § 1-201(b)(3) and (12).
Neither definition turns on a writing.
Correct. The contract can be more than the agreement (gap fillers, implied warranties) or less (a term barred by the SOF or struck as unconscionable).
Reversed.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Agreement vs. contract

q: A contract requires payment before inspection. The goods arrive in sealed crates; inspection later reveals a hidden defect. Was the buyer excused from paying?
o: No, but paying didn't waive its remedies.
No, and paying waived its remedies.
Yes, if it rejects within 10 days.
Yes; nonconformity always excuses payment.
Yes, because it hadn't accepted yet.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-512(1), nonconformity doesn't excuse payment unless it appears without inspection, or the circumstances would justify an injunction against honor (fraud, § 5-109(b)). Under (2), payment isn't acceptance and doesn't impair the right to inspect or any remedy.
Remedies survive.
No such rule.
Not when payment before inspection was agreed.
Payment was due regardless.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Pay before inspection

q: Which feature points toward PUFFING rather than an express warranty?
o: The statement answered the buyer's direct question.
The statement was hedged and freely volunteered.
The statement was specific and measurable.
It would be reasonable for the buyer to rely on the statement.
The statement was stated unequivocally, without qualification.
oe: Points toward a warranty.
Correct. Equivocal or conditional statements, and volunteered ones, lean toward puffing.
Points toward a warranty.
Points toward a warranty.
Points toward a warranty.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Warranty vs. puffing factor

q: In the slides' approach to a title problem, what comes first?
o: Did the buyer pay value for the goods in good faith?
Did the buyer give notice of breach?
Was the seller a merchant?
What rights did the seller purport to transfer?
Did the contract say "as is"?
oe: That matters within the § 2-403 analysis, not first.
That comes later.
Not the first step, and irrelevant to the title warranty.
Correct. Then: did the buyer get good title (§ 2-312)? If not, the warranty is breached.
"As is" doesn't affect title.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Approach to title problems

q: A shutter maker invested heavily to supply Home Depot under an at-will arrangement. Home Depot terminated, and the trial court awarded five years of lost profits. On appeal:
o: the award was affirmed because good faith required a good reason.
the court held the deal had to last a reasonable time first.
the court held good faith doesn't apply to termination.
the lost-profits award was reversed.
the court ordered Home Depot to resume buying.
oe: No reason is required.
It didn't.
It applies, but doesn't override the right.

Correct. Good faith applies to termination, but it can't override § 2-309(2)'s right to terminate "at any time"; no good reason is needed. Remaining claims: fraud in the inducement, breaches before termination, and unreasonable notice.
No.
topic: XIV · Termination & cancellation (§§ 2-106, 2-309) — Santa Fe Custom Shutters

q: Warranties conflict and can't reasonably be read together. Under § 2-317, which is correct?
o: Merchantability displaces fitness for a particular purpose.
Express beats inconsistent implied, except fitness.
A general description displaces exact technical specifications.
A general description beats a sample drawn from the existing bulk.
Implied warranties always displace express ones.
oe: Conflicts are generally resolved in favor of fitness.

Correct. Also, exact or technical specifications displace an inconsistent sample or general description, and a sample from the bulk displaces an inconsistent general description. Fitness wins conflicts unless the buyer furnished specs.
Reversed.
Reversed: the sample from bulk wins.
Reversed.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Cumulation and conflict

q: The price is to be set by an independent appraiser both parties agree on. The buyer refuses to agree on anyone. What may the seller do?
o: Only sue to compel the buyer to name an appraiser.
Charge the market price on the contract date.
Name the appraiser itself and bind the buyer to that appraiser's figure.
Nothing; the contract fails for indefiniteness.
Treat the contract as canceled, or fix a reasonable price.
oe: It has self-help options.
The reasonable price, at the seller's option.
The statute lets the seller fix a reasonable price, not appoint the appraiser.
Section 2-305(3) prevents that.

Correct. Section 2-305(3): when a price left to be fixed other than by agreement fails through one party's fault, the other may cancel or fix a reasonable price (Problem 4-3(c)). Refusing to cooperate is also a breach (cmt. 5).
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Buyer blocks the price mechanism

q: At a yard sale, Ivy hands Jules the posted price for a lamp and walks off with it. Nobody says a word. Under Article 2:
o: there is a completed gift, since nothing was said.
there is no contract, because no one made an offer or a promise.
there is a contract only if the lamp cost $500 or more.
there is an agreement and a contract.
Article 2 does not apply, because neither person is a merchant.
oe: Money changed hands for the lamp; that's a sale.
The UCC asks whether there was a bargain, not a promise.
The $500 figure is the statute of frauds threshold, and a fully performed deal doesn't need a record anyway.

Correct. No one promised anything, but there is a bargain, which is an "agreement," and Article 2 makes it a contract (absent incapacity or contraband). A contract may be made in any manner sufficient to show agreement, including conduct (§ 2-204(1)).
Scope doesn't depend on merchant status.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Yard sale with no words

q: Which act is an acceptance of the goods?
o: Unloading them to inspect.
Reselling some before deciding whether they conform.
Signing the carrier's delivery receipt when the truck arrives.
Paying for them in advance.
Storing them while testing them.
oe: Part of inspecting.
Correct. An act inconsistent with the seller's ownership is acceptance (§ 2-606(1)(c)). So is signifying acceptance after a reasonable chance to inspect, or failing to reject effectively.
Receipt isn't acceptance.
Payment isn't acceptance.
Not acceptance.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — What counts as acceptance

q: After a justified, timely revocation of acceptance, the buyer:
o: may cancel, get its money back, and recover damages.
is limited to specific performance.
must let the seller cure first.
must keep the goods and sue under § 2-714.
may only get a refund, with no damages.
oe: Correct. Plus incidental and consequential damages (§§ 2-711 to 2-713, 2-715).
No.
Not a requirement for revocation remedies.
That's for accepted goods not revoked.
Damages too.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Remedies after revocation

q: Under § 2-209 cmt. 3, "rescission" means:
o: one party's ending of the contract for breach.
a court's refusal to enforce an unconscionable term.
one party's ending of the contract without breach.
the buyer's revocation of acceptance.
None of the above.
oe: That's cancellation.
That's termination.
Correct. None of these. In § 2-209, "modification or rescission" covers abandonment of the contract by mutual consent (cmt. 3); it doesn't include one party's termination or cancellation.
topic: XIV · Termination & cancellation (§§ 2-106, 2-309) — Rescission

q: Which is NOT required for a written confirmation to satisfy § 2-201(2)?
o: The recipient signs the confirmation.
The confirmation is sent within a reasonable time.
Both parties are merchants.
It would satisfy § 2-201(1) against the sender.
No written objection to its contents arrives within 10 days after receipt.
oe: Correct. That's the point of the exception: the recipient who never signed loses the SOF defense ("merchants must read their mail").
Required.
Required: "between merchants" (§ 2-104(3)), using the broad practices sense.
Required: "sufficient against the sender."
Required.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Merchant's confirmation requirements

q: Which of these can the parties vary by agreement?
o: The court's power to police unconscionability under § 2-302.
Whether an agreement was formed under §§ 2-204 to 2-207.
Article 2's scope under § 2-102.
The default place of delivery in § 2-308.
The rights of good-faith purchasers under § 2-403.
oe: Not variable.
Not variable (though parties can require more formality for a future deal).
Not variable: labels can't change scope.
Correct. Gap fillers are defaults. Problem 5-1(b): the slides list § 2-302, § 2-102, §§ 2-204 to 2-207 and § 2-403 as non-variable (plus § 2-201 and good faith).
Not variable: the parties can't alter third parties' rights.
topic: X · Variation by agreement (§ 1-302) — What the parties can change

q: A dealer tells a buyer a used truck "has a rebuilt transmission with under 5,000 miles on it." Nothing is written. Which is correct?
o: It's a warranty only if the dealer regularly sells trucks.
It's unenforceable because express warranties must be written.
It can be an express warranty.
It's an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
It's puffing because it was only said, not written.
oe: Express warranties don't depend on merchant status.
No writing is required for an express warranty.
Correct. It's a specific, verifiable affirmation of fact. On the slides "written" points toward a warranty but is asterisked: oral statements can be warranties too.
Nothing shows a particular purpose or reliance; this is an affirmation of fact.
Oral statements can be warranties.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Oral statements count

q: (1) Before signing, a buyer knows the seller is underpricing its goods and says nothing. (2) After signing, the buyer sees the seller has overlooked a contract clause that hurts the seller and quietly exploits it. Under Market Street:
o: (1) is fine; (2) may be bad faith.
Neither is bad faith, since there's no duty to disclose.
Both are bad faith.
(1) is bad faith; (2) is fine.
Both are fine unless the parties are fiduciaries.
oe: Correct. Before contracting you may exploit superior knowledge. After contracting, deliberately taking advantage of the partner's oversight about its contract rights, when you could correct it at no cost, is sharp dealing.
Exploiting a known oversight during performance can be bad faith.
There's no duty to share superior knowledge before contracting.
Reversed.
Good faith reaches (2) even without a fiduciary relationship.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Before vs. after contracting

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the recurring themes of sales law listed on the Week 1 slides?
o: Responsiveness.
Paternalism.
Certainty.
International.
Laissez-faire.
oe: One of the six themes.
Correct. The six themes are certainty, responsiveness, laissez-faire, simplicity, efficiency and international. Paternalism appears later, at one end of the disclaimer "continuum of protection."
One of the six themes.
One of the six themes.
One of the six themes.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — Recurring themes

q: A buyer says she'll film all-day events and asks whether the battery will last four hours. The seller hands her a camera whose battery lasts two. Which warranty is most clearly breached?
o: Against infringement.
Title.
Merchantability.
Fitness for a particular purpose.
None; she should have tested the battery.
oe: No third-party IP claim.
Ownership isn't at issue.
A two-hour battery may be ordinary; the problem is her particular need.
Correct. The camera chart: scratched lens is merchantability; the four-hour battery for her need is fitness; a stolen camera is title.
She relied on the seller's selection.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Camera battery

q: How much weight does a merger clause carry under § 2-202?
o: None; courts ignore boilerplate.
It bars even course of dealing and usage of trade.
It's strong evidence of full integration, but not conclusive.
It conclusively makes the writing complete and exclusive.
It turns the writing into a modification.
oe: It's highly probative.
Not unless carefully negated.
Correct. Courts differ on whether to look only within the "four corners" or to consider the offered evidence itself (Apex LLC).
Probative, not conclusive.
No.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Weight of a merger clause

q: A seller phones that the wheat is ready for pickup. Before the buyer arrives, fire destroys the seller's storage building. Does it matter whether the seller is a merchant?
o: No; whoever has insurance bears it.
Yes: merchant seller bears it; non-merchant's passed on tender.
Yes. A merchant seller's risk passed when it phoned.
No; the seller bears it either way.
No; the buyer bears it either way.
oe: Insurance isn't the test.

Correct. Problem 4-6(b): merchant status is outcome-determinative. If the seller bears the risk and the wheat was identified at contracting (e.g., "the wheat in bin #3"), § 2-613 may avoid the contract.
Reversed.
A non-merchant's tender passed the risk.
A merchant keeps risk until receipt.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Ready for pickup, then fire

q: How do formation-time doctrines like fraud, duress and mistake apply to Article 2 contracts?
o: They don't; Article 2's own rules displace them for sales of goods.
Only if the contract adopts them.
Through § 1-103(b); Article 2 itself covers only unconscionability.
Through § 2-302 alone.
Through § 2-615.
oe: They supplement it.
They apply by law.

Correct. Section 1-103(b) brings in fraud, duress, mistake and the like; among the formation-time doctrines, Article 2 itself addresses only unconscionability (§ 2-302). Restatement § 266 also excuses a party for an impracticability or frustration that existed, unknown, at formation.
Section 2-302 is unconscionability only.
That's for supervening events.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — How formation doctrines reach Article 2

q: A company leasing a forklift "sells" it to a buyer who knows nothing about the lease. The lessee isn't in the forklift business. Under § 2-403(1), what does the buyer get?
o: Full title, because the buyer acted in good faith.
Full title, because forklifts are goods.
Full title, because the lessee had possession.
Nothing at all.
Only the lessee's leasehold interest.
oe: Good faith alone can't create title the transferor lacked (no voidable title or entrustment to a dealer here).
Irrelevant.
Possession alone isn't title.
It gets whatever the lessee had.
Correct. A purchaser acquires the title its transferor had or had power to transfer; a lessee has only a limited interest.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Lessee sells forklift

q: Which statement about sales law and sales systems is NOT accurate?
o: A sales system's job ends once a contract is formed.
One role of a sales system is to bring buyers and sellers together.
Sales law is broader than commercial law, which focuses on companies' commerce.
A sales system supplies one or more standard sets of terms for the parties' deal.
Sales law is a cumulative subject rather than one single law.
oe: Correct. This is false. Sales systems also supply mechanisms for performing the deal and for resolving disputes.
Accurate. That is the first of the four roles.
Accurate, per the slides.
Accurate. That is the second of the four roles.
Accurate, per the slides.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — Sales law and sales systems

q: A buyer pays in full when signing. Before the buyer picks up the goods, they burn at the merchant seller's shop. Did prepayment shift the risk?
o: Yes; paying in full puts the risk on the buyer.
Yes, because title passed on payment.
Only if the seller gave a receipt.
Yes, unless the seller was negligent.
No; a merchant seller keeps the risk until receipt.
oe: Payment is irrelevant.
Title is irrelevant.
Irrelevant.
Risk stayed with the seller regardless.
Correct. Under § 2-509(3) a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods; prepayment doesn't shift it (Problem 4-6(E); Capshaw v. Hickman).
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Prepayment

q: Rook buys a watch from Sloane with a check that later bounces, then resells it to Tate, who pays value in good faith. Sloane sues Tate for the watch. Who wins?
o: Tate, a good-faith purchaser for value.
Sloane, unless Tate knew of the bounced check.
Sloane, because a bounced check means Rook never got title.
Tate, but only if Tate is a merchant.
Sloane, because the deal was a "cash sale."
oe: Correct. Delivery in exchange for a later-dishonored check gives the buyer voidable title, which it can pass as good title to a good-faith purchaser for value (§ 2-403(1)(b)).
Backwards: if Tate knew, Tate wouldn't be in good faith.
Rook got voidable title.
Any good-faith purchaser for value is protected.
Even a "cash sale" gives voidable title.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Bounced check, then resale

q: Under the test from Royal Business Machines discussed in the text, a statement is more likely a warranty when:
o: the statement concerns the value of the goods.
the seller asserts a fact the buyer doesn't know.
the statement appears in a printed advertisement rather than in conversation.
the seller offers an opinion on something it has no special knowledge of.
the buyer is more expert in the goods than the seller.
oe: Value statements aren't warranties.

Correct. Contrast an opinion on a matter where the seller has no special knowledge and the buyer is expected to form its own judgment. The text questions whether relative expertise should matter, since even an expert buyer may want the warranty as insurance.
The medium isn't the test.
That points toward opinion.
That cuts against the buyer under this test.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Royal Business Machines test

q: Under § 2-202 cmt. 3, evidence of an additional term must be kept from the trier of fact when:
o: the term was first discussed after the writing was signed.
the term is oral.
the term favors the drafter.
the term would certainly have been in the writing.
the writing has no signature block.
oe: Later terms aren't barred.
Oral terms can come in against a partial integration.
Not the test.
Correct. That's also one way courts tell contradiction from supplementation.
Not the test.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Certainly would have been included

q: A merchant seller sends a merchant buyer a confirmation that satisfies § 2-201(2), and the buyer never objects. In the seller's suit, which is true?
o: The buyer is bound only if it signed a delivery receipt for the letter.
The buyer is conclusively bound by the confirmation's terms.
The buyer loses the SOF defense but can still deny there was a deal.
The buyer may still raise the SOF because it never signed anything.
The seller need not show the buyer received the confirmation.
oe: No such requirement.
It isn't conclusive proof of the contract or its terms.
Correct. The confirmation only removes the SOF defense; the seller still must prove the contract, and must prove the buyer received the confirmation (proper dispatch raises a presumption).
That's exactly what § 2-201(2) takes away.
Receipt is an element; the sender must prove it.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Effect of an unanswered confirmation

q: A letter says, "No deal unless we agree on the price." They never agree, but the seller already shipped some goods and the buyer paid a deposit. Result?
o: No contract, and each side keeps what it has.
A contract only for the goods already shipped.
A contract at a reasonable price at the time for delivery.
No contract; goods and deposit go back.
A contract at the seller's list price.
oe: Restitution runs both ways.
No contract at all.
They intended not to be bound without agreement.

Correct. Section 2-305(4): if they intended not to be bound unless the price was agreed, there's no contract. The buyer returns the goods (or pays their reasonable value) and the seller returns the deposit.
No contract.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — No deal without a price

q: A buyer repudiates before delivery. Which is NOT a measure of the seller's damages?
o: Contract price minus market price (§ 2-708(1)).
Contract price minus resale price (§ 2-706).
Value as warranted minus value as accepted.
Incidental damages (§ 2-710).
Lost profit on the deal (§ 2-708(2)).
oe: A seller's measure.
A seller's measure.

Correct. That's the buyer's measure for accepted nonconforming goods (§ 2-714(2)). The seller may withhold or stop delivery, cancel, and recover under § 2-706, § 2-708(1) or § 2-708(2) plus § 2-710 incidentals; the same applies to a wrongful rejection.
Recoverable by the seller.
A seller's measure.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Seller's measures after repudiation

q: The Week 5 slide says every non-variable UCC provision is expressly identified. What does the textbook say?
o: Every provision of Article 2 can be varied.
Only provisions saying "unless otherwise agreed" can be varied.
Only Article 1 provisions are non-variable.
The slide is right; only expressly identified provisions are non-variable.
Exceptions "vary in explicitness"; the SOF can't be varied though it doesn't say so.
oe: Some can't.
Section 1-302(c) rejects that inference.
Article 2 has non-variable rules too.
The text disagrees.

Correct. Section 1-302 cmt. 1. Some provisions are explicit, e.g., § 2-616(3) (can't be negated), § 2-309(3) (dispensing with termination notice invalid if unconscionable), § 2-718(1) (penalty void) and § 2-719(3).
topic: X · Variation by agreement (§ 1-302) — Which rules can't be varied

q: A diner chips a tooth on a pebble in a restaurant's fried rice. Can she sue for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: No. Food is excluded from Article 2.
Yes. Serving food for value is a sale.
No. A restaurant sells a service, not goods.
Only if the restaurant was negligent.
Only if she ate the meal on the premises.
oe: Food is goods.
Correct. Section 2-314(1): serving food or drink for value, on or off the premises, is a sale, and the restaurant is a merchant in food. Liability doesn't depend on negligence.
Section 2-314(1) treats it as a sale.
Implied warranty liability is strict.
On or off the premises.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Pebble in the rice

q: How did Market Street Associates v. Frey come out?
o: The court sent it to trial on intent; bad faith was later found.
The Seventh Circuit ordered specific performance of the buy-back option.
The court held Market Street had to disclose its financing plans before contracting.
The court affirmed summary judgment, holding that not citing ¶ 34 was bad faith as a matter of law.
The court held good faith inapplicable because the deal was a lease of land.
