oe: Correct. Summary judgment for the Trust was reversed because liability turned on Orenstein's state of mind. On remand, the court found he knew the Trust was overlooking ¶ 34 and sent "lulling" letters, so no specific performance (affirmed).
No; it reversed summary judgment and remanded.
The issue arose during performance.
It held summary judgment improper.
It applied good faith.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — What happened in Market Street

q: A dining set of a table and eight matching chairs is a single commercial unit. The buyer keeps one chair and rejects the rest. Effect?
o: It accepted one chair only.
It owes for one chair at a pro-rated price.
The rejection of the rest is effective.
It has accepted the whole set.
The seller must take back all nine pieces.
oe: A commercial unit can't be split this way.
It owes for the unit.
Not for part of a unit.
Correct. Acceptance of any part of a commercial unit is acceptance of the entire unit (§ 2-606(2)).
The buyer accepted the unit.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Part of a commercial unit

q: Which is NOT required before a party may suspend its performance under § 2-609?
o: A demand in writing (an email or other electronic record works).
Suspension must be commercially reasonable.
The other party must already be in breach.
Reasonable grounds for insecurity.
The suspended performance must be one for which it hasn't received the agreed return.
oe: Required; the 2022 amendments confirm a record suffices.
Required.
Correct. Section 2-609 works before any breach: it protects each party's expectation of due performance.
Required.
Required.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Suspending under § 2-609

q: A car floats away in a flood before risk passes to the buyer. If the seller is EXCUSED, which is correct?
o: They split the car's value.
The seller loses the car's value but owes no damages.
The buyer bears the loss of the car.
The buyer must still pay the price.
The seller loses the car and also owes damages.
oe: No splitting.

Correct. Excuse decides who pays damages; risk of loss decides who absorbs the goods' value. If the seller weren't excused, it would lose the car AND owe damages (§§ 2-713, 2-715). Contracts allocate these risks, often with force majeure clauses.
Risk hadn't passed.
No.
That's if it isn't excused.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Excuse vs. risk of loss

q: Article 2 doesn't define "offer." Where does a court look?
o: To usage of trade alone, since the Code is silent.
To § 2-206, which treats any order for goods as an offer.
To § 2-204, which makes every communication about goods an offer.
To § 1-201's definition of "agreement."
None of the above.
oe: Usage can matter, but the common law supplies the definition.
Section 2-206 governs how offers may be accepted, not what is an offer.
Section 2-204 governs formation in general; it doesn't define offers.
"Agreement" is the bargain in fact, not an offer.

Correct. None of these. Article 2 doesn't define "offer," so the common law supplies it through § 1-103(b): Restatement (Second) § 24, a manifestation of willingness to bargain that justifies another in understanding assent is invited. Then ask: firm offer (§ 2-205)? accepted (§ 2-206)? conflicting terms (§ 2-207)?
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Where "offer" is defined

q: To close a sale, a seller knowingly and falsely says, "This ring is worth $10,000." It's an affirmation of value. What claim might the buyer still have?
o: Breach of the warranty of title.
Unconscionability, entitling the buyer to damages.
Fraud or misrepresentation.
Breach of express warranty, because the statement was false.
None; a statement of value is never actionable.
oe: Title concerns ownership, not value.
Section 2-302 doesn't award damages.
Correct. Comment 8: even false statements of value aren't warranties, but they may be remediable under fraud or misrepresentation law.
Affirmations of value don't create warranties.
Fraud law may reach it.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — False statement of value

q: Which is NOT part of the textbook's approach to reading a UCC provision?
o: Start with the Official Comment, since it controls when it conflicts with the text.
Read the whole provision, then read it again, parsing the grammar and finding the pauses.
Test your reading against hypotheticals the provision does and doesn't cover.
Find the definitions, in § 1-201 and in the Article's own definitions sections.
Read the language in light of the provision's purposes and the Code's.
oe: Correct. This is wrong twice over. You start with the text, and the comments, though the most important aid, are not law: the enacted text controls over a conflicting comment.
Part of rule 1. Article 2 is "notorious for its lack of commas."
Part of rule 1.
Rule 2. Never assume a word is undefined.
Rule 3: context and purpose.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — Three rules of interpretation

q: At the buyer's request, the seller leaves the wheat in unlocked bins on its dock for after-hours pickup. Vandals ruin it overnight. What is the seller's best argument?
o: The seller is a merchant, so risk passed on tender.
Risk passes whenever goods are left outdoors.
The buyer's request shifted the risk, or completed the tender.
Vandalism isn't a casualty covered by risk-of-loss rules.
The buyer is liable in tort for the vandals' acts.
oe: For a merchant, receipt is the default test.
No such rule.
Correct. Problem 4-6(C) (McKenzie v. Olmstead): an agreement can shift risk (§ 2-509(4)), and a tender the buyer itself shaped may be complete.
Theft and vandalism are classic casualties.
Not the theory.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Unlocked bins after hours

q: Under § 1-205, what does "seasonably" mean?
o: During the normal selling season for goods of that kind.
Immediately.
Before the other party objects.
Within 30 days.
None of the above.
oe: Not the meaning.
No.
No.
No fixed period.

Correct. None of these. Under § 1-205(b), an action is taken "seasonably" when taken at or within the agreed time or, if no time is agreed, within a reasonable time. What is reasonable depends on the nature, purpose and circumstances of the action (§ 1-205(a)).
topic: X · Variation by agreement (§ 1-302) — Meaning of "seasonably"

q: A hobbyist sells a used guitar and writes on the receipt, "This guitar is merchantable." Which is correct?
o: It disclaims every other warranty.
The statement is void, because only merchants warrant merchantability.
It's puffing, because the hobbyist isn't an expert.
The hobbyist made an express warranty of merchantability.
It creates an implied warranty of merchantability.
oe: Nothing disclaims anything.
Only merchants make the IMPLIED warranty.
It's a specific affirmation.
Correct. A non-merchant can expressly warrant merchantability (§ 2-314 cmt. 4); only merchants make it impliedly.
It's express, not implied.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Non-merchant's written promise

q: A person obtained goods in each situation below. In which one does that person have NO power to pass good title?
o: It was agreed to be a "cash sale," and she never paid.
The seller was deceived about her identity.
She stole them from the seller's warehouse.
She procured delivery through fraud punishable as larcenous.
She paid with a check that was later dishonored.
oe: Voidable title: § 2-403(1)(c).
Voidable title: § 2-403(1)(a).
Correct. A thief has void title and passes nothing. The other four are § 2-403(1)'s voidable-title cases.
Voidable title: § 2-403(1)(d).
Voidable title: § 2-403(1)(b).
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Void vs. voidable title

q: In a heavily negotiated deal, a party simply benefits when the other side fails to send an extension notice by the agreed deadline. Under Vintage Rodeo v. Rent-A-Center, the benefiting party:
o: did nothing wrong, since good faith fills only gaps.
breached good faith by staying silent.
had to remind the other side before the deadline passed.
breached only if the parties were fiduciaries.
must allow a reasonable extension.
oe: Correct. Good faith fills gaps between express terms; it doesn't require warning a sophisticated party about its own deadline.
Silence about the other side's own negotiated deadline isn't bad faith.
No such duty.
They weren't, and it didn't breach anyway.
The deadline is express.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Missed deadline in a negotiated deal

q: Once a buyer accepts goods, which of the following is true?
o: It can no longer reject them.
It must pay for them at the contract rate.
It bears the burden of proving any nonconformity.
It must notify the seller of a breach within a reasonable time or lose any remedy.
All of the above.
oe: True (§ 2-607(2)), but not the best answer.
True (§ 2-607(1)), but not the best answer.
True (§ 2-607(4)), but not the best answer.
True (§ 2-607(3)(a)), but not the best answer.

Correct. All four follow from acceptance under § 2-607. Note what does NOT follow: acceptance doesn't impair the buyer's other remedies, so it can still recover damages for the nonconformity (commonly under § 2-714).
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Consequences of acceptance

q: A buyer accepts the goods and never pays. What is the seller's basic remedy?
o: Nothing until the buyer revokes.
The contract price, plus incidental damages.
Only the difference between contract and market price.
Specific performance of the buyer's promise to pay.
Reclaiming the goods, in every case.
oe: No.
Correct. Sections 2-709 and 2-710. Reclaiming the goods is possible only in narrow cases.
It may recover the full price.
The action for the price is the remedy.
Only in limited circumstances.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Accepted but unpaid

q: Under Speciality Tires v. CIT (quoting ALCOA v. Essex), which statement about foreseeability is correct?
o: Any foreseeable event bars excuse.
Only events the parties named in writing count.
Unforeseeable events always excuse.
It's the most important factor but not decisive.
Foreseeability is irrelevant.
oe: Not decisive.
No.
Still applied sparingly.

Correct. "Foreseeability or even recognition of a risk does not necessarily prove its allocation"; the question is whether the risk was so likely that the obligor should have guarded against it. Excuse is applied sparingly.
It's the most important factor.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Foreseeability

q: Between merchants, how are the reasonableness of grounds for insecurity and the adequacy of an assurance judged?
o: By the words of the demand letter alone.
By a jury's sense of fairness, without regard to trade practice.
By the demanding party's honest belief.
By whatever the contract price implies.
None of the above.
oe: Not the test.
Commercial standards govern.
The test is objective.
Not the test.
Correct. None of these. Between merchants, the reasonableness of grounds for insecurity and the adequacy of any assurance are determined according to commercial standards (§ 2-609(2)).
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Between merchants

q: Which clause most clearly makes a writing complete and exclusive?
o: "This Agreement may not be modified except by a signed writing."
"Time is of the essence of this Agreement."
"This Agreement supersedes all prior agreements, written or oral."
"This is the complete and exclusive statement of our terms."
"This Agreement represents the final agreement of the parties."
oe: That's a NOM clause, about future changes.
Irrelevant to integration.
Helpful but misses contemporaneous oral agreements; pair it with the "complete and exclusive" clause.
Correct. It tracks § 2-202(b).
"Final" tracks only partial integration.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Best merger clause

q: Two merchants trade emails about 40 pallets of tile. The seller ships, and the buyer pays. Neither can say when the deal was struck. Is there a contract?
o: Yes, but only under § 2-207(3), and only if the writings conflict.
Yes, even though the moment of making is undetermined.
No, because the statute of frauds requires a record stating the date of formation.
No, because without an identifiable acceptance there is no contract.
Only if a usage of trade fixes the date of formation.
oe: Section 2-204 is enough; § 2-207(3) addresses writings that fail to form a contract.

Correct. A contract may be made in any manner sufficient to show agreement, including conduct by both parties (§ 2-204(1)), and may be found even though the moment of its making is undetermined (§ 2-204(2)).
Section 2-201 requires a quantity, not a date, and part performance satisfies it anyway.
Article 2 doesn't require an identifiable moment of acceptance.
No such requirement.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Contract by conduct, no clear moment

q: After a phone deal between merchants, the seller sends one of the following. Which is "sufficient against the sender" under Problem 2-10(A)?
o: "Confirming our deal: you buy 500 widgets at $10. /s/ Sam Seller."
A signed letter confirming "our widget deal at $10 each," with no quantity.
A message about "our widget deal" whose only sign of the sender is the "From" field.
An unsigned preprinted invoice for 500 widgets.
"Thanks for your interest. We'd be glad to quote you on widgets. /s/ Sam."
oe: Correct. It is signed by the sender, indicates a contract was made, and states a quantity, so it would bind the sender under § 2-201(1).
No quantity, so it fails § 2-201(1) even against the sender.
Questionable signature and no quantity.
Unsigned, so it couldn't bind the sender.
A quote doesn't indicate a contract was made.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Sufficient against the sender

q: Which statement drawn from the comments to § 2-305 is correct?
o: A posted price can never satisfy good faith.
If a named expert was essential, the expert's failure may end the deal.
An "agreement to agree" on price is unenforceable.
Interfering with the agreed price-fixing machinery carries no legal consequence.
Whether the parties meant to be bound is a question of law.
oe: In the normal case it does (cmt. 3).

Correct. Comment 4 (e.g., a trusted expert to value a unique painting; contrast a named expert grading cotton). Comment 1 rejects the "agreement to agree" defense; cmt. 2 makes intent a fact question; cmt. 5 treats interference with the price machinery as repudiation or a failure to cooperate.
Comment 1 rejects that.
It may be a repudiation (cmt. 5).
Usually a question of fact (cmt. 2).
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Section 2-305 comments

q: A landlord dodges a tenant's repeated requests to close on a lease purchase option for 19 months, never mentioning an unpaid option fee, and then declares the option void. Under Brunswick Hills:
o: The landlord acted in bad faith.
The landlord breached a fiduciary duty.
The option failed, so the landlord owed nothing.
Good faith doesn't apply to real estate options.
The landlord acted properly; the tenant should have read the lease.
oe: Correct. Unlike Vintage Rodeo, the landlord actively evaded the tenant's requests while the problem was curable.
Landlord and tenant aren't fiduciaries; the duty is good faith.
The court found bad faith.
It applied.
The landlord's evasion was the problem.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Evading an option for 19 months

q: A buyer accepts a late, short delivery without complaint. Can it still demand adequate assurance about future deliveries?
o: No; accepting the delivery waived the right.
Only with the seller's consent.
Yes; accepting it doesn't waive the right.
Only if it first rejects the delivery it accepted.
Only if the contract is an installment contract.
oe: It doesn't.
It's a statutory right.
Correct. Section 2-609(3): acceptance of any improper delivery or payment doesn't prejudice the right to demand adequate assurance of future performance.
It can't reject after accepting, and needn't.
The right is general.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Accepting a late delivery

q: Under § 2-305 cmt. 3, in the "normal case" a price set by the seller satisfies good faith if it is:
o: a posted price, price in effect, or market price.
the lowest price available in the market.
any price the seller sets without intending harm.
a price the buyer has agreed to in a writing.
below the seller's cost.
oe: Correct. That's the safe harbor. Mathis held a lack of subjective good faith takes a case outside the "normal case."
Not required.
The safe harbor is about established prices, not motive alone.
Then it isn't seller-set.
Irrelevant.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Safe harbor

q: Goods sit in an independent warehouse and won't be moved. The seller gives the buyer a negotiable warehouse receipt for them. When does risk pass?
o: When the contract is signed.
When the buyer removes the goods from the warehouse.
A reasonable time after the buyer gets the document.
When the buyer receives the negotiable document.
When the warehouse ships the goods.
oe: Not for bailee goods.
Earlier, on receipt of the document.
That rule is for non-negotiable documents.

Correct. Section 2-509(2)(a). Risk also passes on the bailee's acknowledgment of the buyer's right to possession, or a reasonable time after the buyer receives a non-negotiable document or delivery order.
They aren't being moved.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Negotiable warehouse receipt

q: Which statement about excuse is NOT correct?
o: Traditional excuses include death of a promisor of personal services, illegality and destruction of the subject matter.
Force majeure clauses can allocate these risks.
Excuse doctrines are applied sparingly.
A seller can't agree to bear more risk than § 2-615 leaves with it.
The buyer's options under § 2-616 can't be negated except as the seller assumed a greater obligation.
oe: True.
True.
True.
Correct. This is false. Section 2-615 applies "except so far as a seller may have assumed a greater obligation," and §§ 2-613 and 2-614 also yield to agreement.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Excuse: false statement

q: A thief sells a stolen saddle to a good-faith buyer for value, who resells it to a second good-faith buyer. The owner sues the second buyer. Who wins?
o: The owner, but only if she reported the theft promptly.
The second buyer, if it bought from a merchant.
The second buyer, as a good-faith purchaser for value.
The second buyer, because the first buyer had voidable title.
The owner; a thief passes no title.
oe: Reporting doesn't matter.
Entrustment needs the owner to have entrusted the goods.
That protection needs a transferor with voidable title.
The first buyer took from a thief: void.
Correct. A thief has void title, so no one down the chain gets title, however innocent.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Thief down the chain

q: Which is NOT one of the tests courts use to decide whether parol evidence contradicts, rather than supplements, a writing?
o: Whether it lacks reasonable harmony with the writing.
Whether the parties would certainly have included it.
Whether the party offering it is a merchant.
Whether it's a term that might naturally be left out of the writing.
Whether it directly negates a term in the writing.
oe: A test (Alaska Northern).
A test.

Correct. The tests: it directly negates a term; it lacks reasonable harmony with the writing; the parties would certainly have included it (cmt. 3); vs. supplementary if it might naturally be omitted (Restatement § 216). Courts may treat usage as supplemental more readily (Nanakuli).
A test (Restatement § 216).
A test.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Contradiction tests

q: A merchant buyer receives a merchant seller's sufficient confirmation on May 1. On May 8 the buyer emails: "I never agreed to 90-day payment terms." Effect?
o: The buyer is bound, because it waited more than five days.
It defeats the confirmation's effect against the buyer.
None, because the objection disputes only one term.
It matters only if the buyer isn't a merchant.
None, because objections must be sent by certified mail.
oe: The window is 10 days.
Correct. Written notice of objection to the contents within 10 days after receipt defeats § 2-201(2) (Problem 2-10(B)).
An objection to its contents is enough.
If the buyer weren't a merchant, § 2-201(2) wouldn't apply at all.
Any written notice works.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Objection within 10 days

q: A trucking firm will buy all its diesel from a supplier at prices the supplier sets at each delivery. The trucking firm's lawyer wants to pin down "good faith." Which clause works best?
o: "The price will be fair."
Price capped at an index plus a set margin.
"The supplier will set its price in good faith."
"The supplier waives the duty of good faith in pricing."
"The trucking firm may reject any price it dislikes."
oe: Too vague to measure.

Correct. Problem 5-1(a): tie the price to an objective, verifiable standard that isn't manifestly unreasonable (§ 1-302(b)), such as a published index plus a margin or the supplier's lowest price to similarly situated customers.
That just repeats § 2-305(2).
Good faith can't be disclaimed, and the buyer wouldn't want that anyway.
That makes the price "to be agreed."
topic: X · Variation by agreement (§ 1-302) — Defining good faith for a seller-set price

q: Which statement from Problem 3-6 is the clearest express warranty?
o: A new-car dealer: "This is the safest car in its class, bar none."
A memorabilia dealer: "Ortiz's 2013 World Series grand-slam ball."
An art seller: "A beautiful painting by a talented artist."
A clothing seller: "That dress looks good on you."
A neighbor selling a used washer: "It works great."
oe: A split (Gallagher vs. Viking Yacht): superlative puffery, or measurable by crash ratings?
Correct. It's a specific, verifiable statement of provenance.
Puffing: commendation.
Puffing: subjective opinion.
A close call (Petti): present condition vs. casual opinion.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Clearest warranty in Problem 3-6

q: A signed record for 50 drill presses leaves the price and delivery date open. The contract does not fail for indefiniteness if:
o: the missing terms are minor, whatever the parties intended.
a usage of trade or the parties' course of dealing supplies every one of the missing terms.
the parties later agree on the missing terms in a signed writing.
never, because price and delivery are material terms that must be agreed.
the parties intended to contract and there's a reasonably certain basis for a remedy.
oe: Intent to contract is required; minor terms aren't the test.
Gap fillers can supply missing terms too; usage isn't required.
No later agreement is needed; § 2-305 and § 2-309 fill the gaps.
That is the common-law view Article 2 rejected.
Correct. That is § 2-204(3), a big departure from the common law's insistence on all material terms.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Open terms and indefiniteness

q: Which is NOT required to revoke acceptance under § 2-608?
o: Revocation comes within a reasonable time and before a substantial change not caused by the defect.
The buyer accepted expecting a cure, or without discovering a hard-to-find defect.
The defect was caused by the seller's negligence.
The buyer notifies the seller.
The defect substantially impairs the goods' value to the buyer.
oe: Required.
Required. Discovery may also have been delayed by the seller's assurances.
Correct. Revocation doesn't depend on fault.
Required: revocation isn't effective until notice.
Required.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Revocation elements

q: A Delaware court is interpreting § 2-207 and finds a well-reasoned Ohio decision on point. Why may it give the Ohio case weight?
o: Because the Code aims to make the law uniform among jurisdictions.
Because full faith and credit makes another state's UCC rulings binding in Delaware.
It may not; only Delaware decisions can interpret Delaware's enacted Code.
Because the Official Comments direct courts to follow the majority of states.
Because the Permanent Editorial Board certifies other states' decisions as authoritative.
oe: Correct. Uniformity is a § 1-103(a)(3) purpose, so other states' decisions are persuasive (not binding). Other aids follow: treatises, state legislative history, earlier drafts, and finally a tie-breaker policy.
Full faith and credit applies to judgments, not to another state's reading of a statute. The case is persuasive only.
Too narrow. Because the Code is meant to be uniform, out-of-state cases are persuasive authority.
The comments contain no such directive, and they aren't law in any event.
No such certification exists.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — Out-of-state decisions

q: A seller delivers on credit. Six days later it learns the buyer was insolvent when it received the goods. Can the seller reclaim them?
o: Yes, at any time within a year.
Only if the buyer signed a security agreement.
Yes, within three months of delivery.
Yes, by demand within 10 days after the buyer's receipt.
No; a credit seller can never reclaim.
oe: Within 10 days (absent a written misrepresentation).
Not required.
Three months relates to a written misrepresentation of solvency.
Correct. Section 2-702(2). The 10-day limit doesn't apply if the buyer misrepresented its solvency in a writing within three months before delivery.
Section 2-702(2) allows it.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Reclaiming from an insolvent buyer

q: Which seller from Problem 3-9 most clearly makes NO implied warranty of merchantability?
o: A home builder that buys and installs the appliances its clients choose.
A rental company that sells its oldest fleet cars every four months.
An accountant who sells her own stained-glass pieces at a semiannual craft fair.
A dealership selling a new car.
A decorator who locates antiques and takes a finder's fee from the client.
oe: Arguably a merchant in what it regularly supplies, and warranty rules apply in a hybrid.
Likely a merchant: regular, recurring sales.
Likely a merchant in those goods; her day job isn't decisive.
A merchant in cars.
Correct. The decorator isn't the seller, and the warrantor must be the seller. (The intermediary prong works for a principal through its own agent; here the decorator works for the buyer.)
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Problem 3-9 sellers

q: Which statement about the UCC's definitions is correct?
o: The § 1-201 definitions apply only to Article 1.
Article 2's definitions in §§ 2-103 to 2-106 also govern every other Article.
"Goods" excludes the unborn young of animals, since they aren't yet movable.
A word Article 2 doesn't define is undefined everywhere in the Code.
"Purchase" includes taking by gift.
oe: Wrong. Section 1-201's definitions apply throughout the Code; each Article adds its own.
Wrong. Article-specific definitions apply within that Article.
Wrong. Section 2-105(1) expressly includes the unborn young of animals.
Wrong. Never assume a word is undefined; check § 1-201 and cross-referenced definitions (§ 2-103(3)).
Correct. Section 1-201(b)(29) defines "purchase" to include a gift and any other voluntary transaction creating an interest in property. It's one of the text's "surprises."
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — Definitional surprises

q: Same warehouse, but the seller gives the buyer a non-negotiable delivery order. The goods are destroyed an hour later. Who most likely bears the loss?
o: The buyer, because it holds a document of title.
The warehouse.
The buyer, because it didn't object to the order.
The seller, until a reasonable time to present it passes.
They split it.
oe: Not yet, for a non-negotiable one.
As between the parties, the seller.
Not objecting makes the tender sufficient; risk still waits for a reasonable time.

Correct. A non-negotiable document or delivery order is a sufficient tender unless the buyer seasonably objects, but risk (and the risk the bailee won't honor it) stays on the seller until the buyer has had a reasonable time to present it (§§ 2-503(4)(b), 2-509(2)(c)). Compare Problem 4-11 (horse killed two hours after a non-negotiable bill).
No splitting.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Non-negotiable delivery order
pre: Goods sit in an independent warehouse and won't be moved. The seller gives the buyer a negotiable warehouse receipt for them. When does risk pass?

q: A justified written demand for assurance goes unanswered for 35 days. Effect?
o: It's a breach only if the contract says so.
Nothing happens until performance is actually due.
It's a repudiation; the demanding party may cancel and seek remedies.
The demand lapses.
The silent party gets another 30 days.
oe: The statute makes it a repudiation.
It's a repudiation now.

Correct. Failure to provide adequate assurance within a reasonable time not exceeding 30 days after a justified demand is a repudiation (§ 2-609(4)), triggering § 2-610 and cancellation under § 2-703(f) or § 2-711(1).
No.
No.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — No answer for 35 days

q: Evidence of a claimed oral term gets past the parol evidence rule. Which is correct?
o: The term is now established as part of the contract.
The fact-finder may still disbelieve it.
The term now controls over the writing.
The writing is now void.
The other side can't offer contrary evidence.
oe: It must still be proved and believed.
Correct. Getting past the PER only gets evidence to the fact-finder. And the proponent of course of dealing or usage must prove it is more probable than not and give § 1-303(g) notice for usage.
Admissibility isn't priority.
No.
It can.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Past the PER

q: A merchant sells a sealed space heater with a manufacturing defect the merchant couldn't have discovered. The heater fails in normal use. Has the merchant breached the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: No; only the manufacturer is liable for a sealed product.
Yes. Liability is strict.
Only if it was careless in inspecting the heater.
No, because it couldn't have discovered the defect.
Only if the box had been opened before sale.
oe: The retailer, a merchant seller, makes the warranty too.

Correct. Implied warranties rest on strict liability, not negligence; the seller's lack of knowledge is no defense. Usually there's a defect at the time of sale, or a failure to give proper instructions.
Negligence isn't required.
Knowledge is irrelevant.
Irrelevant.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Seller didn't know of defect

q: Which pairing from the class excuse chart is correct?
o: Obstruction of the payment method: Restatement § 263 / UCC § 2-613.
Intervening illegality: UCC § 2-614(1).
Frustration of purpose: UCC § 2-613.
Casualty to identified goods: Restatement § 261 / UCC § 2-615.
Death of a party: Restatement § 262; no UCC rule.
oe: That's § 2-614(2), with no Restatement analog on the chart.
No UCC rule.
Frustration is common law (§ 265).

Correct. The chart: casualty to identified goods, § 263 / § 2-613; obstruction of delivery method, § 270 / § 2-614(1); obstruction of payment method, none / § 2-614(2); damage to facilities or interference with tender, § 261 / §§ 2-615, 2-616; intervening illegality, § 264 / no UCC rule (but § 2-615(a) covers good-faith compliance with regulation). Frustration is § 265.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Restatement and UCC chart

q: A manufacturer prices each order at "80% of our suggested retail price on the day the order is accepted." Planning a 30% cut, it waits for the retailer's large monthly order, accepts it at once, then announces the cut. Best analysis?
o: Likely bad faith in performance, despite the express price term.
Bad faith in negotiation, which § 1-304 forbids.
Fraud, because sellers must disclose all business plans.
A breach of fiduciary duty.
No issue, because parties may always enforce express terms as written.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-2: using control over timing to exploit the partner fits Market Street. Counter: there's no general duty to disclose plans, and the price term is express (Vintage Rodeo). Problem 3-3 adds pretextual rejection after a market drop as another example.
The conduct is in performance; § 1-304 doesn't reach negotiation.
No such duty.
They aren't fiduciaries.
Good faith governs how discretion under express terms is exercised.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Timing an acceptance to exploit a price term

q: Now representing the diesel supplier, how would you limit the trucking firm's "requirements"?
o: Add a merger clause.
Delete the requirements term and let the firm order whatever it wants.
Use an estimate with a floor and cap, and tie it to fuel the existing fleet burns.
Let the supplier refuse any order it considers too large.
Rely on good faith alone.
oe: A merger clause doesn't limit quantity.
That gives up all protection.

Correct. Problem 5-1(a)(2): an estimate is the center of variation and a minimum or maximum is a clear limit (§ 2-306 cmt. 3); excluding resale, stockpiling and new fleets (or requiring notice) tracks the statute.
An arbitrary standard risks being ineffective and may make the deal illusory.
Disproportion and good faith help, but a clause gives certainty.
topic: X · Variation by agreement (§ 1-302) — Limiting a requirements buyer
pre: A trucking firm will buy all its diesel from a supplier at prices the supplier sets at each delivery. The trucking firm's lawyer wants to pin down "good faith." Which clause works best?

q: A buyer rightfully rejects a pallet of printers but keeps two of them running in its office. What is the problem?
o: The seller owes it storage fees for the rest.
It gains title to the two printers.
None; rejected goods may be used until the seller picks them up.
It may keep the two for free.
Using them is an act of ownership that undercuts the rejection.
oe: Not the issue.
No.
Ownership acts are barred.
No.

Correct. After rejection the buyer may not exercise ownership (§ 2-602(2)(a)) and must hold goods in its possession with reasonable care for the seller to remove (§ 2-602(2)(b)). Rejection must come within a reasonable time with seasonable notice (§ 2-602(1)).
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Using rejected goods

q: Before delivery, a seller that agreed to give credit discovers the buyer is insolvent. What may it do?
o: Nothing; it promised credit.
Refuse delivery except for cash.
Demand a letter of credit as of right.
Deliver and reclaim at any time later.
Cancel and sue for lost profits.
oe: Section 2-702(1) gives it a right.
Correct. Section 2-702(1) (including payment for goods already delivered under the contract). Without actual insolvency, use § 2-609 instead (Problem 6-3).
Cash is what § 2-702(1) allows.
Reclamation has a 10-day limit.
Insolvency isn't itself a breach.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Insolvent buyer before delivery

q: Vance obtains a painting by fraud and gives it to his niece, who knows nothing. The defrauded owner sues the niece. Who wins?
o: The owner, because the niece gave no value.
The niece, because Vance could transfer whatever he had.
The niece, because "purchase" includes a gift.
The niece, because she acted in good faith.
The owner, because Vance had void title.
oe: Correct. "Purchase" includes a gift (§ 1-201(b)(29)), so the niece takes Vance's voidable title, but protection against the owner requires a good-faith purchaser FOR VALUE, and she gave none.
He had only voidable title, which the owner can avoid against a donee.
She's a purchaser, but not for value.
Value is also required.
Fraud gives voidable title; the owner wins for another reason.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Gift from a voidable-title holder

q: Which Problem 3-6 statement does the problem present as a split of authority?
o: A dealer's description of a vase as "Ming."
"That dress looks good on you."
"A beautiful painting by a talented artist."
A yacht dealer's statement that a used boat is "seaworthy."
An electronics seller's statement that "replacement parts are readily available."
oe: A description, so a warranty (the question is only what the label means).
Puffing, not a split.
Puffing.
Correct. The problem cites Keith v. Buchanan (warranty) against Sessa v. Riegle.
Likely a warranty: specific and measurable.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Split in Problem 3-6

q: In Mathis v. Exxon, Exxon's dealer tank wagon price was within the range its competitors charged. Why did the bad-faith verdict stand?
o: Exxon never posted its price.
Exxon's price was above the range its competitors charged.
Proof of intent to drive dealers out defeated the safe harbor.
Good faith under § 2-305 is purely objective.
The dealers proved Exxon was negligent in calculating its price.
oe: Not the basis.
It was within the range.
Correct. Good faith under § 2-305(2) has subjective and objective parts; cmt. 3's safe harbor covers only the "normal case."
The court required both prongs.
Negligence isn't the test.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Mathis v. Exxon holding

q: Which is NOT required for the specially manufactured goods exception, § 2-201(3)(a)?
o: The seller made a substantial beginning of manufacture or commitments for procurement.
The goods are specially manufactured for the buyer.
They aren't suitable for sale to others in the seller's ordinary course.
The buyer paid a deposit.
The seller did so before receiving notice of repudiation.
oe: Required.
Required.
Required.
Correct. Payment isn't an element. (Payment and acceptance is the separate part-performance exception.)
Required.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Specially manufactured goods elements

q: A letter of intent between two suppliers says, "No contract exists until both parties sign a definitive agreement." They then agree on every term by phone, and no one signs. Is there a contract?
o: No. They required more formality, and parties may do that.
Yes, if the price is under $500.
No, because a phone call can never form an Article 2 contract.
Yes, because § 2-207 abolished the mirror-image rule.
Yes. Section 2-204 lets a contract form in any manner, and that rule can't be varied.
oe: Correct. Article 2 lowers the formalities for forming a contract, but parties remain free to require more (freedom of contract, § 1-302).
The SOF threshold doesn't override their agreed requirement.
Oral contracts are fine under Article 2 (subject to § 2-201).
Section 2-207 doesn't override the parties' agreed precondition.
Parties can add formation requirements of their own for a future deal.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — No contract until both sign

q: Uma leaves her road bike at a bike shop for a tune-up. The shop, which also sells bikes, sells it to Vic, a buyer in ordinary course. Uma sues Vic. Who wins?
o: Vic, but only if Uma was careless.
Vic, a buyer in ordinary course from a bike dealer.
Uma, because the shop's sale was larcenous.
Uma, unless she authorized the shop to sell.
Uma, because the shop had no title to transfer.
oe: Carelessness isn't required.

Correct. Entrusting goods to a merchant who deals in goods of that kind gives it power to transfer all the entruster's rights to a buyer in ordinary course (§ 2-403(2)), even though the shop's sale was unauthorized or larcenous (§ 2-403(3)).
Section 2-403(3) covers that.
Authorization isn't required.
It had power to transfer Uma's rights.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Bike left for a tune-up

q: An oral deal calls for 50,000 circuits built to the buyer's specs. The seller has finished 8,000 when the buyer repudiates. Under § 2-201(3)(a), the contract is enforceable for:
o: only what the buyer admits in its pleadings.
nothing, since there's no signed record.
at least the circuits made or committed for; the full 50,000 is debatable.
only the circuits the buyer has accepted.
all 50,000 automatically, because every one is custom-made to the buyer's specs.
oe: That's the admission exception.
The exception exists precisely for unsigned deals.
Correct. Problem 2-11 asks whether the exception reaches the whole quantity; it clearly reaches what was made or committed for before notice.
That's the part-performance exception.
The text treats the full quantity as an open question.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Reach of the special-manufacture exception

q: Which is NOT required for § 2-613 to avoid the contract?
o: The goods suffered a casualty.
The goods were identified when the contract was made.
The casualty occurred without fault of either party.
The loss happened before risk passed to the buyer.
The buyer has already paid.
oe: Required.
Required.
Required.
Required.
Correct. Payment is irrelevant. Required: goods identified when the contract was made, a casualty, without fault of either party, before risk passed.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Elements of § 2-613

q: Both parties' forms say they're the "complete and exclusive agreement." The buyer offers (1) usage of trade that fiber makers supply a buyer for its carpet style's market life, and (2) a prior oral promise to the same effect. Which is admissible?
o: (1) only, and only if the forms are ambiguous.
(1) only.
Neither.
(2) only.
Both.
oe: No ambiguity threshold for usage.

Correct. Problem 5-12(a)-(b): usage can supplement even a complete and exclusive record (with notice and proof), but a prior oral term is barred by full integration, and a term that important would certainly have been written down.
Usage comes in.
Reversed.
The prior oral promise is barred.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Fiber supplier: usage vs. prior talks

q: Under § 2-313 cmt. 3, what must a buyer show about reliance?
o: That the statement was the main reason it bought.
That it relied reasonably on the statement.
That the seller intended the buyer to rely on it.
None in particular; taking it out needs clear proof.
That it read or heard the statement before agreeing to buy.
oe: Not required.
Comment 3 says no particular reliance need be shown.
The seller's intent isn't required.
Correct. Affirmations made during the bargain are regarded as part of the description; taking one out "requires clear affirmative proof." The issue is normally one of fact.
Not required by the comment, though some courts demand reliance.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Basis of the bargain and reliance

q: A seller emails an offer to sell 300 drums of resin and says nothing about how to accept. The buyer accepts by overnight courier letter. Is the acceptance effective?
o: Yes, because § 2-206 makes every acceptance effective when dispatched.
Yes, but only because both parties are merchants.
No; an emailed offer must be accepted by email.
Yes, if a letter is a reasonable medium in the circumstances.
No; by emailing, the offeror unambiguously required email.
oe: Section 2-206 says nothing about the mailbox rule; it addresses manner and medium.
Section 2-206(1)(a) applies to everyone.
That is the common-law same-medium presumption, which § 2-206(1)(a) abolished.

Correct. Unless the offer unambiguously indicates otherwise, it invites acceptance in any manner and by any medium reasonable in the circumstances (§ 2-206(1)(a)). The offeror can still be master of the offer by clearly requiring a medium.
Sending an offer by email doesn't unambiguously require an email reply.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Accepting by a different medium

q: Which disclaimer of the implied warranty of merchantability is effective?
o: The seller says out loud, "No guarantees of fitness with this saw."
"No warranty of merchantability," in small gray type in a long contract.
A conspicuous written clause: "Seller disclaims fitness for a particular purpose."
A conspicuous clause: "This saw is guaranteed to work."
The seller says out loud, "I make no warranty of merchantability on this saw."
oe: Doesn't mention merchantability (and fitness disclaimers must be written).
Written, so it must be conspicuous.
Reaches fitness only.
That's a warranty, not a disclaimer.
Correct. Under § 2-316(2), the language must mention merchantability and, IF written, be conspicuous. An oral disclaimer that mentions merchantability works.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Effective merchantability disclaimer

q: A buyer sues for breach of merchantability after a pressure washer fails. Which fact most helps the seller?
o: The buyer put gasoline in the water tank.
The buyer used the washer for its ordinary purpose.
The seller didn't know of any defect.
The buyer never read the warranty card.
The seller is a small family business.
oe: Correct. Comment 13: the buyer must prove the warranty, breach and proximate cause; the seller can show the loss came from events after delivery, and misuse may mean no breach or reduced damages.
That helps the buyer.
Irrelevant to strict liability.
Implied warranties don't depend on reading anything.
Size doesn't matter if it's a merchant in those goods.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Fact that helps the seller

q: Which was NOT evidence the Mathis dealers offered of Exxon's bad faith?
o: After 1994 Exxon barred dealers from buying from jobbers.
The DTW price exceeded the rack price plus delivery cost.
Exxon refused to sell them any gasoline.
Exxon planned to convert stations to company-operated stores.
Many dealers became unprofitable.
oe: Offered.
Offered.
Correct. Exxon sold to them; the dispute was the price it set.
Offered.
Offered.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Mathis evidence

q: Which bailee tender is effective under § 2-503(4)(a)?
o: The seller emails the buyer that the goods are in the warehouse.
The warehouse acknowledges to the seller that the goods have been sold.
The warehouse acknowledges to the buyer the buyer's right to possession.
The seller mails the warehouse a bill of sale.
The seller gives the buyer a photocopy of the seller's own receipt.
oe: Notice alone isn't a bailee tender.
It must be to the buyer.
Correct. The acknowledgment must run to the buyer (Jason's Foods). Tendering a negotiable document also works.
The bailee must acknowledge the buyer's right.
Not a negotiable document or acknowledgment.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Bailee's acknowledgment

q: Without any reasonable grounds, a seller sends a written demand for assurance and stops shipping. What is the risk?
o: The seller's demand and suspension may themselves be a repudiation.
None; any party may demand assurance at any time.
The buyer must answer within 30 days anyway.
The buyer becomes insolvent by law.
The demand is valid if it is in writing.
oe: Correct. The class flowchart: no reasonable grounds and the request could be a repudiation. The three questions are: reasonable grounds? a reasonable request? an adequate response?
Grounds are required.
Only a justified demand triggers § 2-609(4).
No.
Writing is necessary, not sufficient.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Demand without grounds

q: Which is NOT a hallmark of good contract drafting from the Week 1 slides and text?
o: Using traditional legalese, which courts read more favorably.
Knowing the legal rules and the options available for allocating risks.
Anticipating what could go wrong and drafting terms that allocate that risk.
Concise, clear and simple language, with close attention to detail.
Understanding the deal, including the client's business and the usage of trade.
oe: Correct. The text says to avoid legalese and use short sentences and active voice.
A hallmark. The transactional lawyer's main job is risk allocation.
A hallmark of the transactional lawyer's work, e.g., limiting liability if a defective toaster burns down a house.
Hallmarks three and four. The goal is an enforceable agreement that reflects the deal.
A hallmark: first on the slide.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — Good drafting and the lawyer's role

q: Which statement about § 2-725 is correct?
o: It runs from discovery for every warranty claim.
The parties may shorten it to 90 days.
It is two years for consumer goods.
The parties may extend it to six years.
It can be cut to one year by the original agreement, not extended.
oe: Only for warranties of future performance.
Not below one year.
Four years for all.
It can't be extended.
Correct. A cause of action accrues on breach, and a warranty breach occurs on tender unless the warranty explicitly extends to future performance.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Statute of limitations

q: Mid-contract, a seller's costs spike, and it asks for a higher price. The buyer agrees by signed email. Nothing new is given in return. Is the modification enforceable?
o: Yes, whatever the seller's motive.
Yes, if it was sought in good faith.
No; a price change needs a writing signed by both parties.
Yes, but only if it is "fair and equitable" under Restatement § 89.
No; the pre-existing duty rule requires new consideration.
oe: Good faith is required (cmt. 2; Roth Steel).

Correct. Under § 2-209(1) a modification needs no consideration. Comment 2 polices it with good faith: a market shift that makes performance a loss can justify asking, even if it wouldn't excuse performance.
Only if the SOF or a NOM clause requires it, and a signed email by the party charged would satisfy § 2-201.
That's the modern common-law test; Article 2 is even more lenient.
That's the common-law rule § 2-209(1) displaces.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — Price increase without consideration

q: A merchant buyer rightfully rejects a load of fresh strawberries. The seller has no agent nearby and sends no instructions. What should the buyer do?
o: Give them away to a food bank.
Ship them back to the seller at its own expense.
Let them spoil and sue the seller.
Try to resell them for the seller's account.
Keep them as its own.
oe: Not authorized.
Not required.
It must try to sell perishables.

Correct. Section 2-603: a merchant buyer must make reasonable efforts to sell perishables for the seller, keeping expenses and a commission (usual rate, up to 10%), judged by good faith. For non-perishables, § 2-604 lets a buyer store, reship or resell; none of this is acceptance or conversion.
That would be acceptance.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Perishables after rejection

q: A buyer with good reason to worry phones the seller to demand assurance and stops paying. What is the problem?
o: It must first sue for a declaratory judgment.
It must wait 30 days before calling.
It needs a written demand to suspend.
None; a phone demand is enough.
Buyers can't demand assurance; only sellers can.
oe: No.
No.
Correct. The flowchart: no written demand, no right to suspend; the buyer's suspension may itself be a breach.
The statute requires writing (or a record).
Either party can.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Oral demand

q: Which is NOT one of the § 2-314(2) standards for merchantable goods?
o: Be free of every defect, however minor.
Run of even kind, quality and quantity within each unit and among all units, within agreed variations.
If fungible, be of fair average quality within the description.
Pass without objection in the trade under the contract description.
Conform to the promises or affirmations made on the container or label.
oe: Correct. Merchantability means minimal quality, not perfection ("at least" the listed standards).
Standard (d).
Standard (b).
Standard (a).
Standard (f).
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Merchantability standards

q: How do Shell Oil v. HRN and Autry Petroleum v. BP differ from Mathis?
o: They hold seller-set prices are void.
A reasonable, non-discriminatory price is in good faith.
They hold good faith under § 2-305 is purely subjective.
They follow Mathis.
They require the seller to charge the lowest market price.
oe: They uphold them.
Correct. The majority reasons that letting allegations of bad motive defeat the safe harbor would inject uncertainty.
They emphasize the objective test.
They reject it.
Not required.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Majority view after Mathis

q: Which buyer is NOT a buyer in ordinary course of business under § 1-201(b)(9)?
o: A business that buys a delivery van from a van dealer in good faith.
A shopper who buys from a store, unaware the guitar was left there for repair.
A shopper who buys a guitar in good faith from a music store.
A customer who buys a ring on credit from a jeweler in the usual way.
A shopper who buys a used guitar from a pawnshop.
oe: A BIOCB.
A BIOCB: good faith, no knowledge.
A BIOCB.
A BIOCB.
Correct. The definition excludes purchases from a pawnbroker.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Not a buyer in ordinary course

q: A merchant buyer rejects a shipment, saying only "nonconforming." The defect was a missing label the seller could have fixed in time. Effect?
o: The buyer must accept and then sue.
None; a buyer never has to explain a rejection.
It can't rely on that defect to justify rejecting.
The rejection turns into a revocation of acceptance.
The seller loses its right to cure.
oe: The rejection fails as to that defect.
It must state curable defects.

Correct. Section 2-605(1)(a): failing to state a defect ascertainable by reasonable inspection bars relying on it where the seller could have cured. Between merchants, a seller's written request for a full statement has the same effect.
No.
The buyer's silence is what's penalized.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Unstated curable defect

q: A seller offers to indorse to the buyer a negotiable warehouse receipt covering all 200 ovens it sold. The buyer wants to pay for each oven as it resells it. Who is right?
o: The buyer, because it can't inspect ovens in a warehouse.
Neither; the ovens must be moved to the buyer first.
The buyer, because a warehouse receipt is never a tender.
The buyer; paying as goods resell is the default.
The seller; the receipt is a proper tender and payment is due.
oe: It may inspect at the warehouse before paying.
Bailee goods can be tendered without moving them.
A negotiable receipt is the classic tender.
No credit or installment payment is presumed.
Correct. Problem 4-10: tendering a negotiable document is a proper tender (§ 2-503(4)(a)), and absent agreement payment is due on tender in a single lot (§§ 2-307, 2-310).
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Ovens in a warehouse

q: A merchant's form sale contract with a consumer has a no-oral-modification clause in the fine print. The consumer signs only at the bottom. Later the parties orally agree to a new delivery date. Is the oral change barred?
o: No, unless the consumer separately signed the NOM clause.
No; NOM clauses are unenforceable under Article 2.
Yes; any NOM clause in a signed agreement bars all oral modifications.
Yes, because the consumer signed the contract.
Yes, but only if the change involves $500 or more.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-209(2), "except as between merchants such a requirement on a form supplied by the merchant must be separately signed by the other party."
Article 2 enforces them; the common law didn't.
Not on a merchant's form signed by a non-merchant without a separate signature.
A signature at the bottom isn't a separate signature of the clause.
That confuses the NOM clause with the SOF.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — NOM clause on a merchant's form

q: Which statement about remedy limitations is correct?
o: They must be conspicuous, like disclaimers.
They are tested under § 2-316.
Article 2 implies a repair-or-replace limit in every sale.
They must be part of the agreement; the law never implies them.
Article 2 makes them bar tort claims too.
oe: No conspicuousness requirement.
Never implied.

Correct. Ask (1) is it part of the agreement (§§ 2-204 to 2-209) and (2) is it enforceable (§§ 2-718, 2-719, 2-302). Neither LD nor limited-remedy clauses must be conspicuous, and whether they reach fraud or negligence claims is for other law.
That's for other law.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Remedy limitations generally

q: Which statement about "as is" is correct?
o: It disclaims express warranties too.
Absent contrary circumstances, it excludes implied warranties.
It works only if it also mentions merchantability.
It disclaims the warranty of title.
It must be in a separately signed writing.
oe: Express warranties survive.
Correct. Section 2-316(3)(a) ("as is," "with all faults"). It doesn't reach express warranties or the title warranty.
Section 2-316(3)(a) works "notwithstanding" (2).
Title requires specific language or circumstances.
No such rule.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — "As is"

q: Same forms. The buyer offers its prior negotiations to explain what "support the integration of all materials" means. Admissible?
o: Yes, always, because explanation is never barred.
It depends on the court; some require ambiguity first.
Only if the seller consents.
Only if both forms quote the negotiations.
No, never, because the forms are complete and exclusive.
oe: Some courts require ambiguity.

Correct. Problem 5-12(c)(2): explaining a term isn't contradicting or supplementing it, so many courts admit it; others first require a finding of ambiguity. Usage of trade to explain the term comes in either way ((c)(1)).
Not the test.
Not the test.
Explanation is treated differently.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Prior talks to explain a term
pre: Both parties' forms say they're the "complete and exclusive agreement." The buyer offers (1) usage of trade that fiber makers supply a buyer for its carpet style's market life, and (2) a prior oral promise to the same effect. Which is admissible?

q: An art dealer contracts to sell a specific Picasso etching; the buyer will pick it up tomorrow. Overnight it burns in a fire started by a coffee pot the dealer left on. Result?
o: The buyer bears the loss because the contract was signed.
The contract is avoided because the etching was unique.
The buyer must accept a different etching.
No excuse; the dealer is in breach.
The contract is avoided because the dealer didn't intend the fire.
oe: Risk hadn't passed.
Uniqueness isn't enough without the no-fault element.
The contract was for that etching.

Correct. Problem 6-6(a): risk hadn't passed (merchant seller, no receipt), and the goods were identified, but § 2-613 requires no fault, and fault includes negligence (cmt. 1). A lightning strike would avoid the contract instead.
Negligence is fault.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Etching and the coffee pot

q: A buyer orders 100 blue office chairs for prompt shipment. The seller has only green, ships 100 green chairs, and says nothing. What is the result?
o: There is a contract and no breach, because color isn't a material term.
The shipment is treated as an accommodation as a matter of law.
No contract forms, because the goods don't match the order.
The shipment is both an acceptance and a breach.
The shipment is a counteroffer that the buyer may accept or reject.
oe: Under perfect tender, goods that fail in any respect are nonconforming.
Accommodation requires the seller's seasonable notice.
Shipment of nonconforming goods is still an acceptance.

Correct. An order for prompt shipment may be accepted by shipping conforming or nonconforming goods (§ 2-206(1)(b)). Without an accommodation notice, shipping nonconforming goods accepts and breaches at once.
Only if the seller seasonably notified the buyer that it was an accommodation.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Shipping the wrong goods, no notice

q: In its answer, a buyer admits it orally agreed to buy 200 crates but denies agreeing to 600. The seller claims 600. Under § 2-201(3)(b), the contract is enforceable for:
o: 600 crates, because admitting a contract waives the SOF.
Nothing, because only testimony counts as an admission.
200 crates, the quantity admitted.
600 crates if the seller testifies to it.
Nothing, because an answer isn't a signed record.
oe: Enforcement is capped at the quantity admitted.
Pleadings count too.
Correct. An admission in a pleading, testimony or otherwise in court makes the contract enforceable, but "not beyond the quantity of goods admitted."
The seller's testimony isn't the buyer's admission.
An admission in a pleading is enough.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Admission limited to quantity admitted

q: Courts disagree about whether a buyer must prove reliance for an express warranty (Cole v. General Motors). Which is NOT one of the positions?
o: Reliance is required only for oral warranties.
No reliance is required.
Reliance is presumed, but the presumption is rebuttable.
A strict showing of reliance is required.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The three positions are: a strict showing of reliance, no reliance at all, or a rebuttable presumption of reliance.
One of the three positions.
One of the three positions.
One of the three positions.
One of the other choices is correct: Reliance is required only for oral warranties.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Three views of reliance

q: A Wilmington seller agrees to sell machine parts to a manufacturer in Ontario. The U.S. and Canada have both ratified the CISG. The contract says only "governed by Delaware law." What most likely governs?
o: Article 2, because the CISG applies only to consumer sales.
Delaware common law, because the CISG and Article 2 both require a signed writing.
Ontario's sale-of-goods statute, because the goods are going to Ontario.
Delaware's Article 2, because the parties chose Delaware law and that choice controls.
The CISG, unless the contract expressly excludes it.
oe: Backwards. The CISG does not apply to consumer purchases; it covers commercial sales.
The CISG has no statute of frauds (Art. 11), and nothing here displaces both bodies of law.
The CISG, not the buyer's location, governs here unless excluded.
Choosing a state's law alone may select the CISG, which is part of that state's law. The CISG must be expressly excluded.

Correct. The CISG applies to sales between commercial parties whose places of business are in different ratifying nations, and it is federal law in Delaware, so choosing "Delaware law" can pull it in. To get Article 2, the clause must choose Delaware law and expressly exclude the CISG.
topic: I · The UCC, its purposes & interpretation (§§ 1-102, 1-103) — CISG and a choice-of-law clause

q: A used-car dealer's agent says the car "has never been in an accident" and "if it breaks down within 30 days, we'll fix it." The buyer signs: "AS IS. Seller makes no warranty, express or implied." The car breaks down; records show a prior accident. What is the buyer's best route?
o: Express warranty, because § 2-316(1) voids the disclaimer regardless of § 2-202.
The statute of frauds.
Fraud, which the PER doesn't bar.
The implied warranty of merchantability.
Unconscionability, because "as is" is always unconscionable.
oe: Section 2-316(1) is subject to the PER.
Irrelevant.

Correct. Problem 5-13: the statements are express warranties, and § 2-316(1) would make the disclaimer inoperative, but that's "subject to" § 2-202. If the writing is final on warranties, the oral warranties are excluded and "as is" kills the implied ones. Fraud evidence, or an argument that the form wasn't final, are the buyer's best routes.
"As is" excludes it.
It isn't.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — As-is car with oral warranties

q: A receipt says "The goods are sold as is" in the same font as everything else. Does it exclude the implied warranties?
o: No, because "as is" works only in capital letters.
Yes, and it also disclaims express warranties.
By the statute's text, yes; many courts demand conspicuousness.
No, because "as is" must be oral.
No, because it doesn't mention merchantability.
oe: That's the court-made gloss, not the statute's text.
Express warranties survive.
Correct. Problem 5-2(C)(2): subsection (3)(a) has no conspicuousness requirement in its text, but many courts impose one. Circumstances (TVs from a flood) can support it.
No such rule.
Not required under (3)(a).
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — "As is" in ordinary type

q: Which statement about risk of loss is NOT correct?
o: Goods with a bailee pass to the buyer on its receipt of a negotiable document of title.
Nonconforming goods stay at the seller's risk until cure or acceptance.
A non-merchant seller's risk passes on tender.
A buyer who prepays in full takes the risk from a merchant seller.
In a shipment contract, risk passes when the goods are duly delivered to the carrier.
oe: Correct. This is false. A merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods, even if the buyer has paid (§ 2-509(3) cmt. 3).
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Risk of loss: false statement

q: A seller delivers 200 jackets two weeks early; 30 are the wrong color, and the buyer rejects. What may the seller do?
o: Cure at any time within the following year, on notice.
Cure only if the buyer agrees.
Nothing; perfect tender ends the deal.
Insist that the buyer keep them at a discount.
Give notice and deliver conforming jackets on time.
oe: Within the contract time (or a further reasonable time under (2)).
It's the seller's right.
Cure softens perfect tender.
The buyer needn't accept.
Correct. Section 2-508(1): if the time for performance hasn't expired, the seller may seasonably notify its intent to cure and make a conforming delivery within the contract time.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Cure before the deadline

q: For fungible goods, "fair average quality" means:
o: any quality that isn't actually defective.
the middle belt of quality, not the worst that would pass.
the best quality available in the market.
whatever quality the price would suggest, which has no bearing on the warranty.
the quality of the seller's last delivery to this buyer.
oe: Too low: it must be middle-belt.
Correct. Comment 7. The comment also says the price at which a merchant closes a contract is an excellent index of the quality owed.
Too high.
Price is an index of the quality obligation.
Not the test.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Fair average quality

q: An oral deal for 100 chairs at $60 each. The seller delivers 40; the buyer accepts and pays for them, then refuses the rest. The seller sues for the other 60. Result?
o: Enforceable as to all 100, because part performance takes the deal out of the SOF.
Enforceable for the 40 only if the buyer is a merchant.
Unenforceable in full, because there's no signed record.
Enforceable for 100 if the seller tendered all 100.
Enforceable only as to the 40 chairs.
oe: It reaches only the goods paid for or received and accepted.
The exception doesn't depend on merchant status.
The 40 accepted and paid for are enforceable.
A tender the buyer rejected isn't part performance.
Correct. Part performance makes the contract enforceable only for goods paid for and accepted, or received and accepted (§ 2-201(3)(c)).
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Part performance limited to accepted goods

q: Same order for blue chairs, but before shipping green ones the seller emails: "Out of blue. Sending green only as an accommodation." What is the shipment?
o: An acceptance and a breach, because shipping always accepts.
A firm offer the buyer has three months to accept.
An acceptance of the buyer's offer at a reduced price.
An acceptance, but the seller may cure later.
A counteroffer, so the seller hasn't breached.
oe: The accommodation notice changes that result.
A firm offer needs a signed assurance it will be held open; nothing here.
There's no acceptance, and price isn't changed by the notice.
It isn't an acceptance at all.

Correct. Under § 2-206(1)(b), shipping nonconforming goods is not an acceptance if the seller seasonably notifies the buyer it is offered only as an accommodation. The buyer may accept or reject the green chairs.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Accommodation shipment
pre: A buyer orders 100 blue office chairs for prompt shipment. The seller has only green, ships 100 green chairs, and says nothing. What is the result?

q: Under § 2-718(1), an LD amount must be reasonable in light of several factors. Which is NOT one of them?
o: The difficulty of proving the loss.
The inconvenience or nonfeasibility of another adequate remedy.
The anticipated or actual harm caused by the breach.
Whether the clause is conspicuous.
None of the above.
oe: A factor.
A factor.
A factor.

Correct. Nothing requires an LD clause to be conspicuous. The factors: anticipated or actual harm; difficulty of proving loss; and the inconvenience or nonfeasibility of otherwise getting an adequate remedy.
One of the other choices is correct: Whether the clause is conspicuous.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — LD factors

q: Which can supply reasonable grounds for a seller's insecurity about its buyer?
o: The buyer's decision to use a different bank, with nothing more.
The buyer's refusal to renegotiate the price.
The buyer has fallen behind on another, unrelated account with the seller.
A competitor's statement that it would like the buyer's business.
The seller's vague, unexplained unease.
oe: Alone, weak; Problem 6-3 combined it with a credit downgrade and late payments.
Insisting on the contract isn't a ground.
Correct. Comment 3: grounds need not arise from or relate directly to the contract. Grounds are objective; a purely subjective fear isn't enough.
Irrelevant.
Purely subjective.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Grounds unrelated to the contract

q: Same etching, but lightning causes the fire. Result?
o: The contract is avoided; no one owes anything.
The dealer must find another Picasso.
The buyer must still pay.
They split the etching's value.
The dealer must pay the buyer's damages.
oe: Correct. Identified goods, total casualty, no fault, before risk passed: neither party owes the other anything, and the dealer absorbs the loss of the etching.
Identified goods; no substitution.
Risk hadn't passed.
No.
It's excused.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Lightning
pre: An art dealer contracts to sell a specific Picasso etching; the buyer will pick it up tomorrow. Overnight it burns in a fire started by a coffee pot the dealer left on. Result?

q: The price is "the Chicago Board of Trade price on March 15." The board closes on March 14; the last quote (March 13) was $12. The seller tenders at $12; the buyer refuses and buys elsewhere at $11. Result?
o: The seller breached by demanding a price the board never set.
A contract at a reasonable price; if $12, the buyer breached.
No contract, because the only agreed price term failed when the board closed.
The price is $11, what the buyer paid elsewhere.
The price is the market price when they signed.
oe: Its demand matched a reasonable price.
Correct. Problem 4-3(b): the agreed standard wasn't set, so § 2-305(1)(c) supplies a reasonable price at the time for delivery. The last quote is strong evidence.
They intended to be bound.
That's contrary evidence, not the rule.
The time for delivery controls.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Price board closes

q: The textbook examines four factors, in order, to decide which law governs a transaction. Which comes first?
o: What the parties' agreement says about governing law.
The type of property involved.
Whether either party is a merchant.
The nature of the rights transferred, such as a sale or a lease.
Where the parties are located, domestically or internationally.
oe: That is the fourth factor, not the first.

Correct. The order is (1) type of property (goods, real estate, services, IP), (2) nature of the rights transferred (sale, lease, license, lien, gift), (3) location of the parties, and (4) the parties' agreement on governing law.
Not one of the four factors at all. Scope never turns on merchant status.
That is the second factor.
That is the third factor.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Four factors in order

q: A dishwasher's owner's manual, packed in the box, says it is "free of defects in material and workmanship for one year." The buyer never read it before buying. Which is correct?
o: It can still be an express warranty.
It can't be a warranty because the buyer saw it only after the sale.
It can't be a warranty because the buyer never relied on it.
It's puffing, because it appears in a printed manual.
It's an implied warranty of merchantability, not an express one.
oe: Correct. Courts have held owner's manuals and package inserts to be warranties even if unread before purchase (Weinstat, Rite Aid), and a warranty in the written contract needs no proof the buyer read it.
Post-sale language can become part of the bargain (cmt. 7).
Reliance isn't required under cmt. 3, and courts treat such inserts as warranties.
A specific promise in print isn't puffing.
It is an express promise about the goods.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Unread owner's manual

q: Which statement about no-oral-modification clauses is correct?
o: They also bar evidence of prior oral agreements.
Between merchants, the clause must be separately signed.
They make a later waiver impossible.
Article 2 enforces them; the common law generally didn't.
They're unenforceable under Article 2, just as at common law.
oe: That's a merger clause. A NOM clause governs future modifications.
The separate signature applies when a merchant's form goes to a non-merchant.
A failed modification can still operate as a waiver (§ 2-209(4)).
Correct. Section 2-209(2) makes a NOM clause in a signed agreement effective, a "private statute of frauds."
Article 2 reversed the common-law rule.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — NOM clauses generally

q: Buyer contracts to buy a necklace from a jeweler and leaves it with the jeweler to pick up later. The jeweler sells and delivers it to Purchaser, a buyer in ordinary course. Who gets the necklace?
o: Purchaser, because Buyer entrusted the necklace.
Neither; the jeweler still owns it.
Purchaser, but only if Buyer hadn't yet paid.
Buyer, because it had already bought the necklace.
Buyer, because entrusting requires handing goods over.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-12(F): Buyer's acquiescence in the jeweler's keeping possession is an "entrusting" (§ 2-403(3)). Buyer's remedy is against the jeweler.
Purchaser takes good title.
Payment doesn't matter.
Its acquiescence let the jeweler pass its rights.
Acquiescence in retention counts.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Leaving goods with the seller

q: A seller's tender on the delivery date is rejected. When does it get extra time to cure?
o: Always, for 30 days.
If it reasonably thought the tender would be accepted.
Only if the buyer is a merchant.
Only if it offers the buyer a price reduction for the delay.
Never after the contract time.
oe: Not automatic.

Correct. Section 2-508(2): with reasonable grounds to believe the nonconforming tender would be acceptable (with or without a money allowance), the seller gets a further reasonable time on seasonable notice.
Irrelevant.
A money allowance can be part of it, but isn't required.
Section 2-508(2) allows it.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Cure after the deadline

q: A buyer agreed to pay against documents under a C.I.F. term. It then hears rumors the seller's recent shipments elsewhere were poor. Can it demand assurance and refuse to pay against the documents meanwhile?
o: Yes, if the demand is in writing.
Yes, because C.I.F. buyers may inspect before paying.
No; it can't use § 2-609 to escape its promise to pay against documents.
Yes; any rumor is a reasonable ground.
Only if the seller is insolvent.
oe: Writing doesn't change what the buyer assumed.
They pay against documents.
Correct. Comment 3: a buyer who agreed to pay against documents assumed that risk and can't evade it by demanding assurance.
Grounds must be objective, and here the buyer assumed the risk.
Not the point.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — C.I.F. buyer and rumors

q: The price is "to be agreed at delivery." At delivery the market is $12 a sack; the seller demands $15. The buyer refuses and covers at $13. Result?
o: The seller breached; the buyer recovers $2 a sack.
No contract, since the price was never agreed.
The buyer recovers $3 a sack.
Seller breached; buyer recovers about $1 a sack.
The buyer breached by refusing to pay $15.
oe: That measures from cover to an incorrect base.
They intended to be bound.
Measured from the contract (reasonable) price, not the demand.
Correct. Problem 4-3(a): the price is a reasonable one (about $12), so insisting on $15 as a condition of delivery is a breach. Cover damages are $13 minus $12, plus incidentals (§ 2-712).
$15 isn't a reasonable price.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Seller demands too much

q: Under the class governing-law chart, which pairing for a transaction in goods is wrong?
o: Gift of goods: Article 2.
Bequest of goods in a will: the law of wills.
Sale of goods between merchants in two ratifying nations: the CISG.
Security interest in goods: Article 9.
Lease of goods: Article 2A.
oe: Correct. This is wrong. A gift of goods is governed by the common law. Article 2 governs sales.
Right pairing.
Right pairing. The chart's goods-sale cell reads "Art. 2 (or CISG)."
Right pairing.
Right pairing.
