topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Governing-law chart: goods column

q: A specific tractor identified at contracting is damaged, not destroyed, in a flood that is no one's fault, before risk passes. What are the buyer's options?
o: Take the tractor and sue for full damages.
Demand a new tractor.
Rescind and recover lost profits.
Inspect, then avoid or take it with a price allowance.
Nothing; the contract is automatically avoided by the flood.
oe: No further right against the seller.
Identified goods; no substitution.
No damages.
Correct. Section 2-613(b): the buyer may demand inspection and either avoid the contract or accept the goods with due allowance, "but without further right against the seller."
Only a total loss avoids it automatically.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Partial casualty

q: An LD clause sets $500,000 for late delivery of a $20,000 machine whose delay could cause at most a few thousand dollars of harm. Effect?
o: It's enforced if conspicuous.
It's enforced between merchants.
The clause is void as a penalty.
The court rewrites it to equal actual harm.
It's enforced because the parties agreed.
oe: Conspicuousness isn't the test.
The penalty rule applies to everyone.
Correct. A term fixing unreasonably large liquidated damages is void as a penalty (§ 2-718(1)); the buyer must then prove actual damages.
It's void; actual damages are then proved.
Not if unreasonably large.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Huge LD amount

q: Which is NOT one of the slide's factors for deciding whether a statement became part of the basis of the bargain?
o: The seller used the word "warranty."
The price tends to support the buyer's claim.
The seller was more expert than the buyer.
The quality wasn't something the buyer could easily check.
The statement concerned a matter of objective importance to the buyer.
oe: Correct. Formal words aren't needed (§ 2-313(2)). The nine factors include a plain, unambiguous statement; objective importance; a quality the buyer couldn't easily check; a more expert seller; buyer reliance in part; nothing suggesting the seller wasn't serious or putting the buyer on guard; a remedy fair to the seller; and a price that supports the claim.
One of the factors.
One of the factors.
One of the factors.
One of the factors.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Basis-of-the-bargain factors

q: Which Problem 3-12 seller has NOT breached the warranty of title (assuming no colorable claim)?
o: One who bought the necklace, in good faith, from a thief.
One who borrowed the necklace from a friend and sold it.
One who received the necklace as a gift from a thief.
One who stole the necklace from its owner.
One who paid the owner with a check that later bounced.
oe: Breach. Void title.
Breach. No title and no power.
Breach. Void title.
Breach. All sellers warrant title, and a thief has none.
Correct. That seller had voidable title, so its good-faith buyer for value got good title.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Problem 3-12 no breach

q: Which statement uses the terms correctly?
o: A buyer assigns its duty to pay.
A seller delegates its right to payment and assigns its duty to deliver.
A buyer delegates its right to receive the goods.
Rights and duties are both "assigned" under § 2-210.
A seller assigns its right to payment and delegates its duty to deliver.
oe: Duties are delegated.
Reversed.
Rights are assigned.
The section distinguishes them.
Correct. Rights are assigned; duties are delegated. The buyer's right is to the goods; its duty is to pay.
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — Rights and duties

q: A buyer's offer invites acceptance by beginning performance. The seller starts making the goods but never tells the buyer. Three months later the buyer, having heard nothing, buys elsewhere. Who is right?
o: The buyer may treat the offer as having lapsed.
The seller. A contract formed when work began, so the buyer breached.
Neither. Article 2 doesn't allow acceptance by beginning performance.
The seller, but only if the seller is a merchant.
The seller, because beginning performance turns the offer into a firm offer.
oe: Correct. Where beginning performance is a reasonable mode of acceptance, an offeror not notified of acceptance within a reasonable time may treat the offer as lapsed before acceptance (§ 2-206(2)).
Section 2-206(2) protects an offeror who isn't notified within a reasonable time.
It does, when that is a reasonable mode of acceptance.
Merchant status is irrelevant to § 2-206(2).
A firm offer requires a merchant's signed assurance; beginning performance doesn't create one.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Beginning performance without notice

q: An oral deal: 100 widgets for $400. Before delivery, the parties orally agree to 200 widgets for $800. Result?
o: The $800 deal binds only if the seller is a merchant.
The modification fails without a record; the $400 deal stands.
The $800 deal is enforceable because the original was oral too.
Both are enforceable, since modifications need no consideration.
Neither is enforceable; the failed modification taints the original.
oe: Merchant status alone doesn't satisfy § 2-201.
Correct. The contract as modified is within § 2-201, so § 2-209(3) requires a signed record. The failed modification may still operate as a waiver (§ 2-209(4)).
The modified contract must satisfy § 2-201 on its own.
Consideration isn't the problem; the SOF is.
The original $400 deal needed no record and survives.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — Problem 3-4(a)

q: In a shipment contract, when does risk of loss pass to the buyer?
o: When the buyer pays.
When the goods reach the buyer.
When title passes at the destination.
When the seller duly delivers the goods to the carrier.
When the carrier bills the buyer.
oe: Payment is irrelevant.
That's a destination contract.
Title is irrelevant, and in a shipment contract it passes at shipment anyway.
Correct. Section 2-509(1)(a). In a destination contract, risk passes when the goods are duly tendered at the destination (§ 2-509(1)(b)).
Irrelevant.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Shipment contract risk

q: Which was NOT part of the court's reasoning in Casazza v. Kiser (the 52-foot sailboat)?
o: Promissory estoppel failed under every approach Minnesota recognized.
Accepting the navigation software wasn't accepting the boat; they weren't one commercial unit.
Article 2 didn't apply because both parties were individuals.
The typed terms were never signed by Kiser.
Hoping Kiser would admit the deal in a deposition wasn't an admission.
oe: Part of the reasoning.
Part of the reasoning.
Correct. Article 2 applied, and so did § 2-201, even though neither party was a business. That is why the oral $200,000 deal failed.
Part of the reasoning.
Part of the reasoning.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Casazza reasoning

q: A bold clause just above the signatures says: "There are no warranties, express or implied, included in this transaction." Which is correct?
o: It excludes nothing, because it doesn't say "as is."
It can exclude fitness; its effect on merchantability is doubtful.
It excludes every warranty, express and implied.
It excludes merchantability, because it is conspicuous.
It excludes the warranty of title.
oe: It can still exclude fitness.

Correct. Problem 5-2(C)(1): it fails § 2-316(2) for merchantability because it doesn't mention it, and courts split on whether it is "other language" that works under (3)(a). Fitness needs only a conspicuous writing.
Express warranties that are part of the bargain survive, and merchantability is doubtful.
Under (2), it must also mention merchantability.
Title needs specific language.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — "No warranties, express or implied"

q: A new car meets every safety regulation but rates below average in crash tests. A buyer seriously injured in a head-on collision sues for breach of merchantability. Likely result?
o: Breach, because regulatory compliance is irrelevant.
No breach, because personal injuries can't be recovered for warranty breach.
Breach of fitness, because every buyer wants safety.
Breach, because the car wasn't the safest on the market.
No breach; the car need only be reasonably safe.
oe: Compliance is strong, though not conclusive, evidence.
Injury to person from breach of warranty can be consequential damages.
Fitness needs a communicated particular purpose (compare Problem 3-11(B)).
The standard is minimal, not best.
Correct. Problem 3-10(d): merchantable goods must be reasonably safe for ordinary use, not the safest; compliance is strong evidence of merchantability.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Low crash rating

q: Unknown to both parties, the specific painting they contract for burned the day before they signed. Does § 2-613 apply?
o: Only if the buyer had paid.
Only if the seller knew.
No; it applies only to casualties after contracting.
Yes; it covers goods already destroyed at contracting.
No; the contract is void for mistake instead, and § 2-613 can't apply.
oe: Irrelevant.
Unknown to both.
It covers both.

Correct. Comment 2: it applies whether the goods were already destroyed at contracting (unknown to both) or destroyed later but before risk passed. The key question is whether the seller undertook responsibility for the goods' continued existence. (It also applies in a proper case under a "no arrival, no sale" term, § 2-324.)
Section 2-613 expressly covers this.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Destroyed before signing

q: Which statement about title under Article 2 is correct?
o: Risk of loss passes with title.
In a shipment contract, title passes on tender at the destination.
Most Article 2 rules apply regardless of title.
Title always passes when the contract is signed.
Article 2 has no rule on when title passes.
oe: Risk turns on tender and breach, not title.
At shipment.

Correct. Section 2-401 de-emphasizes title; § 2-312 and § 2-403 are the main exceptions. Title still matters for creditors, insurance, taxes and bankruptcy. In a shipment contract it passes at shipment; in a destination contract, on tender there.
It depends on the delivery terms.
Section 2-401(2) has one.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Title under Article 2

q: A bill of sale warrants a painting's authenticity. Before closing, an independent curator tells the buyer she doubts the attribution. The buyer closes anyway and later sues. Under Rogath v. Siebenmann:
o: The buyer loses, because express warranties require reliance.
The buyer loses, because anyone who closes knowing of doubts waives the warranty.
The buyer loses, because he no longer believed the painting was authentic.
The buyer can recover; he may have bought the warranty as insurance.
The buyer wins only if he expressly reserved his rights at closing.
oe: Rogath rejects a strict reliance test.
Waiver applies when the SELLER disclosed the facts.
Belief in the fact isn't the test.

Correct. The question is whether the buyer believed he was buying the seller's promise, not whether he believed the fact. Knowledge from a third party doesn't bar recovery; the buyer may have bought the warranty as insurance.
Reservation matters when the seller made the disclosure.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Doubts from a third party

q: Which pairing from the governing-law chart is correct?
o: Sale of a negotiable promissory note: Article 9 only.
Lease of an office building: Article 2A.
Sale of investment securities: Article 8 and securities law.
Bailment of goods for repair: Article 2, as a transaction in goods.
License of a patent: Article 2.
oe: Wrong. The chart puts sales of negotiable instruments under Articles 3 and 4.
Wrong. Real property leases are governed by real property law. Article 2A covers leases of goods.
Correct. Securities are excluded from "goods" and governed by Article 8 and securities laws (Article 9 for security interests in them).
Wrong. A bailment transfers possession, not title; it's governed by common law (and sometimes Article 7).
Wrong. IP transfers are governed by common law and federal law.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Governing-law chart: other columns

q: Which subsections of § 2-210 deal with delegation of duties?
o: (4) only.
(5) only.
oe: Prohibitions.
(2) is assignment.
Assignment.
Correct. (2) and (3) cover assignment; (4) reads prohibition language; (5) says what an assignment of "the contract" transfers.
What "the contract" transfers.
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — Structure of § 2-210

q: A pharmacy resells sealed boxes of gloves labeled "latex free." They contain latex. What is the buyer's best theory against the pharmacy?
o: Title, because mislabeled goods aren't rightfully transferred.
Express warranty, because the pharmacy itself made the label statement.
None; only the manufacturer answers for its label.
Fitness, because every glove buyer has a particular purpose.
Merchantability: goods must conform to the label.
oe: Labeling has nothing to do with title.
The text doubts a reseller makes the label statements as express warranties.
The retailer is a merchant seller.
Avoiding latex may be an ordinary expectation; fitness needs a particular purpose and reliance.
Correct. Section 2-314(2)(f). A retailer reselling packaged goods probably doesn't make the label statement as its own express warranty, but it impliedly warrants that the goods conform to it.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Mislabeled gloves

q: A seller offers 1,000 pens at 75¢ each. The buyer replies: "Price too high. Can't buy for more than 68¢." Which is correct?
o: The reply is a counteroffer, not an acceptance.
A contract exists at a reasonable price under § 2-305.
The reply accepts with a different price term under § 2-207(1).
A contract exists at 68¢, because the last communication wins.
A contract exists at 75¢, the offeror's term.
oe: Correct. It isn't a definite expression of acceptance at all, so § 2-207(1) never applies. By contrast, a catalog order is an offer, and a reply like "Received your order; expect to ship Sept. 10" can accept it.
There's no agreement to contract with an open price; the buyer rejected the price.
A response that rejects the price isn't a "definite and seasonable expression of acceptance."
There is no "last shot" rule under Article 2, and no acceptance here.
No acceptance occurred.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — "Price too high" reply

q: Casazza described three approaches to promissory estoppel and the SOF. Under the Restatement approach, estoppel overcomes the SOF when:
o: refusing to enforce would let the defendant perpetrate a fraud.
never; the statute can't be avoided by estoppel.
the promise was to put the agreement in writing.
the plaintiff's reliance cost more than $500.
the plaintiff relied in any foreseeable way.
oe: That is the least restrictive approach.
That is the restrictive approach.
Correct. The restrictive view never allows it; the least restrictive allows it only where refusing to enforce would let a party perpetrate a fraud. Casazza lost under all three.
No such test.
No approach goes that far.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Promissory estoppel approaches

q: A seller's used tractor sits in its yard, available to look at, but the seller never asks the buyer to inspect it, and the buyer doesn't. A cracked engine block, which a quick look would have shown, surfaces later. Does § 2-316(3)(b) exclude implied warranties as to it?
o: Yes, because used goods carry no implied warranties.
No; there was no examination and no demand.
Yes, because a cracked block is obvious.
Yes, because the buyer had the chance to look.
Only if the buyer is a merchant.
oe: They carry a reduced one.
Correct. Section 2-316(3)(b) needs an actual pre-contract examination, or a refusal to examine after the seller DEMANDS one (cmt. 8). Mere availability isn't enough.
Only if there was an examination or a refusal after demand.
Availability isn't enough.
Status matters to what an examination should reveal, not here.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Tractor available but not inspected

q: A contract says "Ship to Buyer, Dover. Seller pays freight." There's no F.O.B. term. The goods are destroyed in transit. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because it agreed to pay freight to Dover.
The buyer; it's still a shipment contract.
They split it.
Only the carrier.
The seller, because the contract names a destination.
oe: Paying freight is a cost term, not a risk term.

Correct. Shipment contracts are presumed; the destination contract is "the variant" (§ 2-503 cmt. 5). Naming where the goods are going and agreeing to pay freight don't make it a destination contract.
No splitting.
As between the parties, the buyer, who may sue the carrier.
Every shipping contract names one.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Ship to, freight paid

q: An oral deal: 100 widgets for $1,000 (no record). The parties then orally agree to 40 widgets for $400. Is the new deal enforceable?
o: Yes, because as modified it's under $500.
No; a reduction needs consideration.
No; nothing built on an unenforceable $1,000 deal can be enforced.
Yes, but only for the original 100.
Only if the buyer signs a record.
oe: Correct. The contract as modified isn't within § 2-201, so no record is needed.
Modifications need no consideration (§ 2-209(1)).
The modified (or new) $400 deal stands on its own.
The original is unenforceable without a record.
No record is needed under $500.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — Problem 3-4(b)

q: An LD clause sets the buyer's recovery at $1 for any breach. What is the main concern?
o: It may be struck as unconscionable.
It must be conspicuous to be valid.
It's automatically valid because it's small.
It converts the contract into an option.
It's a penalty against the seller.
oe: Correct. Comment 1 to § 2-718: an unreasonably small amount may be unconscionable. LD may be an amount or a formula, and down-payment forfeitures are often enforced.
No such rule.
Too small can be unconscionable.
No.
Penalties are unreasonably large.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Tiny LD amount

q: A buyer effectively rejects goods that actually conform to the contract. What is the result?
o: The rejection is ineffective, so the buyer has accepted the goods.
It's effective but wrongful: the buyer is in breach.
The rejection is rightful.
No one has breached.
The seller must cure.
oe: It was effective (timely, with notice).
Correct. The seller then has its § 2-703 remedies. A rightful rejection of nonconforming goods, by contrast, preserves the buyer's § 2-711 remedies.
The goods conformed.
The buyer has.
Nothing to cure.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Rejecting conforming goods

q: Absent agreement, which statement about the parties' basic obligations is correct?
o: The seller must deliver, but the buyer has no duty to accept the goods.
The seller must deliver on credit unless told otherwise.
If neither party tenders, both are in breach.
The buyer must pay before the seller tenders.
Tender of goods and of payment are concurrent conditions.
oe: The buyer must accept and pay.
No credit is presumed.
Neither is.
Neither goes first by default.

Correct. Section 2-301 states the duties (seller transfers and delivers; buyer accepts and pays); §§ 2-507(1) and 2-511(1) make the tenders concurrent. If neither tenders, neither is in breach. The problems assume the seller tenders first.
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — Basic obligations

q: Which is a ground for insecurity that the Code itself supplies?
o: Any late delivery under any contract.
The other party's merger with a competitor.
A drop in the market price.
The other party's choice of a new lawyer.
An assignment that delegates the other party's performance.
oe: It may be a ground, but not a statutory one.
Not statutory.
Market changes can contribute (Top of Iowa), but aren't a statutory ground.
No.

Correct. Section 2-210(6). Separately, a buyer's insolvency lets a seller refuse delivery except for cash (§ 2-702(1)); "insolvent" means ceasing to pay debts in the ordinary course, being unable to pay them as they come due, or insolvency under bankruptcy law.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Statutory ground

q: A buyer orders 5,000 bicycle lights from a manufacturer that regularly sells them, built to the manufacturer's own design. A patent holder claims the lights infringe. Which is correct?
o: The buyer must indemnify the seller.
The warranty applies only once the patent claim is proved valid.
No warranty, because only express warranties cover patents.
The seller warranted against rightful infringement claims.
Every seller, merchant or not, makes this warranty.
oe: Only if the buyer supplied the specs.
The buyer needn't prove validity.
Section 2-312(3) implies one.
Correct. Unless otherwise agreed, a merchant regularly dealing in goods of the kind warrants delivery free of rightful third-party infringement claims (§ 2-312(3)).
Only merchants regularly dealing in such goods.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Infringement warranty arises

q: In a single-delivery contract for 1,000 bolts, 10 have slightly off threads. Under § 2-601, the buyer may:
o: reject only the 10 defective bolts.
reject only after giving the seller a chance to cure.
reject only if the defect substantially impairs the bolts' value.
reject all, accept all, or keep some commercial units.
only accept and sue for damages.
oe: It may do more.
Cure is the seller's right in limited cases, not a precondition to rejecting.
That's the installment test.
Correct. If the goods or tender "fail in any respect," the buyer may reject the whole, accept the whole, or accept any commercial units and reject the rest.
It may reject.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Perfect tender options

q: A buyer pays a $2,000 deposit on a $10,000 sale, then breaches. There's no LD clause, and the seller proves no damages. How much must the seller return?
oe: No.
The seller may keep the smaller of 20% or $500.
Forfeiture is limited absent a valid LD clause.
Correct. Section 2-718(2)(b): the buyer recovers what exceeds 20% of the price ($2,000) or $500, whichever is smaller. The seller keeps $500 (subject to offset for proved damages).
That's what the seller keeps.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Breaching buyer's deposit

Only if the buyer was forced to stop using the goods altogether.
