oe: Correct. The claim must cast a "substantial shadow" on the buyer's use (Sun Coast); a more lenient view excepts only frivolous claims (Pacific Sunwear). No eviction is needed (cmt. 4).
No such standard.
Frivolous claims don't.
Eviction isn't required.
Validity isn't required.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Proving an infringement claim

q: Which statement about acceptance and rejection is NOT correct?
o: A seller who blocks the buyer's inspection is in breach.
Waiting too long to inspect can cost the buyer its right to reject.
A buyer may accept some commercial units and reject others.
A buyer may hold goods indefinitely, neither accepting nor rejecting.
A buyer can't both accept and reject the same commercial unit.
oe: True.
True.
Correct. This is false. Failing to reject within a reasonable time after an opportunity to inspect is acceptance (§ 2-606(1)(b)), so the buyer can't do neither.
True.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Acceptance and rejection: false statement

q: A big retailer's form lets it demand from its supplier, "whenever it desires," "whatever assurances [it] deems appropriate," and suspend meanwhile. Effect?
o: Void only if the supplier is a consumer.
Enforceable, because good faith can be disclaimed.
Enforceable if conspicuous.
Enforceable; parties may vary § 2-609 freely.
Likely ineffective, because the standard is arbitrary.
oe: Not the test.
It can't be.
Conspicuousness doesn't fix arbitrariness.
Not with arbitrary standards (§ 1-302(b)).

Correct. Comment 6: clauses can fix the time for assurance or define adequacy in a commercially reasonable way, but arbitrary standards are ineffective (compare § 1-309: a "deems itself insecure" clause requires a good-faith belief). Problem 6-4, Clause 2.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — "Whatever assurances it deems appropriate"

q: An oral modification fails because a NOM clause requires a signed record. Can the attempt have any legal effect?
o: No, it's void for all purposes.
Only if supported by consideration.
Yes, it binds both parties as to all future performance.
Only between merchants.
Yes, it can operate as a waiver.
oe: Section 2-209(4) says otherwise.
No consideration is needed.
A waiver of an executory term can be retracted; it isn't a binding modification.
Section 2-209(4) isn't limited to merchants.
Correct. Section 2-209(4): an attempt at modification that doesn't satisfy (2) or (3) can operate as a waiver.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — Failed modification as waiver

q: A warranty says "Seller will repair or replace defective parts," but doesn't say this is the buyer's exclusive remedy. Is the buyer limited to repair?
o: No, because it isn't expressly exclusive.
Yes, once the seller attempts a repair.
Yes, if the seller is a merchant.
Only if the buyer is a consumer.
Yes; any agreed remedy is exclusive.
oe: Correct. Resort to an agreed remedy is optional unless expressly agreed to be exclusive (§ 2-719(1)(b)); clauses are presumed cumulative (cmt. 2).
Attempting a repair doesn't make it exclusive.
Irrelevant.
Irrelevant.
Only if expressly exclusive.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Optional unless exclusive

q: What governs a clause limiting the buyer's remedy to repair or replacement of defective parts?
o: Nothing; such clauses are unenforceable.
§ 2-316(2), so it must mention merchantability.
§ 2-316(3)(a), so it must say "as is."
§ 2-312(2), so it needs specific language.
oe: They're common and generally enforceable.
That's for disclaimers.
No.
Correct. Section 2-316(4). A disclaimer attacks the "breach" element (no warranty); a remedy limitation applies only after a breach and limits damages.
That's the title warranty.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Remedy limits aren't disclaimers

q: Under § 1-201(b)(10), who decides whether a term is conspicuous, and by what test?
o: The seller, by labeling the clause "conspicuous."
The court: whether it's printed entirely in capitals.
The parties, by agreeing that a clause is conspicuous.
The jury: whether this buyer actually noticed it.
The court: whether a reasonable person ought to have noticed it.
oe: Labels don't decide it.
Capitals help but aren't the test.
It's a decision for the court.
Objective, and for the court.
Correct. Examples: a heading in capitals as large as or larger than surrounding text, or contrasting type, font or color; body text in larger or contrasting type or set off by symbols.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Conspicuous

q: A buyer wants to send a sample of delivered wheat for a two-week lab test for genetic modification before accepting. The seller objects. When is that a reasonable inspection?
o: Only if the seller consents to it.
If GMO-free is a contract term and the test is reasonable.
Never; inspection must happen on the spot.
Only if the buyer pays the seller for the two weeks of delay.
Always; buyers may run any test they like.
oe: The right exists by default.

Correct. Problem 4-5(b): otherwise the test checks for nothing the contract requires. The buyer may hold the wheat without accepting, must reject within a reasonable time, and pays the test cost unless the wheat fails and is rejected.
Reasonable time and manner.
Not required.
Inspection must be reasonable.
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Two-week GMO test

q: A weaver buys five dye lots of "Magenta No. 02" yarn and sees color differences between lots. In this trade, weavers know to buy one dye lot for a project. Breach of merchantability?
o: Yes; the seller had to warn her about dye lots.
Yes; goods must always run of even kind and quality.
Likely not, given the trade's dye-lot practice.
Yes, because the lots were sold under a single description.
No, because yarn isn't goods.
oe: Trade usage already charges her with that knowledge.
Within permitted variations.

Correct. Problem 3-10(c): goods must run of even kind and quality "within the variations permitted by the agreement," and the agreement includes usage of trade. Variation within a single lot, or beyond trade tolerances, would be different.
The description is read with trade usage.
Yarn is goods.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Dye lots

q: For months a buyer has let the seller deliver after the contract's "by the 5th" deadline. Can the buyer now insist on on-time delivery?
o: No; a waiver, once made, is permanent.
Yes, by reasonable notice, unless the seller has materially relied.
Only if the seller agrees in a signed record.
Yes, and the retraction also revives claims for past late deliveries.
Yes, immediately and without notice.
oe: Waivers of future performance are retractable.

Correct. Under § 2-209(5) a waiver of an executory portion may be retracted by reasonable notification that strict performance will be required, unless that would be unjust because of a material change of position in reliance.
Retraction is unilateral.
Retraction works going forward; past claims depend on § 2-607(3)(a) notice and whether the conduct waived them.
Reasonable notification is required.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — Retracting a waiver

q: A buyer is sued for infringement over goods it bought. What must it do to preserve its warranty claim against the seller?
o: Nothing; notice is required only for quality defects.
Win the infringement suit first, then sue the seller for its costs.
Sue the seller within 30 days.
Return the goods to the seller.
Notify the seller within a reasonable time.
oe: Section 2-607(3)(b) addresses infringement suits.
Not required.
No such deadline.
Not required.
Correct. Section 2-607(3)(b): otherwise it is barred from any remedy over for liability established by the litigation.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Buyer sued for infringement

q: Payment is due on delivery. The seller delivers and demands payment; the buyer takes the goods but doesn't pay. Under § 2-507(2):
o: the buyer gets 30 days of credit by default.
the seller may only sue for the price.
the buyer owns the goods outright once they're delivered.
the buyer's right to keep the goods depends on paying.
title could never have passed.
oe: No credit is presumed.
It may have a right to reclaim.
Its right is conditional.
Correct. Where payment is due and demanded on delivery, the buyer's right to retain or dispose of the goods is conditional on paying, so the seller may be able to reclaim them (a "cash sale").
Title can pass; the buyer's right against the seller is conditional.
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — Payment due on delivery not made

q: What do most courts require to find a term unconscionable?
o: Only substantive unconscionability: a one-sided term is enough.
Proof that the complaining party is a consumer.
Only procedural unconscionability, such as fine print.
Both procedural and substantive unconscionability.
A price at least twice the seller's cost.
oe: Most courts want some procedural element too.
Most successful claims are consumer cases, but status isn't an element.
Most courts want an oppressive term as well.

Correct. Procedural (unfair surprise: fine print, no meaningful choice, unequal bargaining power) plus substantive (oppressive, one-sided terms). Some courts use a sliding scale, so much of one offsets little of the other. Comment 1: "prevention of oppression and unfair surprise."
There is no such formula; the text prefers comparing price to value, not cost.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Procedural and substantive

q: Debra buys a used sofa for $80 at her neighbor's garage sale. Which statement is correct?
o: Article 2 governs, but no implied warranty of merchantability arises.
Article 2 governs, and every seller impliedly warrants merchantability.
Article 2 doesn't apply because neither party is a merchant.
The common law governs because the price is under $500.
Article 2 governs only the title warranty, and the common law governs everything else.
oe: Correct. Article 2 applies to consumer-to-consumer sales (Problem 1-4, Bev Smith v. Atwell), but § 2-314 requires a seller who is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind.
Wrong. Only a merchant in goods of that kind makes the § 2-314 warranty. Every seller makes the title warranty.
Wrong. Article 2's scope never depends on merchant status.
The $500 threshold is the statute of frauds, not scope.
Wrong. Article 2 governs the whole sale.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Garage-sale sofa

q: Under "F.A.S. vessel" at a named port, the seller must:
o: deliver alongside and tender a receipt.
insure the goods to the destination.
load the goods on board.
pay the ocean freight to the destination port.
deliver the goods to the buyer's door.
oe: Correct. Section 2-319(2): deliver alongside in the usual manner (or on a dock the buyer designates) and obtain and tender a receipt in exchange for which the carrier must issue a bill of lading.
That's C.I.F.
That's F.O.B. vessel.
That's C.I.F. or C. & F.
No.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — F.A.S.

q: A merchant tells a customer in person, "I'll hold this price for 30 days." On day 10 the merchant revokes. What result?
o: The revocation is effective.
The revocation is ineffective because the customer is a merchant.
The revocation is ineffective for a reasonable time, up to three months.
The revocation is ineffective because a merchant's assurance binds for the time stated.
The revocation is effective only if the customer hadn't started preparing to perform.
oe: Correct. A firm offer needs a signed record. An oral assurance without consideration isn't a firm offer, so the offer remained revocable.
The offeree's status doesn't create a firm offer.
That applies only to a written, signed firm offer.
Only an assurance in a signed record does.
Preparation isn't acceptance unless the offer invited acceptance by performance.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Oral promise to hold a price

q: When is a delegate liable to the other party to the original contract?
o: Never; only the delegator is liable.
Always, once a delegation occurs.
Only if the other party consented.
When it assumes the duty.
Only if it's a merchant.
oe: It is if it assumed.
Only if it assumes the duty.
Consent isn't the trigger.
Correct. The other party is then an intended beneficiary of the promise; it gets only one satisfaction. An assignee "of the contract" who accepts makes such a promise (§ 2-210(5)).
Irrelevant.
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — When a delegate is liable

q: A mower's warranty says it "will start on the first pull for five years." It stops starting 4.5 years after tender, and the buyer sues promptly. Is the suit timely?
o: No. Warranty claims accrue on tender, and four years have passed.
Yes. The claim accrued on discovery of the breach.
Yes, because implied warranties last as long as the goods.
No, because the statement is puffing.
Yes, because the parties effectively extended the limitations period.
oe: That's the default, but this warranty explicitly extends to future performance.
Correct. A warranty that explicitly extends to future performance accrues on discovery (§ 2-725(2)), not on tender.
This is an express warranty, and implied warranty claims accrue on tender.
A specific promise about future performance is a warranty.
Parties can shorten the period to one year but can't extend it.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Warranty of future performance

q: The same retailer's form also says the supplier may never demand assurance or suspend its performance. Is that enforceable?
o: Void because the retailer is a merchant.
Enforceable only if the supplier is a merchant.
Vulnerable as unconscionable.
Clearly enforceable; it's just a waiver.
Clearly void; § 2-609 can never be waived.
oe: Not the test.
Not the test.

Correct. Problem 6-4, Clause 1: arguably a permissible waiver, but imposed by a party with overwhelming market power it's exposed to § 2-302 and good-faith attacks. The supplier also keeps its rights on an actual repudiation or insolvency.
Arguable, but vulnerable.
It's not that clear.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Total waiver of § 2-609
pre: A big retailer's form lets it demand from its supplier, "whenever it desires," "whatever assurances [it] deems appropriate," and suspend meanwhile. Effect?

q: Which is NOT an example of a limited remedy failing of its essential purpose?
o: A replacement period that ends before a latent defect can surface.
Repair-or-replace where repeated repairs never fix the defect.
A repair remedy the seller performs promptly and successfully.
Replacement parts only, when one defect destroys the whole machine.
A store-credit remedy from a retailer that goes bankrupt.
oe: An example.
Classic (Razor; Adams v. J.I. Case).
Correct. If the remedy works, it hasn't failed. When one does fail, the buyer gets ordinary UCC remedies (§ 2-719(2)).
Classic.
Problem 5-7 (the Circuit City example).
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Failure of essential purpose examples

q: Payment was to be by transfer from the buyer's bank, which regulators seize, freezing the account. The seller is ready to deliver. Which is correct?
o: The buyer is excused because the government caused the problem.
The seller must deliver on credit.
The seller must wait until the account is unfrozen.
The contract is avoided under § 2-613.
The buyer isn't excused and must offer an equivalent way to pay.
oe: Section 2-614(2) doesn't excuse the buyer.
It may withhold.
It may demand an equivalent.
No casualty to goods.

Correct. Section 2-614(2) (Problem 6-8(b)): if the agreed means of payment fails because of governmental regulation, the seller may withhold delivery unless the buyer provides a commercially substantial equivalent.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Frozen bank account

q: A contingency whose non-occurrence was a basic assumption makes a seller's performance impracticable. What else must the seller do for its delay or nondelivery not to be a breach?
o: Prove the event was unforeseeable in every respect.
Deliver to its regular customers first, then to contract buyers.
Seasonably notify the buyer and, if capacity is partly affected, allocate fairly.
Pay the buyer's cover costs.
Get the buyer's written consent.
oe: Foreseeability matters but isn't decisive.
Allocation must be fair and reasonable.
Correct. Section 2-615(b)-(c). Good-faith compliance with a governmental regulation is also a basis under (a).
Excused nondelivery isn't a breach.
Not required.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Section 2-615 conditions

q: Under an F.A.S. term, the buyer never tells the seller which vessel, berth or sailing date to use. Effect?
o: The seller must choose a vessel and bear the risk until it sails.
The contract is void for indefiniteness.
It's a failure of cooperation that excuses the seller's resulting delay.
The seller must deliver to the buyer's warehouse instead.
Risk passes to the buyer immediately at contracting.
oe: The buyer's failure is the problem.
No.
Correct. Section 2-319(3): the buyer must seasonably give needed instructions; failing to do so is a failure of cooperation under § 2-311.
No.
Not as such; the seller is excused and may proceed reasonably.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — F.A.S. buyer gives no instructions

q: A C.I.F. buyer pays against the documents without reservation. When the goods arrive, they have a defect the documents didn't show. Which is correct?
o: It must sue the carrier instead of rejecting.
Paying against the documents was an acceptance.
It may reject only for defects shown in the documents.
It can't reject anything once it has paid.
It can still inspect and reject.
oe: Rejection is available for nonconforming goods.
Payment isn't acceptance.
Backwards: those are the ones it can't later raise.
It may still reject.

Correct. Agreeing to pay against documents waives inspection before payment, not before acceptance (§ 2-512(2)). Paying without reservation bars recovery only for defects apparent on the documents (§ 2-605(2)).
topic: VIII · Inspection, acceptance, rejection & cure (§§ 2-508, 2-512, 2-513, 2-601 to 2-612) — Paying against documents

q: Which statement about unconscionability is NOT correct?
o: Parties can't contract out of § 2-302.
Most successful claims involve consumers.
A disclaimer that satisfies § 2-316 can't be unconscionable.
Courts are generally reluctant to interfere with freedom of contract.
Comparing price to value is more telling than comparing price to cost.
oe: True (Problem 5-1(b)).
True, e.g., Williams v. Walker-Thomas; modern cases often involve consumer arbitration clauses.
Correct. This is false. Complying with § 2-316 is necessary but not always sufficient; a compliant disclaimer can still be unconscionable.
True.
True, per the text's Problem 2-15.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Unconscionability: true and false

q: Problem 3-10(b) cites Webster v. Blue Ship Tea Room against Mexicali Rose and Schafer for a diner who chokes on a bone in a restaurant's salmon fillet. What question do the cases frame?
o: Whether the diner relied on the chef's skill and judgment in choosing the dish.
Whether a fillet with a bone is fit for ordinary use.
Whether the restaurant disclaimed fitness.
Whether serving food for value is a sale.
Whether a restaurant can be a merchant.
oe: That's fitness.
Correct. Serving food for value is a sale (§ 2-314(1)); the cases disagree on how to measure merchantability for things like bones in food.
No disclaimer is involved.
The statute settles that it is.
It is a merchant in food.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Bone in the fillet

q: A buyer tenders a personal check for the price. The seller wants cash. Which is correct?
o: The seller may demand cash but must allow time to get it.
A check is absolute payment once it is handed over to the seller.
The buyer is in breach at once for not bringing cash.
The seller may cancel the contract immediately.
The seller must take the check.
oe: Correct. Payment by any means current in the ordinary course is sufficient unless the seller demands legal tender and gives a reasonable extension of time to procure it (§ 2-511(2)).
Payment by check is conditional (§ 2-511(3)).
A check is an ordinary-course means.
It must allow time.
It may demand legal tender.
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — Check or cash

q: Which statement about the warranty against infringement is correct?
o: Any seller of goods makes it.
It applies to a one-time seller who doesn't regularly deal in such goods.
"As is" clearly disclaims it under § 2-316(3)(a).
It arises "unless otherwise agreed"; how to disclaim it is unclear.
It can be disclaimed only by specific language, exactly like title.
oe: Only merchants regularly dealing in the goods (cmt. 3: none from a non-dealer).
A non-dealer makes no infringement warranty.
That's unsettled.
Correct. Nothing says how the agreement must be shown, and it's unclear whether it is an "implied" warranty subject to § 2-316(3).
Section 2-312(2) speaks only of the title warranty in subsection (1).
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Disclaiming noninfringement

q: Under § 2-106(1), a "sale" is:
o: the identification of existing goods to a contract.
the passing of title from seller to buyer for a price.
a promise to deliver goods at some future time.
any transaction in goods, including a lease or a bailment.
the delivery of possession of goods in exchange for a price.
oe: Identification (§ 2-501) is a separate concept that gives the buyer an insurable interest.
Correct. A "contract for sale" includes a present sale and a contract to sell at a future time; a "present sale" is one accomplished by making the contract.
That is a contract to sell, which is one kind of contract for sale, not the definition of "sale."
Leases and bailments transfer possession without title; they aren't sales.
Possession isn't the test; a sale passes title.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Definition of "sale"

q: Which statement about express warranties is NOT correct?
o: A seller's opinion becomes a warranty if the buyer relied on it.
A sample from the bulk warrants that the whole of the goods will conform to it.
Statements made at delivery can be warranties without new consideration.
The seller needn't intend to make a warranty.
Oral statements can be warranties.
oe: Correct. This is false. An affirmation merely of value, or the seller's opinion or commendation, doesn't create a warranty, whatever the buyer's reliance (§ 2-313(2)).
True: cmt. 7.
True.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Express warranties: false statement

q: In Roth Steel v. Sharon Steel, why was Sharon's price increase unenforceable?
o: Sharon got it by threatening to stop shipping.
The modification lacked consideration.
Sharon proved impracticability under § 2-615, which made the increase unnecessary.
Sharon wasn't losing money, so no ordinary merchant would have sought it.
Roth never signed a written modification.
oe: Correct. Sharon passed the objective prong (the market shift made the deal a loss) but failed honesty in fact: its threat was coercion, and its contract-based excuse surfaced only at trial.
Section 2-209(1) dispenses with consideration.
The district court rejected Sharon's § 2-615 defense.
The court found the objective prong satisfied.
The problem was bad faith, not form.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — Roth Steel holding

q: A seller never demanded assurance before its buyer repudiated. The buyer argues the seller should have used § 2-609 first. Result?
o: The seller recovers only half its damages.
The argument fails; § 2-609 is optional.
The repudiation is cured by the missing demand.
The argument wins; a demand is a precondition to suing.
The seller must now wait 30 days before suing.
oe: No.
Correct. Section 2-609 permits, but never requires, a demand.
No.
It isn't.
No.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Must you demand first?

q: A seller sends a carpet sample and a form stating "Seller makes no express warranties." The buyer inspects the sample and signs. The delivered carpet doesn't match the sample. Does the disclaimer protect the seller?
o: Yes, because express warranties are disclaimed like implied ones.
Yes, if the disclaimer is conspicuous.
Only if the form mentions the sample by name.
Yes, because the buyer signed it.
No, if the sample was part of the basis of the bargain.
oe: They're nearly impossible to disclaim.
Conspicuousness doesn't matter here.
Not the test.
Signing doesn't save an irreconcilable disclaimer.

Correct. Words creating a warranty and words negating it are read consistently where reasonable; where they can't be, the negation is inoperative (§ 2-316(1)). A general disclaimer can't cut down the seller's obligation as to the sample or description.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Sample plus "no express warranties"

q: A seller's quote (the offer) limits suits to one year. The buyer's purchase order "accepts," but boilerplate on the back says acceptance "is expressly limited to the terms of this order." Under the view Daitom adopted, the purchase order is:
o: a counteroffer, because any term that materially favors the buyer makes acceptance conditional.
a rejection, because it conflicts with the quote's one-year term.
an acceptance only after the seller ships.
an acceptance, because the boilerplate doesn't clearly say the buyer won't proceed otherwise.
a counteroffer, because it is expressly limited to its own terms.
oe: That is the Roto-Lith view, which Daitom rejected.
Under § 2-207(1), a response with different terms can still accept.
If it is an acceptance, the contract forms on the writings themselves.

Correct. Daitom followed Dorton: to be "expressly conditional," the offeree must clearly communicate it is unwilling to proceed unless its terms are accepted. This boilerplate isn't enough, so the PO is an acceptance under § 2-207(1).
That reading would revive the mirror-image rule; Daitom rejected it.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Expressly conditional acceptance

q: Which exclusion of consequential damages is prima facie unconscionable under § 2-719(3)?
o: Any exclusion in a merchant-to-merchant contract.
One excluding a business buyer's lost profits.
One excluding damage to a factory's equipment.
One excluding the cost of cover.
One excluding personal-injury damages from a consumer product.
oe: Generally fine.
Commercial loss: not prima facie unconscionable.
Commercial loss.
Not personal injury.
Correct. A limitation for injury to the person in the case of consumer goods is prima facie unconscionable; a limitation of commercial loss is not.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Prima facie unconscionable exclusion

q: A small bakery's requirements contract for flour is assigned by the bakery to a national bakery chain. The seller objects. Likely result?
o: It's ineffective only if the contract bans assignment.
It's effective if the bakery remains liable.
It's effective because the seller's consent is never needed.
The assignment is likely ineffective.
It's effective; rights are always freely assignable.
oe: The statutory limit applies anyway.
Remaining liable doesn't cure a material change.
The materiality limit applies.

Correct. Rights are assignable unless the assignment would materially change the other party's duty, materially increase its burden or risk, or materially impair its chance of return performance (§ 2-210(2)). A requirements buyer swapping in a much larger buyer is the classic example (cmt. 4).
Not if it materially changes the seller's burden.
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — Assignment of a requirements buyer's rights

q: A dealer sells a used car with hidden flood damage that it didn't know about. Breach of merchantability?
o: No, because the car is used.
Likely yes; the dealer's ignorance doesn't matter.
No, because the dealer didn't know.
Only under fitness for a particular purpose.
Only if the buyer inspected the car before buying.
oe: Used goods carry a reduced, not absent, warranty.
Correct. Text Problem 3-10(G): a flood-damaged car is likely unmerchantable even for used goods, and the dealer's ignorance is irrelevant to strict warranty liability (though relevant to fraud).
Knowledge doesn't matter.
Merchantability applies.
An inspection that couldn't reveal it doesn't matter.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Hidden flood damage

q: A contract is silent on where delivery happens, but in eight prior deals the seller always delivered to the buyer's dock. Does § 2-308's default (the seller's place) apply?
o: No, because the contract fails for indefiniteness.
Yes, because gap fillers override course of dealing.
No, because course of dealing fills the term.
Yes, because the express terms are silent on delivery.
Only if the buyer gave notice of the course of dealing.
oe: It doesn't fail; the term is supplied.
Backwards; gap fillers come last.

Correct. Gap fillers apply only if the agreement, including course of dealing and usage of trade, leaves a gap. Problem 3-8(B): with a history of seller delivery, the seller breached by refusing to deliver.
The agreement includes course of dealing.
Notice under § 1-303(g) is for usage of trade.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — No gap, no gap filler

q: In Daitom, the seller's offer required suits within one year of delivery; the buyer's acceptance reserved "all rights and remedies available at law." The buyer sued about three years after delivery. What happened?
o: The seller's one-year term controlled, because the seller made the offer.
The buyer's term controlled, because its form was the last one sent.
The suit was barred because the buyer let the dryers sit crated for a year.
Both terms applied, so the shorter one controlled.
Both terms dropped out and the UCC's four-year period applied.
oe: That was the district court's (and the dissent's) view. The majority applied the knock-out rule.
Article 2 rejects the last-shot rule.
The court stressed that the one-year period would have run before the dryers were even installed, which supported its fairness reasoning.
Conflicting terms can't both apply.
Correct. The terms conflicted, so under the knock-out rule (cmt. 6) neither applied, and § 2-725's four years filled the gap. The suit was timely; summary judgment for Pennwalt was reversed.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Daitom result

q: Which statement about § 2-719(3) and personal injury is correct?
o: The presumption can never be rebutted.
It voids every warranty disclaimer in consumer sales.
Article 2 defines "personal injury" in § 2-103.
A seller that validly disclaims warranties may avoid the presumption.
It applies to commercial buyers as well as consumers.
oe: It's prima facie, so rebuttable.
It addresses remedy limitations.
It's undefined.
Correct. If there's no warranty, there's no contract liability to limit (§ 2-719 cmt. 3), though tort law may still apply. Article 2 doesn't define "personal injury"; other law does.
Consumer goods only.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Sidestepping § 2-719(3)

q: On March 1, Fern signs a contract stating that she "hereby sells" to Glen the 12 chairs she will build in June. What is the legal effect?
o: It is a present sale, because the contract says Fern "hereby sells" the chairs.
It is a bailment until the chairs are built and delivered.
It isn't a sale of goods, because the chairs aren't movable things yet.
It is a services contract, because Fern must still build the chairs.
It operates as a contract to sell.
oe: The label can't make a present sale of goods that don't exist yet.
Nothing is entrusted to anyone; this is a contract for sale.
Goods include specially manufactured and future goods; movability is judged at identification.
Making the goods is part of supplying specially manufactured goods; the deal is for chairs.
Correct. Goods that are not both existing and identified are "future" goods, and a purported present sale of future goods operates as a contract to sell (§ 2-105(2)).
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Present sale of future goods

q: Which is NOT a seller's duty under a C.I.F. term?
o: Preparing an invoice and other required documents.
Bearing the risk of loss until the goods arrive.
Putting the goods in the carrier's possession and getting a negotiable bill of lading.
Obtaining insurance payable to the buyer.
Forwarding and tendering the documents to the buyer.
oe: Correct. C.I.F. is a shipment contract: risk passes at shipment, even though the seller pays freight and insurance.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — C.I.F. seller's duties

q: Under Roth Steel's two-part test, which fact satisfies the OBJECTIVE prong of good faith in seeking a modification?
o: The seller offered a token payment as consideration.
The buyer had no other source of supply.
Unforeseen market changes have made performance a loss.
The seller threatened to stop performing unless paid more.
The seller honestly believed it could sell elsewhere for more.
oe: A technical consideration can't support a bad-faith modification (cmt. 2).
That shows the buyer's vulnerability, not a legitimate reason.
Correct. The single most important consideration is whether market changes or other unforeseeable conditions have made performance unprofitable, so an ordinary merchant would seek a change.
That goes to the subjective prong, and it's evidence of bad faith.
A chance to profit elsewhere isn't a reason an ordinary merchant would seek a modification.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — Roth Steel objective prong

q: Which event is LEAST likely to excuse a seller under § 2-615?
o: A local crop failure that destroys its expected supply.
An embargo that cuts off its only source.
An unforeseen shutdown of major sources of supply.
War that shuts down major supply sources.
A sharp rise in the market price of its raw materials.
oe: Can excuse.
Can excuse.
Can excuse.
Can excuse.
Correct. Comment 4: increased cost alone doesn't excuse, and a rise or collapse in the market is exactly the risk fixed-price contracts cover (Problem 6-9).
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Least likely excuse

q: A contract bars either party from assigning any rights. After the seller totally breaches, the buyer assigns its damages claim to a collection firm. Is the assignment effective?
o: Only if the claim is under $500.
Yes; that kind of right is assignable despite a ban.
Only if the seller consents.
No, because damages claims are things in action.
No; the ban covers all rights.
oe: No such rule.

Correct. A right to damages for breach of the whole contract, or a right arising from the assignor's due performance of its entire obligation, can be assigned despite agreement otherwise (§ 2-210(2)).
Not needed.
Things in action aren't goods, but they can be assigned.
This kind of right is assignable despite a ban.
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — Damages claim assigned despite a ban

q: Which statement about merchant status is NOT correct?
o: The $500 writing requirement of § 2-201(1) applies only between merchants.
Additional terms in an acceptance can join the contract without assent only between merchants.
A NOM clause on a merchant's form must be separately signed by a non-merchant.
The confirmation exception requires both parties to be merchants.
Only the offeror must be a merchant for a firm offer.
oe: Correct. This is false. Section 2-201(1) applies to every sale of goods for $500 or more (Casazza). Only the confirmation exception in § 2-201(2) is limited to merchants.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — Merchant-only rules

q: In Top of Iowa Coop v. Sime Farms, what supplied reasonable grounds for insecurity?
o: Nothing; the court found no reasonable grounds.
A late delivery under a different contract.
The Coop's own financial trouble.
The inverted market, the AG's statement and Sime's silence.
Sime's written refusal to deliver, sent before any demand was made.
oe: The jury found grounds, and it was affirmed.
Not the basis.
Not the basis.

Correct. Grounds are objective and needn't come from the other party's own conduct. Sime had rolled its hedge-to-arrive deliveries, sold its corn elsewhere, faced a $1.30 inverse, and never got back to the Coop.
Sime's lawyer refused only after the demand.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Top of Iowa grounds

q: Which buyer gets good title, free of the original owner's claim?
o: A good-faith buyer for value from a bounced-check buyer.
A buyer from a pawnshop that took the goods in pledge from a thief.
A buyer who knew the owner was disputing its seller's title.
A donee who received the goods from someone who got them by fraud.
A good-faith buyer for value from a thief.
oe: Correct. Delivery for a dishonored check gives voidable title, which can pass good title to a good-faith purchaser for value (§ 2-403(1)(b)).
Void title, and a pawnshop purchase isn't a buyer-in-ordinary-course purchase anyway.
Not in good faith.
A donee gives no value.
A thief has void title.
topic: VI · Title, entrustment & infringement (§§ 2-312, 2-401, 2-403) — Who gets good title

q: A buyer claims the salesperson orally made an express warranty; the signed writing says "no warranties, express or implied." What is the seller's best tool?
o: The "as is" rule of § 2-316(3)(a).
The statute of frauds.
§ 2-719's limitation of remedies.
The parol evidence rule.
§ 2-316(2), because the disclaimer is conspicuous.
oe: "As is" doesn't reach express warranties.
The SOF governs enforceability of the contract, not oral warranty terms.
A limitation doesn't negate a warranty.

Correct. Section 2-316(1) is "subject to" § 2-202. If the writing is final on warranties, evidence of prior or contemporaneous oral warranties that contradict it is excluded (Problem 5-13). Comment 2 also notes "lack of authority" clauses.
(2) is for implied warranties.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Seller's defense to oral warranty

q: Which statement about risk of loss is correct?
o: It falls on whichever party caused the casualty.
It passes to the buyer when title passes.
It decides who bears a casualty to the goods, and it doesn't follow title.
It stays with the seller until the buyer pays.
It is the same question as whether either party breached.
oe: Causation by a party is a fault question; risk rules handle casualties no one caused.
That was the pre-Code approach.
Correct. Risk of loss is about who absorbs a fire, theft or flood. It isn't the same as performance or breach, and Article 2 ties it to tender and breach, not title (§ 2-401).
Payment doesn't move risk.
Related (§ 2-510) but different.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — What risk of loss is

q: A buyer pays by check and the seller delivers. The check bounces on presentment. What is the effect between buyer and seller?
o: The payment is defeated.
The seller must redeposit the check before doing anything else.
The buyer has paid; the seller can sue only on the check.
The buyer never got title, so no later purchaser can get any.
The contract is void.
oe: Correct. Payment by check is conditional and is defeated as between the parties by dishonor on due presentment (§ 2-511(3)). (The buyer still gets voidable title, which it can pass to a good-faith purchaser for value under § 2-403(1)(b).)
Not required.
Payment by check is conditional.
The buyer has voidable title.
The buyer is in breach for nonpayment.
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — Bounced check

q: A signed record for one skid loader at $20,000 says nothing about delivery, and the parties have no history. The buyer demands delivery; the seller says pick it up. The buyer refuses to pick up or pay. Who breached?
o: The seller, because a seller must deliver to the buyer unless agreed otherwise.
Neither, because the contract fails without a delivery term.
Neither; each must bear half the delivery cost.
The buyer, by refusing to pick up and pay.
The seller, because tender requires transporting the goods.
oe: The default is the seller's place.
Gap fillers supply the term.
No such rule.
Correct. The contract is enforceable (intent plus a basis for a remedy), and § 2-308(a) makes the seller's place of business the place of delivery. The buyer's refusal is the breach.
Tender requires holding conforming goods at the buyer's disposition with notice.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — Problem 3-8(A) skid loader

q: States choose among three versions of § 2-318. Which is the narrowest?
o: Alternative B.
Whichever the seller selects in the contract.
Alternative C.
They're the same; the letters show only which states adopted them.
Alternative A.
oe: Broader than A.
States choose; the seller can't exclude § 2-318.
The broadest.
They differ in scope.

Correct. A: natural persons in the buyer's family or household, or guests in the home, injured in person. B: any natural person reasonably expected to use, consume or be affected, injured in person. C: any person reasonably expected to be affected, for any injury. The seller can't exclude the section's coverage.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Narrowest § 2-318 alternative

q: Which of the following is NOT "goods" under § 2-105(1)?
o: A lottery ticket, a right to claim a prize.
A machine the seller must specially manufacture for the buyer.
Liquid oxygen sold to fill hospital tanks.
A calf not yet born.
Wheat now growing in the seller's field.
oe: Correct. A lottery ticket is a thing in action, a right to claim a prize, which § 2-105(1) excludes along with investment securities and the money in which the price is paid.
Goods. The definition expressly includes specially manufactured goods.
Goods. Liquids and gases are movable things (Problem 1-1).
Goods. Section 2-105(1) includes the unborn young of animals.
Goods. Growing crops are included.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — What counts as goods

q: Courts take several approaches when an acceptance states terms "different" from (in conflict with) the offer's. Which is NOT one of them?
o: Apply the knock-out rule drawn from comment 6, as Daitom did.
The later form controls, because it was the last shot.
Knock out both conflicting terms and fill the gap with the UCC.
Treat them like additional terms, so they drop out as material alterations.
Let them simply fall out because § 2-207(2) mentions only additional terms.
oe: The same approach; Daitom preferred it.
Correct. The last-shot rule was the common-law result that § 2-207 abolished.
One approach: the knock-out rule.
One approach; the offeror's terms then control.
One approach; the offeror's terms control.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Approaches to different terms

q: Which is NOT one of the principles behind the risk-of-loss rules (§ 2-509 cmt. 3)?
o: The party in breach should bear it.
The party in control of the goods should bear it.
The party that has paid more of the price should bear the risk.
The party most likely to have insurance should bear it.
None of the above.
oe: A principle.
A principle.
Correct. Payment isn't a principle. The three are: the party in control (best able to avoid loss), the party most likely insured, and the party in breach (§ 2-510).
A principle.
One of the other choices is correct: The party that has paid more of the price should bear the risk.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Principles behind the rules

q: Which is NOT an element of a course of performance under § 1-303(a)?
o: The other party accepts or acquiesces in it without objection.
The other party has an opportunity to object.
The agreement involves repeated occasions for performance.
The conduct occurred in the parties' earlier contracts.
The other party knows the nature of the performance.
oe: An element.
An element.
An element.
Correct. Conduct in previous transactions is course of dealing (§ 1-303(b)), which comes before contracting. Course of performance arises under this contract, after contracting.
An element.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Elements of course of performance

q: A seller grants its bank a security interest in its rights under a sales contract. Does that materially change the buyer's duty?
o: Yes; any security interest in the contract is a material change.
No, unless enforcing it delegates material performance.
Yes, unless the buyer consents.
Only if the bank is a merchant.
No, and the buyer can never object.
oe: Not under § 2-210(3).
Correct. Section 2-210(3). Even then the security interest stays effective, but the seller is liable for any resulting damages and a court may grant other relief.
No consent needed.
Irrelevant.
If enforcement delegates material performance, it can.
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — Security interest in seller's rights

q: How might a seller rebut the presumption that excluding consumer personal-injury damages is unconscionable?
o: Show the injury was severe.
Show the buyer didn't read the clause.
Show the buyer took a lower price to assume the risk.
Show the clause was printed in bold capital letters on page one.
Show the seller is a large company.
oe: That cuts against the seller.
That cuts against the seller.
Correct. Problem 5-8 themes: a bargained price for the risk, obvious inherent dangers, extensive warnings and negotiated terms.
Conspicuousness alone doesn't rebut it.
Irrelevant.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Rebutting the presumption

q: What did the textbook note about Man Industries v. Midcontinent (Tex. App. 2013)?
o: A seller needn't face a loss to seek a price increase in good faith.
It adopted Roth Steel's two-part test, loss requirement and all.
It held a threat to stop performing is always lawful.
It held NOM clauses unenforceable between merchants.
It held modifications always require consideration.
oe: Correct. The text then asks whether cmt. 2 is right at all, since § 1-304 covers performance and enforcement and § 2-209's text doesn't mention good faith.
It departed from the loss requirement.
Not its holding.
Not its holding.
No.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — Man Industries

q: A requirements contract states an estimate of 10,000 units a year. Which demand may the seller refuse?
o: A demand for 11,000 to meet the buyer's steady growth.
An honest demand for 30,000 after the buyer lands a huge new customer.
A good-faith demand for 10,500.
A good-faith demand for 9,000 units after a slow first quarter.
A demand for 10,000, spread unevenly across the year's twelve months.
oe: Normal good-faith growth is within the contract.

Correct. Section 2-306(1) has two limits: good faith, and no quantity "unreasonably disproportionate to any stated estimate." An honest demand can still fail the second (Problem 4-2(A)). The estimate is the center around which variation is expected.
Close to the estimate and in good faith.
Close to the estimate and in good faith.
Timing within the year isn't a disproportion problem.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Honest but disproportionate demand

q: Goods are shipped "F.O.B. seller's city." The contract says nothing about when payment is due. When is it due?
o: Before shipment.
When the seller sends its invoice.
When the seller delivers the goods to the carrier.
Within 30 days of the invoice.
None of the above.
oe: Not by default.
Not the trigger.
That's when risk passes, not when payment is due.
No credit is presumed.

Correct. None of these. Unless otherwise agreed, payment is due at the time and place the buyer is to receive the goods, "even though the place of shipment is the place of delivery" (§ 2-310(a)), and the buyer may inspect after arrival before paying (§ 2-310(b); Problem 4-8).
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — When payment is due

q: The Coop demanded, as assurance, payment of margins (or a letter of credit) and a signed promise to deliver. Was that demand itself a repudiation?
o: Not as a matter of law; the jury could find it reasonable.
No, because Sime had already breached.
Yes; any demand beyond the contract is a repudiation.
Yes, because the contracts were illegal.
Yes, because letters of credit are never adequate assurance.
oe: Correct. "All demands for adequate assurance call for more than was originally promised," and a demand for more than the contract calls for isn't in itself a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2).
The issue was the demand's reasonableness.
Not by itself.
The jury rejected that defense.
They're common assurances.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Top of Iowa demand
pre: In Top of Iowa Coop v. Sime Farms, what supplied reasonable grounds for insecurity?

q: A seller's sole contemplated supplier fails because of a fire. When is the seller excused?
o: Always; the failure was beyond its control.
Only if the buyer named the supplier.
Never; supplier failures are the seller's risk.
Only if it took all due measures to secure it.
Only under § 2-613.
oe: Due measures are required.
"Contemplated" source suffices.
Can excuse if due measures were taken.
Correct. Comment 5 (§ 2-615, not § 2-613). An excused seller must also turn over its rights against the defaulting supplier to the buyer.
Section 2-615.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Failure of a contemplated source

q: How does a "C. & F." term differ from "C.I.F."?
o: It's a destination contract.
The buyer may inspect before paying.
The seller has no duty to insure.
The seller bears the risk in transit.
The buyer pays the freight.
oe: Still a shipment contract.
It pays against documents.
Correct. C. & F. (cost and freight) is C.I.F. minus the insurance obligation. Both are shipment contracts in which the buyer pays against documents.
The buyer does.
The price includes freight.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — C. & F. vs. C.I.F.

q: On the disclaimer "continuum of protection" in the slides, which transaction calls for the MOST protection for the buyer?
o: A merchant-to-merchant sale of commercial goods.
A manufacturer buying specially made commercial goods.
A custom equipment deal between two manufacturers.
A sale of used goods.
A consumer buying prepackaged new goods.
oe: Near the freedom end.
The freedom-of-contract end.
The freedom-of-contract end.
In the middle.
Correct. The continuum runs from freedom of contract (specially made commercial goods) through merchant-to-merchant commercial goods and used goods to paternalism (prepackaged new consumer goods).
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Continuum of protection

q: In Pittsburgh-Des Moines Steel v. Brookhaven Manor, why did the "assurance" demands fail?
o: The demand came after the 30-day period.
They sought to redraft the deal, beyond adequate assurance.
PDM had no grounds at all for insecurity about Brookhaven's financing.
Letters of credit can't be demanded.
The demands weren't in writing.
oe: Not the problem.

Correct. PDM would be "assured" only by a personal guarantee, escrow financing or an ownership interest, which was more than adequate assurance as a matter of law. Section 2-609 "does not give the alarmed party a right to redraft the contract."
The problem was the scope of the demand.
No letter of credit was involved.
Not the problem identified.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — PDM v. Brookhaven

q: Under an "ex-ship" term, when does risk of loss pass to the buyer?
o: When they leave the ship's tackle or are unloaded.
When the ship sails.
When the goods finally reach the buyer's own warehouse.
When the goods are loaded on the ship.
When the buyer receives the documents.
oe: Correct. Section 2-322: delivery is from a ship that has reached the usual unloading place at the named port; the seller must also discharge carriers' liens and furnish a direction to deliver. It works like a destination term.
No.
Earlier: at unloading.
That's F.O.B. vessel.
No.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Ex-ship

q: A strike was widely expected in the industry when the parties signed. It occurs and slows the seller's output. Does § 2-615 excuse the delay?
o: Only under § 2-614.
Yes; strikes always excuse.
Probably not; a foreshadowed risk was part of the bargain.
Yes, if the seller gives notice.
No, because strikes are never excuses.
oe: Not a delivery-method problem.
Not if foreshadowed.
Correct. Comment 8: no excuse if the contingency was sufficiently foreshadowed to be among the dickered risks. Agreements may enlarge or narrow the exemption.
Notice is required but doesn't create an excuse.
An industry-wide strike can excuse if not foreshadowed.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Foreshadowed contingency

q: A merchant seller's acknowledgment adds a merchantability disclaimer that the merchant buyer's order didn't contain. Before applying § 2-316, what is the seller's first problem?
o: The disclaimer probably isn't part of the contract at all.
The buyer must separately sign it.
The disclaimer fails to mention merchantability.
It isn't conspicuous.
Merchants can't disclaim merchantability to each other.
oe: Correct. A disclaimer is a material alteration (§ 2-207 cmt. 4), so it drops out between merchants absent express assent. Threshold questions: did the warranty arise, and is the disclaimer part of the contract?
That's the NOM-clause rule.
It does mention it.
We don't get there.
They can, by agreement.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Disclaimer in an acknowledgment

q: Which of the following is NOT one of Article 2's gap fillers?
o: § 2-310's time for payment.
§ 2-308's place for delivery.
§ 2-305's open price term.
§ 2-201's signed-record requirement.
§ 2-314's implied warranty of merchantability.
oe: A gap filler.
A gap filler.
A gap filler.

Correct. The statute of frauds is an enforceability rule, not a default term. Gap fillers include §§ 2-304 to 2-311 (price, quantity, lots, place, time, payment, cooperation), the warranties, §§ 2-507 and 2-511, and § 2-512.
A gap filler.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — Which is not a gap filler

q: Goods are destroyed while the seller still bears the risk of loss. When must the seller still deliver?
o: Only if the seller is a merchant.
When the goods are fungible, such as wheat from general stock.
Only if the buyer has already paid.
Never; bearing the risk always excuses the seller.
When the goods were identified at contracting and destroyed without fault.
oe: Merchant status doesn't matter here.

Correct. Fungible goods aren't "identified when the contract is made," so § 2-613 doesn't apply; the seller must tender substitutes or breach. Unique, identified goods destroyed without fault are a different story.
Payment doesn't matter.
Bearing the risk means absorbing the loss, not being excused.
That's the § 2-613 case: the contract is avoided.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Seller with the risk

q: A manufacturer grants a distributor the exclusive right to sell its mowers in Delaware. The contract says nothing about effort. Under § 2-306(2):
o: neither side owes more than honesty and good faith.
each side owes best efforts: to supply, and to promote.
only the manufacturer owes best efforts.
the deal is illusory, since no quantity or effort is stated.
only the distributor owes best efforts.
oe: Section 2-306(2) adds best efforts.
Correct. A lawful exclusive-dealing agreement imposes, unless otherwise agreed, best efforts by the seller to supply the goods and by the buyer to promote their sale.
Both sides do.
Exclusivity plus best efforts supplies the commitment.
Both sides do.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Exclusive dealing

q: In the lumber trade, sellers don't usually shrink-wrap boards. On each of a buyer's last six orders, this seller did. This time it didn't, and rain damaged the lumber. What best supports the buyer's claim that wrapping was required?
o: Nothing; the express terms are silent on wrapping.
Usage of trade.
Course of performance.
Course of dealing.
The implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
oe: Course of dealing fills in what the express terms don't say.
The trade usage is NOT to wrap.
That needs repeated performances under this contract; these were separate earlier orders.
Correct. Conduct in previous transactions between these parties establishes a common basis of understanding and supplements the agreement (§ 1-303(b), (d)). Usage of trade cuts the other way.
Nothing shows a particular purpose or reliance.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Prior orders, new omission

q: What does comment 1 to § 2-719 say about limited remedies?
o: Remedy limits must be conspicuous.
Limited remedies apply only to consumer goods.
Limited remedies are disfavored and presumed exclusive.
Parties may eliminate all remedies.
At least minimum adequate remedies must remain available.
oe: No such rule.
They apply generally.
They're presumed cumulative.
Not entirely.
Correct. It is of the essence of a sales contract that a "fair quantum of remedy" exist; a clause that fails or strips the substantial value of the bargain must give way.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Fair quantum of remedy

q: Two merchants. The buyer's order says nothing about late payment. The seller's acknowledgment adds "1.5% monthly interest on overdue invoices," which is customary in the trade. The buyer says nothing. Is the interest term part of the contract?
o: No, because the acknowledgment was a counteroffer.
No, because additional terms are always mere proposals.
Yes, but only if the buyer signs the acknowledgment.
Yes: between merchants, a non-material term joins unless objected to.
No, because any term adding cost to the buyer is a material alteration.
oe: It's an acceptance that states an additional term.
That's the rule only when a party isn't a merchant.
Silence works between merchants for a non-material term.

Correct. Additional terms are proposals, but between merchants they become part of the contract unless the offer limited acceptance, they materially alter it, or the other side objects. Interest on overdue invoices within trade practice isn't material (cmt. 5).
Comment 5 lists interest on overdue invoices as not material.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Customary interest term between merchants

q: Which item from Problem 1-1 is the clearest example of goods?
o: Excess electricity from a homeowner's solar panels.
1,000 shares of certificated Microsoft stock.
A state lottery ticket.
100,000 yen credited to a brokerage account.
A 1908 gold coin bought from a coin dealer.
oe: A split. Some courts treat electricity as goods once metered; others treat its supply as a service.
Not goods. Investment securities are excluded, even when certificated.
Not goods: a thing in action.
Unlikely goods. A credit entry is a financial asset (a thing in action), not a movable thing.
Correct. Money is excluded only as "the money in which the price is to be paid." A collectible coin is the subject of the sale, not the payment.

q: A seller claims the parties modified their contract. What is the first question?
o: Is the modification unconscionable?
Is the modification in a signed writing?
Did the parties agree to modify, under §§ 2-204 to 2-207?
Is the modification supported by new consideration from the party who benefits?
Does the contract contain a merger clause?
oe: That comes later, if at all.
Only if the SOF or a NOM clause requires one.

Correct. First, was there an agreement to modify (the formation rules apply)? Second, is it enforceable: no consideration needed, but good faith, the SOF (§ 2-209(3)), a NOM clause (§ 2-209(2)) and general defenses like duress can bar it.
Consideration isn't required.
A merger clause addresses prior agreements, not later modifications.

q: Which is NOT required for an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose?
o: The purpose is particular rather than ordinary.
The buyer actually relies on the seller.
The seller has reason to know the buyer is relying on its skill or judgment.
At contracting, the seller has reason to know the buyer's particular purpose.
The seller is a merchant.
oe: Required; ordinary purposes are covered by merchantability.
Required.
Required.
Required. Reason to know is a fact question.
Correct. Fitness can arise even with a non-merchant seller (cmt. 4), though usually it's a merchant with the needed skill.

q: A contract gives the buyer 30 days' credit but doesn't say when the 30 days begin. The seller postdates its invoice. Under § 2-310(d):
o: credit runs from shipment, but postdating delays the start.
credit runs from the contract date.
credit runs from acceptance of the goods.
credit isn't allowed unless the contract states a start date.
credit runs from the buyer's receipt of the goods.
oe: Correct. Where the seller is to ship on credit, the credit period runs from the time of shipment, but postdating the invoice or delaying its dispatch correspondingly delays the start.
From shipment.
From shipment.
The contract allowed credit; § 2-310(d) fills the start date.
From shipment.

q: A seller assigns its right to payment to a bank, and the buyer is notified to pay the bank. The buyer pays the seller anyway. Later the goods prove defective. Which is correct?
o: The buyer owes the bank and loses its defenses.
Paying the seller discharged the buyer.
The buyer still owes the bank, but may raise the defects against it.
The bank must collect from the seller only.
The assignment was void because the buyer never consented.
oe: Defenses survive.
Not after notification.
Correct. After notification, the buyer can discharge its obligation only by paying the assignee (§ 9-406(a)). The assignee steps into the assignor's shoes, so the buyer keeps its defenses.
The buyer remains liable to the bank.
Consent isn't required.

q: For a fitness warranty, must the buyer's reliance on the seller be reasonable?
o: No; reliance isn't an element at all.
Yes; unreasonable reliance defeats the warranty.
No, but it must be actual.
Yes, and it must be shown in writing.
Only if the buyer is a consumer.
oe: Actual reliance is required.
Reasonableness isn't an element.
Correct. Wholly unreasonable reliance may, however, mean the seller had no reason to know of it.
No writing is needed.
Not a factor.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Must reliance be reasonable?

q: A landowner contracts to sell each of the following, and in each case the BUYER will do the severing. Which is goods under § 2-107?
o: Coal to be mined from a seam on the property.
Standing timber the buyer will cut.
Gravel to be dug out of the seller's land.
A barn to be dismantled and hauled away.
Oil and gas under the land.
oe: Not goods: minerals must be severed by the seller.
Correct. Under § 2-107(2), timber to be cut and growing crops are goods whether the buyer or the seller severs them.
Not goods: minerals "or the like" must be severed by the seller.
Not goods under § 2-107(1): a structure is goods only if the seller removes it.
Not goods. Minerals including oil and gas are goods only if the seller severs them (§ 2-107(1)); a buyer's right to extract is an interest in land.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Severance from realty

q: A disclaimer complies with § 2-316. Which is NOT a way it might still fail?
o: A state consumer statute restricting disclaimers.
Unconscionability.
The seller's fraud.
The buyer later regrets the purchase.
Magnuson-Moss, if the seller gave a written warranty.
oe: Can defeat it.
Can defeat it.
Can defeat it (Sorchaga v. Ride Auto).

Correct. Regret isn't a defense. Compliance is necessary but not sufficient: seller fraud can defeat "as is" ("unless the circumstances indicate otherwise"), the clause may be unconscionable, Magnuson-Moss bars a supplier who gives a written warranty from disclaiming implied warranties, and state consumer laws may limit disclaimers.
Can defeat it.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Compliant but still defeated

q: A seller lobbies for a regulation that then makes its own performance impracticable. Is it excused?
o: No; a seller that brings about the regulation loses the excuse.
Yes, unless the buyer objects.
Yes, if the regulation is valid.
Yes; good-faith compliance with regulation excuses.
Only under § 2-614.
oe: Correct. Comment 10: governmental interference must truly supervene; a seller that causes or colludes in the governmental action loses the exemption.
No.
Validity isn't the issue.
Not if the seller caused it.
No.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Seller causes the regulation

q: Which statement about express warranties and gap fillers is correct?
o: They're made by the parties; only § 2-313's creation rules act as gap fillers.
Once an express warranty exists, it displaces every implied warranty and gap filler.
Express warranties fill gaps only in contracts between merchants.
Express warranties are implied by law whenever the contract is silent on quality.
Section 2-313 supplies a quality term whenever the agreement says nothing about quality.
oe: Correct. The text's footnote: express warranties themselves aren't gap fillers.
Express warranties displace only inconsistent implied warranties, and not fitness (§ 2-317).
Merchant status is irrelevant.
That describes implied warranties.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — Express warranties and gap fillers

q: Under § 2-209 cmt. 3, how far does part performance go to satisfy the SOF for an oral modification of a $500-plus contract?
o: To any goods the seller has identified.
To the whole modified contract.
It never applies to modifications.
To the full quantity in the original record.
Only to goods already accepted.
oe: Identification isn't acceptance.
It doesn't reach future deliveries.
It applies to goods accepted.
The original record already covers that; the issue is the modification.
Correct. The "delivery and acceptance" test is limited to the past; a future $500-plus modification can't be conjured up by oral testimony.

q: A contract says "Buyer may not assign this contract." The buyer assigns only its right to receive the goods. Is that barred?
o: It's barred only as to the buyer's right to sue.
Yes, because buyers can never assign the right to goods.
Yes; "this contract" includes every right under it.
Yes, unless the seller consents.
No; the ban reaches only delegation.
oe: No.
They can, subject to § 2-210(2).
Section 2-210(4) reads it narrowly.
It isn't barred at all.
Correct. Unless the circumstances indicate otherwise, a prohibition on assigning "the contract" bars only the delegation of duties, not the assignment of rights (§ 2-210(4)).
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — "May not assign this contract"

q: Risk has passed to the buyer when a fire destroys the goods. The buyer refuses to pay. Result?
o: The buyer owes nothing, since it never got to use the goods.
The contract is avoided under § 2-613.
The parties split the loss.
The seller recovers the price.
The seller must tender replacement goods.
oe: Risk had passed.
Section 2-613 applies only before risk passes.
Article 2 doesn't split losses.
Correct. Section 2-709(1)(a): the seller may recover the price of conforming goods lost or damaged within a commercially reasonable time after risk passed.
It performed; the loss is the buyer's.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Buyer with the risk

q: Which statement about output and requirements terms is correct?
o: They're limited by good faith alone, with no proportionality limit.
Section 2-306 implies a requirements term whenever the quantity is left open.
A requirements term satisfies § 2-201's quantity requirement.
A requirements buyer may demand any quantity in good faith, however large.
They're unenforceable because the quantity is indefinite.
oe: Both limits apply.
It never implies one.
Correct. An output or requirements commitment states a quantity for SOF purposes. Section 2-306 interprets such a term; it never implies one.
Not if unreasonably disproportionate.
Section 2-306 validates them.

q: A seller must deliver 100 bushels and tenders 95, promising 5 more next week. The contract says nothing about lots. Was the tender proper?
o: Yes, because the seller offered to cure.
No, but only if the buyer is a merchant.
Yes, because 95% is substantial performance.
No; the goods must conform and come in a single lot.
Yes, if the seller cuts the price proportionally.
oe: Cure may fix a bad tender; it doesn't make this one proper.
Merchant status doesn't matter.
Perfect tender, not substantial performance, governs.

Correct. Goods conform only if they match the contract (§ 2-106(2)), and § 2-307 requires a single delivery unless otherwise agreed. The buyer may reject (§ 2-601), though the seller may be able to cure (Problem 4-4(a)(1)).
The buyer needn't accept a partial tender.
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — 95 bushels

q: Why should a drafter know whether a contract incorporates Incoterms?
o: They may define the same terms differently from §§ 2-319 to 2-322.
The UCC bans parties from changing shipping terms.
Incoterms apply only to consumer sales.
Incoterms and the UCC define every term identically.
Incoterms override the UCC by federal statute.
oe: Correct. E.g., Incoterms use F.O.B. only for sea and inland waterway shipment, meaning loaded on board. The UCC terms are defaults that parties may vary (§ 1-302).
Parties may vary them.
They're commercial terms.
They differ.
They're incorporated by agreement.

q: Between merchants, which additional term in an acceptance would most likely NOT materially alter the contract?
o: A clause requiring complaints within 3 days where 30 days is customary.
A clause letting the seller cancel whenever any invoice is paid late.
A clause guaranteeing 100% deliveries where the trade allows leeway.
A clause disclaiming the implied warranty of merchantability.
A reasonable force-majeure clause excusing delay.
oe: Material (cmt. 4): materially shorter than customary. A customary period would not be.
Material (cmt. 4).
Material (cmt. 4).
Material (cmt. 4): it would cause surprise or hardship.
Correct. A reasonable force-majeure-type clause is listed in cmt. 5 as not material.

q: A seller learns its buyer's credit rating fell and it is paying suppliers late. The contract gives the buyer 15 days after each delivery to pay. Should the seller just insist on cash on delivery?
o: Yes; credit trouble always justifies cash only.
No; unless the buyer is insolvent, that risks repudiation.
Yes, because sellers may change payment terms on insecurity.
No; it must keep delivering on credit no matter what.
Yes, if it gives 10 days' notice.
oe: Only insolvency does.
Correct. Problem 6-3(a): § 2-702(1) allows a cash-only demand only on insolvency. Unilaterally changing the credit term risks a repudiation by the seller; use a § 2-609 demand instead.
Section 2-609 lets it suspend and demand, not rewrite.
It may use § 2-609.
No such rule.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Problem 6-3: cash on delivery

q: A one-year contract calls for monthly deliveries. In month one, the buyer accepts a short delivery without comment. Is there a course of performance?
o: Yes; acceptance without objection creates one.
No; one occasion isn't enough.
Yes, but only as to that one delivery.
Yes, if the buyer is a merchant.
No, because it requires a signed acknowledgment.
oe: Repeated occasions are needed.
Correct. A single occasion of conduct doesn't create a course of performance (former § 2-208 cmt. 4).
A course of performance is a pattern; one delivery isn't one.
Merchant status doesn't matter.
No writing is required.

q: In Razor v. Hyundai, the repair-or-replace remedy failed of its essential purpose. What happened to the separate exclusion of consequential damages?
o: It was enforced because it was in capital letters.
It was struck as a penalty.
It was held unconscionable because the buyer couldn't see it before signing.
It fell automatically when the repair remedy failed.
It was enforced because consumer exclusions of economic loss are valid.
oe: Unavailability before signing made it unconscionable.
Penalties concern LD.
Correct. The exclusion was in the owner's manual in the glove box; clear capital letters don't matter if the buyer had no access to it at contracting. The case was remanded for § 2-714(2) damages.
That's the dependent approach, which Razor rejected.
Here it was unconscionable.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Razor result

q: Of the four doctrines that can bar a buyer's late-delivery claim, which requires mutual assent and binds both past and future performance?
o: Modification.
Course of performance.
Usage of trade.
Estoppel.
Waiver.
oe: Correct. Waiver is retractable going forward (so it matters mostly for the past); course of performance binds but must be consistent with express terms; estoppel needs reasonable, detrimental reliance.
It rests on repeated performance and acquiescence, not mutual assent.
Not one of the four bases.
Estoppel rests on reliance, not assent.
Waiver is a voluntary relinquishment, retractable for the future.

Yes, unless it materially alters the contract.
No, because arbitration clauses are unconscionable in consumer contracts.
Yes, because the retailer's acknowledgment was the last form.
No, unless the consumer assents to it.
oe: The 10-day rule belongs to the merchant's confirmation exception to the SOF, and it doesn't apply to consumers.
That test applies only between merchants.
They aren't automatically unconscionable; the issue here is formation.
No last-shot rule.
Correct. Where either party isn't a merchant, additional terms in an acceptance are mere proposals; they need the other party's assent, and silence isn't enough under most views.

q: Which is NOT one of the seller's duties in a shipment contract under § 2-504?
o: Putting the goods in the carrier's possession.
Making a reasonable contract for their transportation.
Promptly notifying the buyer of the shipment.
Insuring the goods for the buyer's benefit.
Obtaining and promptly delivering any documents the buyer needs.
oe: A duty: (a).
A duty: (a).
A duty: (c).
Correct. Section 2-504 doesn't require insurance; one purpose of the notice duty is to let the buyer insure. (C.I.F. adds an insurance duty by agreement.)
A duty: (b).

q: A buyer tells a hardware clerk she needs paint for a pool's interior and insists on Brand X. The clerk sells Brand X, which peels underwater. Fitness warranty?
o: Likely not, because she didn't rely on the seller.
Yes, because merchants always warrant fitness.
Yes, because the clerk knew the purpose.
Yes, unless the clerk disclaimed it orally.
No, because painting a pool is an ordinary purpose.
oe: Correct. Insisting on a brand (or supplying precise specs) normally negates reliance (cmt. 5). Had the clerk chosen or recommended Brand X as suitable, a fitness warranty would likely arise (Problem 3-11(A)).
Fitness needs reliance.
Knowledge of purpose isn't enough without reliance.
A fitness disclaimer must be written anyway.
It's a particular use; the problem is reliance.

"Any attempted assignment is void."
"This contract is personal."
"The parties agree to act in good faith."
"Neither party may assign its rights."
oe: Too weak.
Correct. "May not assign its rights" might only make an assignment a breach; saying an attempted assignment is void is what makes it ineffective (subject to § 9-406(d) for rights to payment).
Ambiguous.
Irrelevant.
Might only make it a breach.

q: To provide a reasonably certain basis for a remedy, which term will Article 2 NOT supply by default (outside output and requirements deals)?

Time for payment.
Quality.
Quantity.
Place of delivery.
oe: Supplied by § 2-305.
Supplied by § 2-310.
Supplied by the implied warranties.
Correct. Price, quality and delivery are all gap-filled; quantity isn't, and § 2-306 only interprets an agreed output or requirements term.
Supplied by § 2-308.
