q: Which statement about usage of trade is NOT correct?
o: Its existence and scope must be proved as facts.
It must be ancient or universal in the trade.
It is a practice so regularly observed in a place or trade that it is expected to be observed here.
The party offering it must give notice sufficient to prevent unfair surprise.
If it is embodied in a written trade code, interpreting the code is a question of law.
oe: True.
Correct. This is false. Comment 4 rejects any requirement that a usage be "ancient," "immemorial" or "universal."
True.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Usage of trade: false statement

q: A dealer recommends an engine for a fisherman's boat; he buys it. At delivery he signs a receipt whose back, in larger type, disclaims all implied warranties "including merchantability." What is his strongest argument?
o: The dealer didn't sign the receipt.
Disclaimers are never valid against an experienced merchant buyer.
The dealer made no implied warranties.
It came after formation, so it isn't part of the deal.
It doesn't mention fitness.
oe: The disclaimer would bind the buyer who signed, if it were part of the contract.
They can be.
Both arose: a merchant dealer, and a particular purpose with reliance.

Correct. Problem 5-4: a post-formation receipt term is at most a proposed modification or an additional term that materially alters (§§ 2-207, 2-209). If it were part of the deal, it would mention merchantability and cover fitness in writing, leaving only the question whether a term on the back is conspicuous.
Fitness disclaimers needn't mention fitness.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Disclaimer on a delivery receipt

q: Which describes the "independent" approach Razor adopted?
o: The jury decides unconscionability.
A failed limited remedy automatically takes the exclusion down with it.
Exclusions in consumer contracts are always void.
Both clauses are tested only for conspicuousness.
The exclusion survives a failed remedy unless itself unconscionable.
oe: It's for the court.
That's the dependent approach (Adams v. J.I. Case).
Judged case by case.
Neither must be conspicuous.

Correct. The majority approach (Chatlos): "two concentric walls." Repair-or-replace is tested by failure of essential purpose; the consequential exclusion by unconscionability. The seller's willful failure to repair can bear on unconscionability. The dissent warned the ruling burdens manufacturers.

q: A buyer arrives with a small truck and asks to take half the wheat today and half tomorrow. The seller insists on one delivery and full payment now. Who is right?

Neither; the price must be split per load.
The seller; a single delivery is the default.
The buyer, if it's a merchant.
The buyer, because delivery in lots is the default.
oe: The buyer supplies the facilities.
Only if delivery in lots is agreed.

Correct. Section 2-307 presumes a single delivery, and the buyer must furnish facilities reasonably suited to receipt (§ 2-503(1)(b)). The seller may demand the full price on tender (Problem 4-4(a)(5)).
Irrelevant.
A single lot is the default.

All 60,000 to new customers paying today's higher price.
A fair, reasonable proration that may take regular customers into account.
Nothing to either until the plant is rebuilt.
All 60,000 to the customer the seller likes best.
oe: Not fair and reasonable.
Contract customers come first.
Correct. Section 2-615(b) and cmt. 11 (Problem 6-7(B)): when prices have risen, contract customers should be favored and supplies prorated evenly regardless of price.
The seller must allocate.
Not fair.

q: When does a buyer get an insurable interest in goods it has contracted to buy?
o: When risk of loss passes to it under § 2-509.
When it pays for them in full.
When it receives them.
When title passes.
On identification, even if nonconforming.
oe: Earlier: on identification.
Identification, not payment.
Earlier.
Identification is enough.

No; fixtures are things in action.
No; whatever is sold with real estate is governed by real property law.
Only if the contract separately prices them.
Only if Hollis removes them before closing.

A thing in action is an intangible right. Appliances are tangible and movable.
Too broad. Things attached to realty that can be severed without material harm are goods.
Price allocation matters for hybrid predominance, not for whether appliances are goods.
Who severs matters for minerals and structures, not for things severable without material harm.

A fixed percentage of requirements, or an estimate.
Adding a merger clause.
Calling it a "requirements contract" in the heading.
Setting a price above market.

Irrelevant to mutuality.

Price doesn't fix the mutuality problem.

A letter of credit is always the only adequate assurance.
Likely inadequate from a shaky buyer, though proof of solvency could do.
The seller may cancel at once.
The buyer has repudiated simply by refusing to provide the letter of credit.

Other assurances may be adequate.

Not before a reasonable time (up to 30 days) runs.
Not necessarily.

No, but it may recover damages for lost interest.
No, because no delay or loss resulted.
Yes, within 10 days of arrival.

Nothing was lost.

No such rule.

The whole contract is terminated.
The buyer is deemed to accept its quota.
The seller must deliver in full.

No.
Only the affected deliveries, unless the whole is substantially impaired.
Silence means lapse, not acceptance.
It was excused.

Only between merchants.
Yes, always; otherwise it's estoppel.
Only if the contract has a NOM clause.
No, never.

The split is general.

Only if both knew at contracting the goods were there.
Whenever the warehouse is the seller's closest facility to the buyer.
Never; delivery must be at the buyer's place.
Only if the buyer owns a truck big enough.

Correct. Section 2-308(b). Otherwise the default is the seller's place of business, or its residence if it has none (§ 2-308(a)). (Documents may be delivered through customary banking channels, (c).)
Not the test.

Irrelevant.

o: No, because a brand name defeats reliance.
Only if the store is the exclusive Brand X dealer.
No, because the clerk isn't the manufacturer.
Yes, likely; the buyer relied on the clerk's choice.
Only if the recommendation was in writing.

Irrelevant.
The retailer is the seller.
Correct. A trade name the seller recommends as adequate doesn't negate reliance; the buyer relied on the seller's judgment.
No writing is needed to create the warranty.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Seller recommends the brand
pre: A buyer tells a hardware clerk she needs paint for a pool's interior and insists on Brand X. The clerk sells Brand X, which peels underwater. Fitness warranty?

q: A contract says "Assignment is prohibited and any attempted assignment is void." The seller assigns its right to payment to a factor. Result?
o: The void clause controls, so the factor gets nothing.
The assignment is void because rights to payment are personal.
The assignment is effective, and it isn't a breach.
The assignment is effective only if the buyer consents.
The assignment is effective but a breach.
oe: Section 9-406(d) overrides it.
They're freely assignable.

Correct. Under § 9-406(d), a term restricting assignment of an account (a right to payment for goods sold) is ineffective, and the assignment isn't a breach (Problem 6-2(b)). The policy favors free assignment of receivables.
No consent needed.
Not a breach either.
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — Right to payment despite a void clause

q: Same facts, but the dealer isn't a merchant in engines. Which implied warranty can still arise?
o: Merchantability, but not fitness.
None.
Merchantability.
Only an express warranty.
Fitness for a particular purpose.
oe: Reversed.
Fitness can.
Requires a merchant in goods of the kind.
Fitness can still be implied.
Correct. Problem 5-4(C): without merchant status there is no merchantability warranty at all, but fitness doesn't require a merchant if the seller had reason to know the purpose and the reliance.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Non-merchant engine dealer
pre: A dealer recommends an engine for a fisherman's boat; he buys it. At delivery he signs a receipt whose back, in larger type, disclaims all implied warranties "including merchantability." What is his strongest argument?

q: Under § 2-105(6), a "commercial unit" is:
o: all goods identified to the contract at the same moment, whether or not used together.
a single whole in commerce, whose division would impair its character or value.
goods listed on one invoice.
any goods that are shipped together in one container, rail car or truckload, whatever they are.
the smallest quantity the seller will sell.
oe: Identification is a different concept (§ 2-501).
Correct. Examples include a single machine, a suite of furniture, or a bale, gross or carload. Accepting part of a commercial unit accepts the whole (§ 2-606(2)).
An invoice can list many separate units.
Shipping together doesn't make goods a single commercial unit; a carload can be, but because of trade usage.
That's a minimum order, not a commercial unit.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Commercial unit

q: Which clause is liquidated damages rather than a remedy limitation?
o: "Seller is not liable for consequential damages."
"Seller's liability shall not exceed the purchase price."
"Buyer's remedy is limited to return of the goods and refund."
"Seller shall pay $500 for each day of delay."
"Seller's sole obligation is to repair or replace."
oe: An exclusion: a limitation.
A cap: a limitation.
A limited remedy.

Correct. Problem 5-9: LD fixes the amount (or formula) in advance, higher or lower than actual loss, and is tested for reasonableness and penalty. A limitation caps or removes categories, the buyer still proves actual loss, and it's tested by essential purpose and unconscionability.
A limited remedy.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — LD or limitation

q: In the text's steps for determining a contract's terms, which comes LAST?
o: What are the express terms?
What do course of performance, course of dealing and usage add?
Was an agreement reached?
Which gaps should Article 2's defaults fill?
Is there a reasonably certain basis for a remedy?
oe: Second.
Third.
First.
Fourth.

Correct. The steps: was an agreement reached; what are the express terms and did the parties intend to contract; what do CoP, CoD and UoT add; what gaps remain for Article 2 to fill; and finally, is there a reasonably certain basis for a remedy.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — Order of analysis for terms

q: A contract expressly says "delivery by the 5th." The parties' course of performance shows deliveries by the 10th, and trade usage allows the 15th. If these can't reasonably be reconciled, which controls?
o: Course of dealing.
Whichever favors the party not in breach.
Usage of trade, because it reflects the whole industry.
The course of performance, because it is the most recent conduct.
The express term, under § 1-303(e).
oe: Course of dealing ranks below course of performance and express terms.
No such rule.
Usage ranks last.
It ranks just below express terms.

Correct. Under § 1-303(e), construe them consistently if reasonable; if not, express terms prevail over course of performance, which prevails over course of dealing, which prevails over usage of trade.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Which controls: the hierarchy

q: An output seller closes its plant. In which case does it most likely act in good faith?
o: It closes to pressure the buyer into paying more.
It closes merely to cut its losses on the fixed-price contract.
It closes because it has no orders for the product.
It closes to sell the plant's output elsewhere at the higher market price.
It closes after the market price rises well above the contract price.
oe: Coercive, not good faith.
Comment 2 says that isn't good faith.
Correct. Comment 2: a shutdown for lack of orders may be permissible; one merely to curtail losses would not.
Diversion is bad faith.
That timing suggests opportunism.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Output seller shuts down

q: Between merchants, an additional term in an acceptance becomes part of the contract unless an exception applies. Which is NOT one of the exceptions?
o: The offer expressly limits acceptance to the terms of the offer.
The offeror objects within a reasonable time after notice of the term.
The term imposes an obligation the offer never mentioned.
The term would materially alter the contract.
None of the above.
oe: An exception: § 2-207(2)(a).
An exception: § 2-207(2)(c).

Correct. Every additional term does that, so it can't be an exception. The three exceptions are (a) the offer expressly limits acceptance to its terms, (b) the term materially alters the contract, and (c) the offeror objects, already or within a reasonable time.
An exception: § 2-207(2)(b).
One of the other choices is correct: The term imposes an obligation the offer never mentioned.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Exceptions in § 2-207(2)

q: Which is NOT advisable in the seller's demand letter?
o: Demanding a letter of credit as the only acceptable assurance.
Setting a response deadline within 30 days.
Listing the specific grounds for insecurity.
Reserving the right to suspend performance.
Offering several kinds of acceptable assurance.
oe: Correct. Problem 6-3(c): offer several options (a letter of credit, a guaranty, payment in advance or on delivery, "other assurances might also be adequate") so the demand stays "adequate" rather than becoming a repudiation.
Advisable.
Advisable.
Advisable.
Advisable.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Problem 6-3: demand letter
pre: A seller learns its buyer's credit rating fell and it is paying suppliers late. The contract gives the buyer 15 days after each delivery to pay. Should the seller just insist on cash on delivery?

q: Under § 2-501, which pairing of goods with the time they are identified is WRONG (absent agreement)?
o: Goods to be made from stock: when the seller marks or designates them for the contract.
Chairs the seller will build next month: when the contract is made.
A specific painting on a gallery wall: when the contract is made.
A crop to be harvested within 12 months: when it is planted.
Calves to be born within 12 months: when they are conceived.
oe: Right.
Correct. That's wrong. Future goods are identified when the seller ships, marks or otherwise designates them as the contract goods.
Right: existing, identified goods.
Right (or the next normal harvest season).
Right.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Identification timing

q: Among the policies the text discusses for choosing gap fillers, a "penalty default" is:
o: a default rule that applies only to consumers.
a punitive damages award for breach of contract.
a liquidated damages clause.
a default rule chosen because most parties would have agreed to it anyway.
a default that pushes the better-informed party to bargain.
oe: Not the concept.
Not a default rule.
That's an agreed term, not a default rule.
That's a majoritarian default.
Correct. Other policy choices: the fairest rule, the most efficient, the one most parties would choose, one neutral between buyers and sellers, and whether to treat consumers and merchants alike.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — Penalty default

q: A rotor-blade maker can't deliver on time. Which cause is most likely to excuse it?
o: A rail strike when trucking is a reasonable substitute.
A strike by the seller's own employees.
Tripled metal prices from a market boom.
Its decision to accept more orders than it could fill.
An industry-wide metal workers' strike that blocks all supply.
oe: Section 2-614(1): use the substitute.
Usually within its control.
Market event: no excuse.
Self-inflicted (Roth Steel's § 2-615 defense failed for this reason).

Correct. Problem 6-7(A)(2): a capacity event that shuts down major sources of supply. A market boom tripling prices doesn't; a strike by its own workers usually doesn't; a rail strike calls for a reasonable trucking substitute (§ 2-614); a fire at its only plant may.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Problem 6-7 events

q: A seller phones: "Pick up the wheat within two hours or I'll sell it to someone else." Is that a proper tender?
o: No, because tender always requires 24 hours.
Probably not; two hours likely isn't a reasonable period.
Yes; any notice is enough.
Yes, if the buyer is nearby.
Yes, because the seller sets the time.
oe: No fixed rule; reasonableness.

Correct. Goods must be kept available for the period reasonably necessary for the buyer to take possession (§ 2-503(1)(a)); two hours likely isn't, depending on distance and trade practice. The threat may also be a repudiation (Problem 4-4(a)(3)).
The holding period must be reasonable.
Still must be a reasonable period.
Not unilaterally.
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — Two-hour pickup

q: Which is NOT within a requirements contract under § 2-306 cmt. 2?
o: A sudden expansion of the buyer's plant.
A good-faith reduction because the buyer's orders fell off.
Normal good-faith growth in the buyer's business.
Variation around the stated estimate.
Seasonal swings in the buyer's needs.
oe: Correct. A sudden expansion isn't within the contract, though normal good-faith expansion is; a market price far above the contract price is a factor.
Good-faith variations are allowed, even to discontinuance.
Within the contract.
Expected.
Ordinary variation.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — What a requirements contract covers

q: A contract requires delivery to the buyer's plant by the 5th of each month. The first delivery arrives on the 7th, and the buyer accepts it without complaint. What has the buyer lost?
o: Its damages claim, because acceptance waives it.
Nothing, and it never needs to tell the seller.
Its claim, because it accepted knowing the delivery was late.
Nothing yet, if it gives the seller timely notice of breach.
Its right to on-time delivery in the future, by course of performance.
oe: Acceptance doesn't waive damages.
Notice is required to preserve the claim.
Accepting with knowledge bars revocation for that defect, not damages.

Correct. One occasion isn't a course of performance, there's no modification, and acceptance doesn't impair other remedies (§ 2-607(2)). But a buyer that doesn't notify the seller within a reasonable time is barred from any remedy (§ 2-607(3)(a)). Problem 3-5(A).
One delivery isn't a course of performance.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — One late delivery accepted

q: Under a shipment contract, the carrier's careless forklift driver crushes the goods. Which is correct?
o: The contract is avoided.
Only the seller can sue the carrier.
The buyer owes nothing, because a third party caused the loss.
The buyer must still pay the seller and may pursue the carrier.
The seller must replace the goods.
oe: No.
The buyer, who bears the loss, can.
Risk had passed to the buyer.
Correct. Risk passed on delivery to the carrier, so the buyer owes the price (§ 2-709(1)(a)) and may sue the carrier (§ 2-722; § 7-309) or claim on its insurance.
Risk had passed.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Carrier crushes the goods

q: Which of the following is NOT a "hybrid transaction" under § 2-106(5)?
o: A dealer sells a laptop and licenses the operating software installed on it.
A contractor sells and installs kitchen cabinets.
A buyer pays for a truck with cash plus painting the seller's shop.
A roofer sells and installs a skylight.
A dealer sells a boat and leases the buyer a trailer to haul it for the season.
oe: Hybrid: a sale of goods plus a license of non-goods property.
Hybrid: goods plus installation services.
Correct. A hybrid needs the SELLER to supply the services or other property. Services the buyer gives in exchange for goods are just the price (§ 2-304: price may be payable in money or otherwise).
Hybrid: goods plus services from the seller.
Hybrid: a sale of goods plus a lease of other goods.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Not a hybrid transaction

q: In Ingram River v. Pott, the barge builder argued that carrying and heating heavy oil was just the ordinary use of heating-coil barges. What did the court hold?
o: A particular purpose must be unique to the buyer.
Fitness can't arise where the buyer uses goods the way they're usually used.
A purpose needn't be unique, just different from customary use.
Barges are services, not goods.
Only merchantability can apply to barges built to order.
oe: It need not be unique.
The court rejected the seller's ordinary-use argument as a matter of law.

Correct. Whether the goods were "tank barges" (many cargoes) or "heating-coil barges" was a fact question, like buying climbing shoes at a general shoe store vs. a climbing store. Cmt. 2's example: shoes for walking vs. for mountain climbing.
They're goods.
Fitness could arise.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Ingram River barges

q: The seller's acknowledgment states that acceptance is expressly conditional on the buyer's assent to the seller's terms. The buyer never assents, but the seller ships and the buyer pays. What are the contract's terms?
o: The terms on which the writings agree, plus Article 2's gap fillers.
None; there is no contract because the writings failed.
Whatever the party who performed first proposed.
The seller's terms, because the buyer accepted them by paying for the goods.
The buyer's terms, because the buyer made the offer.
oe: Correct. The writings didn't form a contract, but conduct recognizing one does under § 2-207(3), the third of the three § 2-207 questions.
Conduct by both parties recognizing a contract is enough.
No such rule.
That is the common-law last-shot result § 2-207(3) displaces.
Under (3), neither side's unique terms control.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Contract by conduct terms

q: A course of performance can't be reconciled with an express term. How can it still matter?
o: It overrides the express term automatically, as the most recent conduct.
It matters only if the contract has a merger clause.
It turns the deal into one for successive performances.
It can show a waiver or modification of the term, subject to § 2-209.
It can't matter at all once the express term controls.
oe: Express terms prevail over course of performance under § 1-303(e).
A merger clause has nothing to do with it.
No.
Correct. That's § 1-303(f). Because it's subject to § 2-209, a NOM clause can block a modification by conduct, though the conduct may still be a waiver.
Section 1-303(f) gives it another role.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Inconsistent course of performance

q: A store lets a customer take a vacuum home for a one-week trial, returnable if she doesn't like it. During the trial a fire, no one's fault, destroys it. Who bears the loss?
o: The customer, because using it was an acceptance.
The store, until the customer accepts.
They split it.
The customer, because she had possession.
The customer, because return is at the buyer's risk.
oe: Trial use isn't acceptance.

Correct. Goods delivered primarily for use are a sale on approval (§ 2-326); risk and title stay with the seller until acceptance, and trial use isn't acceptance (§ 2-327(1)). Section 2-509(4) makes the risk rules subject to § 2-327.
No splitting.
Possession doesn't shift risk on approval.
That's a sale or return.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Sale on approval

q: A seller assigns "all my rights under the contract" to another manufacturer, which accepts. What has happened?
o: Only an assignment of the right to payment.
An assignment of rights only, because duties must be named.
A novation releasing the original seller.
Nothing, because duties can't be transferred.
Assignment plus delegation, with a promise to perform.
oe: General language also delegates.
Not under § 2-210(5).
The seller stays liable.
They can be delegated.

Correct. Section 2-210(5): unless the language or circumstances (e.g., an assignment for security) indicate otherwise, the assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform, enforceable by the assignor or the other original party.
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — "All my rights under the contract"

q: Which statement about remedy clauses is NOT correct?
o: An agreed remedy is optional unless it is expressly exclusive.
A limited-remedy clause must be conspicuous to be enforced.
Excluding consequential damages for commercial loss isn't prima facie unconscionable.
An unreasonably large liquidated damages term is void as a penalty.
If an exclusive remedy fails of its essential purpose, ordinary Code remedies become available.
oe: Correct. This is false. Nothing in § 2-719 (or § 2-718) requires conspicuousness; that requirement belongs to some warranty disclaimers.
topic: XI · Liquidated damages & limited remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719) — Remedy clauses: false statement

q: Which is a repudiation rather than a breach by nonperformance?
o: Before delivery is due, the seller says it won't deliver.
The seller delivers nonconforming goods.
The buyer pays three days late.
The seller simply fails to deliver anything on the due date.
The buyer rejects conforming goods.
oe: Correct. Repudiation is signaling before performance is due, by words or acts, that you won't perform. Failing to perform when due is a breach.
A breach.
A breach.
A breach.
A wrongful rejection, a breach.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Repudiation vs. breach

q: Which sale most clearly excludes the warranty of title by circumstances?
o: A dealer's sale stating "no warranties, express or implied."
An Article 9 secured party's foreclosure sale with no disclaimer.
A sheriff's sale of goods seized from a debtor.
A pawnbroker's "as is" sale of a car.
A neighbor's garage sale.
oe: General disclaimers don't reach title.
Such a disposition carries a title warranty unless properly excluded (§ 9-610).
Correct. Comment 5 to § 2-312: sales by sheriffs, executors and certain foreclosing lienors are so out of the ordinary that buyers know the seller isn't claiming title personally.
"As is" doesn't disclaim title (Hagerty).
Every seller warrants title.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Title excluded by circumstances

q: Outside a sheriff's sale, when would a buyer sensibly agree to an express disclaimer of title?
o: Whenever the goods are used.
Only if the buyer is a merchant.
When the seller is a merchant.
Never; a title disclaimer is void.
When provenance is uncertain and priced in.
oe: Used goods still carry title warranties.
Irrelevant.
Merchant status is irrelevant to title.
Specific language works.

Correct. Problem 5-5: e.g., a quitclaim-style sale of art with provenance gaps, salvage, an estate's unsorted property or a storage-unit auction. Circumstances alone can do it at storage-unit, police or executor's auctions.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Why accept a title disclaimer

q: After a phone deal, each merchant sends a confirmation. The seller's requires arbitration; the buyer's says disputes go to court. Neither objects. What happens to those clauses?
o: The buyer's clause controls because it was sent last.
No contract exists, since the confirmations conflict.
Both clauses apply, so the parties must arbitrate before suing.
Both drop out; each is treated as objecting to the other.
The seller's clause controls because it was sent first.
oe: There is no last-shot rule.
The contract was formed by phone; only the terms are at issue.
Conflicting terms can't both apply.
Correct. Comment 6 to § 2-207: where confirmations conflict, each party is assumed to object to the other's clause, and the conflicting terms don't become part of the contract.
There is no first-shot rule.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Dueling confirmations

q: A contract for a commercial oven says nothing about when it will be delivered. When must the seller deliver?
o: Within a reasonable time.
Immediately on signing.
Within 30 days.
Never; the contract fails for want of a delivery date.
Whenever the seller chooses.
oe: Correct. Section 2-309(1). Factors include the nature of the goods, the buyer's purpose, what the seller knows of the buyer's plans, transportation conditions and the market.
A reasonable time.
No fixed period.
The gap filler supplies it.
A reasonable time.
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — No delivery date

q: Under § 1-303(d), course of dealing and usage of trade may do which of the following?
o: Give particular meaning to specific terms of the agreement.
Supplement the terms of the agreement.
Qualify the terms of the agreement.
Help ascertain the meaning of the parties' agreement as a whole.
All of the above.
oe: True, but not the best answer.
True, but not the best answer.
True, but not the best answer.
True, but not the best answer.

Correct. Section 1-303(d): they are relevant in ascertaining the meaning of the agreement, may give particular meaning to specific terms, and may supplement or qualify the terms. What they can't do is override an express term they can't reasonably be reconciled with (§ 1-303(e)).
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — What course and usage can do

q: A requirements contract states: "estimated 5,000 units; minimum 4,000; maximum 6,000." Which is correct?
o: The estimate of 5,000 is a firm minimum.
The estimate is the center; min and max are firm limits.
The seller may refuse anything over 5,000.
The minimum and maximum are just more estimates.
The buyer may demand 7,000 units, so long as it acts in good faith.
oe: An estimate isn't a floor.
Correct. Comment 3: an agreed estimate is the center around which variation is expected; a minimum or maximum sets a clear limit.
Variation up to the maximum is expected.
They're firm limits.
The maximum is a clear limit.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Estimate, minimum and maximum

q: Under a destination contract, fungible goods are lost in transit. What must the seller do?
o: Collect the price from the buyer anyway.
Nothing; § 2-613 excuses it.
Tender substitute goods in time, or be in breach.
Nothing; the carrier must deliver substitutes.
Split the loss with the buyer.
oe: The buyer didn't have the risk.
Fungible goods aren't identified at contracting.
Correct. The seller bore the transit risk; it can claim against its insurer or the carrier.
The seller's obligation remains.
No splitting.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Destination contract loss

q: A wholesaler delivers 200 books to a bookstore "for resale; unsold copies returnable." The bookstore ships the unsold copies back, and they're lost in transit. Who bears the loss?
o: Only the carrier.
The bookstore, which bears the risk of return.
They split it.
The wholesaler, because this is a sale on approval.
The wholesaler, because risk never passed.
oe: As between the parties, the bookstore.
Correct. Goods delivered primarily for resale are a sale or return; return is at the buyer's risk and expense (§ 2-327(2)).
No splitting.
Delivered for resale, so it's a sale or return.
In a sale or return, the buyer had the goods and bears the return risk.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Sale or return

q: Which is NOT a factor under the pre-2022 predominant purpose test?
o: The nature of the supplier's business.
Whether it makes sense to apply Article 2.
Whether the claim concerns the goods or the services.
The relative value of the materials compared with the services provided.
The language of the contract.
oe: A factor.
A factor. Under this all-or-nothing test, if goods predominate Article 2 governs everything; if services do, nothing.
Correct. That is the gravamen-of-the-claim test (Anthony Pools), the main alternative to predominant purpose.
A factor.
A factor.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Predominant purpose factors

q: Same contract, which has a NOM clause. The buyer accepts three late deliveries without objection. Which is most accurate?
o: The NOM clause bars any waiver argument.
The buyer can't insist on on-time delivery again.
No modification, but possibly a waiver it can retract going forward.
A course of performance modified the due date after three deliveries, despite the NOM clause.
The NOM clause strengthens the seller's estoppel argument.
oe: Section 2-209(4) says failed modifications can operate as waivers.
It can retract by reasonable notice.

Correct. Problem 3-5(C): the NOM clause blocks an unwritten modification (and § 1-303(f) is subject to § 2-209), but § 2-209(4) lets conduct operate as a waiver. The clause also makes the seller's reliance less reasonable, weakening estoppel.
Course of performance is subject to § 2-209.
It weakens it, because reliance becomes less reasonable.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — NOM clause and late deliveries
pre: A contract requires delivery to the buyer's plant by the 5th of each month. The first delivery arrives on the 7th, and the buyer accepts it without complaint. What has the buyer lost?

q: A buyer tells a dealer she drives winding mountain roads and needs a car that will keep her safe in a serious crash. The salesperson recommends a model with poor crash ratings. Compared with Problem 3-10(d), she:
o: has no case, since safety is an ordinary purpose.
wins only on express warranty.
loses unless the dealer made the car.
has the same weak merchantability case.
has a stronger case, under fitness.
oe: Her stated need makes it particular.
Fitness is the better route.
The selling dealer makes the warranty.
She adds a fitness claim.
Correct. Problem 3-11(B): a communicated particular purpose plus reliance on the recommendation creates a fitness warranty likely breached.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Mountain roads
pre: A new car meets every safety regulation but rates below average in crash tests. A buyer seriously injured in a head-on collision sues for breach of merchantability. Likely result?

q: Which statement correctly contrasts the parol evidence rule with the statute of frauds?
o: The PER applies only when there is no writing at all.
The SOF applies only to final, integrated writings.
Both bar enforcement of oral contracts.
The PER governs evidence of terms; the SOF, enforceability.
If the PER excludes a term, the whole contract becomes unenforceable.
oe: It applies only when there is a final writing.
That's the PER's trigger.
Only the SOF concerns enforceability.

Correct. PER problems arise only when there is a record adopted by both parties; SOF problems arise when there is no signed record. If the PER excludes a term, the rest of the agreement stays enforceable. Both encourage memorializing deals.
The rest remains enforceable.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — PER vs. SOF

q: A plumber contracts to buy 12,000 sewer fittings with no other use for a town's new sewer system. The supplier, in the same small town, knows this. The town cancels the project. The plumber's best argument?
o: Unconscionability.
Section 2-614(2), because the town's payment failed.
Impracticability, because buying fittings is now impossible.
Frustration of purpose.
Section 2-613, because the fittings lost their value.
oe: Nothing unfair at formation.
That's about payment methods.
Buying is possible; the purpose is gone.

Correct. Problem 6-8(a): common-law frustration (Restatement § 265) applies through § 1-103(b), and § 2-615 cmt. 9 says a supply contract tied to a particular construction venture may excuse the buyer. Counter: the plumber took a foreseeable risk.
No casualty to identified goods.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Sewer project canceled

q: A farmer trades 100 bushels of corn for a neighbor's used tractor. No money changes hands. Which is correct?
o: Only the farmer is a seller; the neighbor is a buyer.
Each party is a seller of the goods it transfers.
It's a hybrid transaction, since two kinds of goods are involved.
It's governed by the common law of barter.
Article 2 doesn't apply because no money changed hands.
oe: Each side transfers goods.

Correct. Under § 2-304, the price may be payable in money or otherwise; if payable in goods, each party is a seller of the goods it transfers. (If part of the price were realty, Article 2 would govern only the goods side.)
A hybrid needs services, a lease or non-goods property from the seller.
Article 2 governs.
The price may be payable in goods.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — Barter of goods

q: A contract prohibits assignment and delegation by either party. Which transfer is still permitted?
o: The seller's assignment of its right to payment.
Delegation of either party's duties, if the other has no substantial interest.
The seller's delegation of its duty to deliver.
The buyer's delegation of its duty to pay.
The buyer's assignment of its right to the goods.
oe: Correct. Problem 6-1's chart: with a contractual prohibition, the buyer's assignment of its right to the goods and both delegations are barred, but the seller's right to payment stays assignable (§§ 2-210(2)-(3), 9-406).
The agreement bars it.
Barred.
Barred.
Barred (unless a claim for breach of the whole, or after full performance).
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — Prohibition chart

q: Which is NOT a way a repudiation can arise?
o: Accepting a late delivery without complaint.
Conduct showing performance won't be forthcoming.
An unjustified demand for assurance, with performance conditioned on it.
Words clearly saying a party won't perform.
Failing to answer a justified demand within 30 days.
oe: Correct. That may raise waiver questions, but it isn't a repudiation.
A repudiation.
Can be a repudiation by the demanding party.
A repudiation.
A repudiation (§ 2-609(4)).
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Sources of repudiation

q: In a shipment contract, goods conform when handed to the carrier but are damaged in transit. May the buyer reject?
o: Yes; perfect tender lets it reject anything.
Only if the seller failed to insure.
No; the transit damage is the buyer's risk.
Yes, if it inspects promptly on arrival.
Yes; they don't conform on arrival.
oe: The tender to the carrier was perfect.
No duty to insure.
Correct. In a shipment contract the buyer can reject only if the goods were nonconforming when delivered to the carrier. That gives the buyer an incentive to inspect at origin.
Timing of inspection doesn't change risk.
Conformity is measured at delivery to the carrier.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Conformity at the carrier

q: The slides cite § 1-205 for course of dealing and usage of trade, and § 2-208 for course of performance. Where are these rules found today?
o: They are still in §§ 1-205 and 2-208.
oe: Not in the current Official Text.
That is the parol evidence rule, which refers to them.
That is the duty of good faith.
Correct. Revised Article 1 consolidated them; § 2-208 was deleted, and § 1-205 now covers "reasonable time" and "seasonably."
That is variation by agreement.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Where the old sections went

q: Why are fitness claims usually limited to the immediate seller?
o: Only merchants make fitness warranties.
Manufacturers never make fitness warranties.
Section 2-318 excludes fitness claims by anyone other than the buyer.
Fitness warranties can't be assigned.
Reliance usually runs to the buyer's own seller.
oe: Any seller can.
They can, by specific assurances.
Section 2-318 extends warranties to some non-buyers.
Not the reason.
Correct. A manufacturer could be liable if it gave the buyer specific assurances.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Fitness and privity

q: The seller arrives at the buyer's farm on the agreed date with the wheat. The buyer's storage isn't cleaned out, and the buyer asks the seller to come back in two hours. Result?
o: The seller breached by not waiting as long as the buyer needed.
The buyer may reject for late tender.
The seller must store the wheat at its own expense indefinitely.
The contract is avoided.
The tender was proper, and the seller is excused for the delay.
oe: The buyer caused the delay.
The tender was timely.
No such duty.
No casualty or excuse.

Correct. The buyer failed to cooperate (§ 2-503(1)(b)), so under § 2-311(3) the seller is excused for any resulting delay and may proceed in a reasonable manner, or treat a material failure as a breach (Problem 4-4(a)(6)).
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — Buyer's bins not ready

q: Before applying § 2-509's carrier, bailee and direct-tender rules, what should you check first?
o: Whether the seller was negligent.
Which party carried insurance.
Any contrary agreement, and whether anyone is in breach.
Which party had paid.
Who held title when the goods were lost.
oe: Fault matters for § 2-613, not for passing risk.
Insurance matters only within § 2-510(2)-(3).

Correct. The sequence: what is the seller's tender obligation; has anyone breached (§ 2-510 vs. § 2-509); then the carrier, bailee, direct-tender or other-agreement rule. Contrary agreement (including usage and course of dealing) controls under § 2-509(4).
Payment is irrelevant.
Title is irrelevant to risk.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Check first

q: A contract for 1,000 shirts leaves the size assortment and the shipping arrangements unspecified. Under § 2-311, unless otherwise agreed:
o: the buyer picks the assortment; the seller, the shipping arrangements.
the seller picks both.
the seller picks the assortment and the buyer picks the shipping arrangements.
the buyer picks both.
the contract fails for indefiniteness.
oe: Correct. Particulars left to one party must be specified in good faith and within limits of commercial reasonableness.
Assortment is at the buyer's option.
Reversed.
Shipping arrangements are at the seller's option.
Section 2-311 fills the gap.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — Assortment and shipping options

q: Which set of online terms is most likely part of the buyer's contract?
o: Terms on a page the buyer could reach only by scrolling past the checkout button.
Terms shown in the box where the buyer clicks "I agree."
Terms printed inside the shipping box, under the Klocek view of § 2-207.
Terms behind a link labeled "Site map" in the page footer.
Terms posted on the website a week after the purchase.
oe: Hidden terms don't give reasonable notice.
Correct. Terms displayed where the buyer manifests assent are part of the contract. Hyperlinked terms bind only if a reasonable buyer would have been aware of them.
Klocek treated in-the-box terms as mere § 2-207 proposals, so they don't bind without assent. (Hill v. Gateway took the opposite, rolling-contract view.)
Mislabeled, hard-to-find links don't give reasonable notice.
Terms added after formation aren't part of the deal without assent.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — Online terms that bind

q: In Anthony Pools v. Sheehan, a defective diving board injured a homeowner. The board was supplied under a pool-building contract in which services predominated. What did the Maryland court hold?
o: Article 2 applied to the whole contract, because a pool is a fixture.
Article 2 applied to the board, because the claim concerned goods.
The disclaimer was valid because Article 2 didn't govern the board.
Only tort law could apply to personal injuries from a service contract.
Article 2 didn't apply, because services predominated.
oe: The court looked at the claim, not at fixture status, and didn't extend Article 2 to the services.
Correct. Under the gravamen test, Article 2 governed both the merchantability warranty and whether the disclaimer worked, since the board kept its character as goods after the work was done.
Article 2 did govern, including the disclaimer analysis.
The court applied the contract warranty of merchantability.
That's the predominant purpose result the court avoided.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Anthony Pools

q: A contract has both a merger clause and a no-oral-modification clause. Which pairing is correct?
o: Merger: later changes. NOM: prior and contemporaneous deals.
Merger: prior and contemporaneous. NOM: later changes.
Neither has any effect under Article 2.
Both govern only later modifications.
Both govern only prior agreements.
oe: Reversed.
Correct. The merger clause works with § 2-202; the NOM clause with § 2-209(2).
Both can matter.
The merger clause looks back.
The NOM clause looks forward.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — Merger vs. NOM

q: Same contract, but it has both a NOM clause and a clause saying any waiver is effective only if signed by the waiving party. The buyer accepts three late deliveries without objection. Does the seller still have a waiver argument?
o: Yes; anti-waiver clauses are void under § 1-302.
Yes, but only if the seller is a merchant.
No, but the seller automatically wins on estoppel.
Maybe; courts split on whether conduct can waive that clause.
No; every court enforces anti-waiver clauses exactly as written.
oe: They aren't void.
Merchant status doesn't decide it.
Estoppel is weak here.

Correct. Problem 3-5(D): many courts enforce anti-waiver clauses; others hold the clause itself can be waived by conduct. Estoppel remains possible but weak, and the buyer must still give § 2-607(3)(a) notice for past deliveries.
Courts split.
topic: IV · Modification, waiver & estoppel (§ 2-209) — Anti-waiver clause
pre: A contract requires delivery to the buyer's plant by the 5th of each month. The first delivery arrives on the 7th, and the buyer accepts it without complaint. What has the buyer lost?

q: Which is NOT a way to exclude the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose?
o: The seller's oral statement that it "makes no warranty of fitness."
A conspicuous writing that never mentions fitness.
The buyer's pre-contract examination, as to defects it should have revealed.
"As is."
Usage of trade.
oe: Correct. A fitness disclaimer under § 2-316(2) must be in writing and conspicuous. The other routes: a conspicuous writing (no magic words), "as is," examination or refusal after demand, and course of dealing or usage. Specs or brand insistence keep the warranty from arising at all.
Works.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Ways to exclude fitness

q: In NIPSCO v. Carbon County Coal, a utility locked into a fixed-price coal contract sought excuse when energy costs fell steeply. The court held:
o: the seller had to lower its price.
the contract was unconscionable.
the utility was excused by frustration of purpose.
a fixed price puts market drops on the buyer, who can't walk away.
the utility could terminate on reasonable notice.
oe: The contract set the price (with a floor and escalation).
No.
No excuse.
Correct. Excuse doctrines "have no place when the contract explicitly assigns a particular risk"; a buyer who forecasts wrong "has only himself to blame."
It wasn't an indefinite contract.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — NIPSCO

q: A seller writes, "We'll deliver as agreed, but we expect you to cover our extra fuel costs." Is that a repudiation?
o: Yes, if the buyer is a merchant.
Yes; any demand beyond the contract is a repudiation.
Not by itself, unless delivery is conditioned on the payment.
No, unless the seller was in bad faith.
No; demands for money can never be repudiations.
oe: Not the test.
Not by itself.
Correct. Section 2-610 cmt. 2: a demand for more than the contract calls for isn't in itself a repudiation, but a statement that the party won't perform except on conditions beyond the contract is.
The test is conditioning, not motive.
They can be, if performance is conditioned on them.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Demand for extra costs

q: A requirements buyer's needs drop from 50,000 to 5,000 in a recession. How do courts treat decreases?
o: They split on whether disproportion applies.
Decreases are never limited at all.
Any decrease is a breach.
Decreases are limited only by a stated estimate.
Every court applies both limits.
oe: Correct. Several apply only good faith, even to going out of business (Empire Gas; HML: the seller assumes the risk of good-faith variations); others apply both tests (Simcala).
Good faith always applies.
Good-faith decreases are allowed.
Not the rule.
Some apply only good faith.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Decreases in requirements

q: A seller agrees to sell 100 standard steel I-beams, F.O.B. its plant. It assigns "the contract" to Manufacturer, which accepts. Which is correct?
o: The contract is void because the beams were sold F.O.B.
The original seller is released.
The buyer may refuse, since any delegation requires the buyer's consent.
The buyer must pay the original seller, not Manufacturer.
It must take and pay for Manufacturer's beams; the seller stays liable.
oe: Irrelevant.
No novation.
Consent isn't needed.
Manufacturer is the assignee of the right to payment.
Correct. Problem 6-2(c): assignment plus delegation (§ 2-210(5)); no substantial interest in who supplies standard beams (§ 2-210(1)); the buyer may demand assurances from Manufacturer (§ 2-210(6)).
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — Assignment of the contract for I-beams

q: An appliance store sells a refrigerator, takes full payment and says it's ready for pickup Saturday. On Friday night the store's warehouse floods and ruins it. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer, because title passed at contracting.
They split it.
The store, until the buyer receives it.
The buyer, because the store tendered by notifying it.
The buyer, because it paid in full.
oe: Title is irrelevant.
No splitting.

Correct. A merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods (§ 2-509(3)), even if the buyer has paid and been told the goods are ready (cmt. 3): the merchant still controls them and can insure them.
Tender moves risk only for a non-merchant seller.
Payment doesn't shift risk.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Paid, ready for pickup, flood

q: A fuel distributor's supplier refuses to honor its fixed-price contract after storms and unrest spike prices; the distributor is losing $1 a gallon on its own resale contracts. What's the best plan?
o: Rescind under § 2-613.
Claim impracticability under § 2-615, since the spike was unforeseen.
Stop delivering to its own customers.
Raise its own prices unilaterally.
Seek a good-faith modification; draft escalation clauses.
oe: No casualty.
Market increases don't excuse.
That's a breach.
That's a breach or repudiation.

Correct. Problem 6-9: § 2-615 likely won't excuse a market spike (cmt. 4), and the distributor has a claim against its supplier. A market shift that makes performance a loss can justify seeking a modification in good faith (§ 2-209 cmt. 2).
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Supplier price spike

q: Which statement about disclaiming warranties is NOT correct?
o: Course of dealing can exclude or modify implied warranties.
"As is" disclaims the warranty of title.
A refusal to examine after the seller's demand excludes defects an examination would have revealed.
A fitness disclaimer must be written and conspicuous.
A merchantability disclaimer may be oral if it mentions merchantability.
oe: Correct. This is false. Title is excluded only by specific language or circumstances (§ 2-312(2)); § 2-316 doesn't govern it.
topic: X · Warranty disclaimers (§§ 2-316, 2-312(2)) — Disclaimers: false statement

q: A form contract says, "No usage of trade shall apply to this agreement." A buyer later offers proof of a specific trade usage. The clause is most likely:
o: effective, because parties may vary any provision of the Code.
void as a violation of good faith.
effective only between merchants.
a merger clause that makes the writing complete and exclusive.
ineffective, because a usage must be specifically negated.
oe: Variation is allowed, but a general clause probably doesn't negate a particular usage.
It's simply ineffective, not a breach of good faith.
Merchant status isn't the issue.
Even a complete and exclusive writing can be supplemented by usage.
Correct. Usage is assumed to be part of the deal unless "carefully negated" (§ 2-202 cmt. 2); a blanket clause likely doesn't do that (Problem 3-1).
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Clause excluding all usage

q: Same beams, but the contract says "any attempted assignment is void." Must the buyer accept Manufacturer's beams?
o: No; the delegation is barred.
Yes, if Manufacturer gives adequate assurance.
No, but it must still pay Manufacturer.
Yes, because standard beams involve no substantial interest.
Yes; § 9-406(d) overrides the clause.
oe: Correct. Text Problem 6-2(D): the clause bars delegation, and § 9-406(d) doesn't help, because under § 9-109(d)(6) Article 9 doesn't apply to an assignment of a right to payment to an assignee that is also obligated to perform.
Assurance doesn't cure a barred delegation.
Not if the transfer is ineffective.
The contractual prohibition controls.
Article 9 doesn't apply here.
topic: XIII · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210, § 9-406) — Void clause and a delegating assignee

q: Which is NOT one of the ways Article 2 changed the common law of offer and acceptance?
o: An offeree may accept after an effective revocation.
Acceptance may be sent by any reasonable method.
A seller may accept by shipping the goods.
A merchant's firm offer binds without consideration.
A written confirmation can operate as an acceptance.
oe: Correct. Nothing in Article 2 revives a revoked offer. The five changes are: any reasonable method of acceptance, acceptance by shipping, firm offers without consideration, no mirror-image rule, and confirmations as acceptances.
A change: § 2-205.
topic: II · Formation, firm offers & the battle of the forms (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) — How Article 2 changed offer and acceptance

q: Under § 2-202, terms in a writing intended as a final expression may NOT be contradicted by:
o: a contemporaneous written agreement.
a prior agreement or a contemporaneous oral agreement.
course of performance.
evidence that the writing was procured by fraud.
a later oral modification.
oe: Not barred: § 2-202 reaches contemporaneous ORAL agreements.

Correct. They may be explained or supplemented by course of dealing, usage of trade or course of performance, and by consistent additional terms unless the writing is also complete and exclusive. (Terms on which the parties' confirmatory memoranda agree are treated the same way.)
Course and usage can explain or supplement.
Not barred.
The PER never bars later agreements.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — What § 2-202 bars

q: A repudiation substantially impairs the contract's value to the aggrieved party. What may that party do?
o: Only wait for performance, until the original due date finally arrives.
Only sue after the due date passes.
Only demand adequate assurance.
Await performance or resort to remedies, suspending either way.
Must keep performing its own side.
oe: It may resort to remedies at once.
Not required.
It may do more.
Correct. Section 2-610(a)-(c). A seller may also identify goods or salvage unfinished goods (§ 2-704). Substantial impairment uses the installment-contract test (cmt. 3).
That was the traditional rule; it may suspend.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Options after repudiation

q: Assuming it appears in a conspicuous writing, which language excludes the implied warranty of fitness?
o: "Buyer acknowledges that the goods were available for viewing in the showroom."
"Seller disclaims the implied warranty of merchantability."
"No fitness warranty," in tiny gray type on page 6.
"No warranties extend beyond the description on the face hereof."
The same sentence, said orally at the counter.
oe: Mere availability isn't an examination after the seller's demand.
That reaches merchantability only.
Not conspicuous.
Correct. That's § 2-316(2)'s own example. A fitness disclaimer must be written and conspicuous but needn't mention fitness.
Fitness disclaimers must be in writing.
topic: VI · Merchantability, fitness, cumulation & privity (§§ 2-314 to 2-318) — Words that exclude fitness

q: Which statement about the tests for hybrid transactions is NOT correct?
o: Most states adopted the gravamen test after Anthony Pools.
Under the gravamen test, one deal can face more than one statute of limitations.
It is unclear under the gravamen test whether irritating contact lenses are a goods or a services claim.
A few courts applied Article 2 to the goods aspects and other law to the services.
The predominant purpose test is all-or-nothing.
oe: Correct. This is false. The gravamen test got little traction; no court outside Maryland expressly adopted it, and Maryland itself seems to use predominant purpose now.
True; the slides flag this as a difficulty.
True. That's the slide's example of how hard the test is to apply.
True: the bifurcation approach, which the 2022 amendments partly adopt.
True.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — Tests for hybrids: true and false

q: For the transaction described, which person is NOT a merchant under § 2-104(1)?
o: A rancher who sells cattle through a licensed livestock broker.
A lawyer buying fishing tackle for her own weekend use.
A hardware store selling hammers.
An antique dealer selling a Victorian desk.
A university's purchasing office ordering lab equipment.
oe: Merchant status can be attributed through an agent or broker who holds itself out as having the knowledge or skill.
Correct. Comment 2: even "practices" merchant status requires acting in a mercantile capacity; a lawyer buying for personal use isn't a merchant.
Deals in goods of the kind.
Deals in goods of the kind.
For the "practices" provisions, even universities and banks can be merchants in their mercantile capacity.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — Who is not a merchant

q: In Orange & Rockland v. Amerada Hess, a utility doubled its oil "requirements" so it could sell the extra on the market. What did the court hold?
o: The utility acted in bad faith, so disproportion didn't matter.
Requirements contracts with estimates are void.
The demand was enforceable because estimates are only estimates.
The doubling was unreasonably disproportionate.
The seller could cancel the entire contract.
oe: The court treated disproportion as its own limit.
They're valid.
It was excessive.
Correct. The disproportion limit is separate from good faith; it applies "even where one party acts with complete good faith."
The holding limited the demand.
topic: VII · Quantity & price (§§ 2-305, 2-306) — Orange & Rockland holding

q: Assuming each becomes part of the basis of the bargain, which creates an express warranty under § 2-313?
o: A description of the goods in the contract.
A model shown because the goods themselves aren't on hand.
The seller's statement that the goods are "a great value at this price."
All of the above.
A and B only.
oe: Creates one (§ 2-313(1)(b)), but it isn't the only correct item.
Creates one (§ 2-313(1)(c)), but it isn't the only correct item.
Doesn't. An affirmation merely of value, or the seller's opinion or commendation, creates no warranty (§ 2-313(2)).
Wrong, because C is an affirmation of value, which creates no warranty.

Correct. Express warranties come from (a) an affirmation of fact or promise relating to the goods, (b) a description, or (c) a sample or model, each part of the basis of the bargain. A statement of value or opinion doesn't count.
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — What creates an express warranty

q: Custom windows are to be "shipped properly crated ... and delivered to" the buyer's New York construction site. Properly crated, they're destroyed in transit. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because the windows were custom-made.
They split it.
The buyer, under a shipment contract.
The carrier alone, as between the parties.
The seller, because it agreed to deliver to the site.
oe: Irrelevant to risk.
No splitting.
Correct. Problem 4-7(a) (Windows, Inc. v. Jordan Panel): "delivered to" just names where the goods are going; without an express undertaking of transit risk, it's a shipment contract.
As between the parties, the buyer.
Naming a destination doesn't create a destination contract.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Windows "delivered to" the site

q: Chapter 4 treats three tender scenarios with different rules. Which is NOT one of them?
o: The seller tenders directly to the buyer.
The seller ships the goods by carrier.
The buyer manufactures the goods itself.
Goods held by a bailee are delivered without being moved.
None of the above.
oe: One of the three.
One of the three.

Correct. The three are: the seller tenders directly; the seller ships by carrier; and goods held by a bailee are delivered without being moved. Within each, tender, inspection, acceptance and payment can unfold in several sequences.
One of the three.
One of the other choices is correct: The buyer manufactures the goods itself.
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — Three tender scenarios

q: Which wording most clearly puts transit risk on the SELLER?
o: "Windows to be properly crated for transit."
"Seller pays freight to the site."
"F.O.B. Buyer's construction site."
"Delivered to the construction site."
"Ship to Buyer at the construction site."
oe: A packaging duty, not a risk term.
A cost term.

Correct. Problem 4-7(c): an F.O.B. destination term, or an express statement that the seller bears the risk until tender at the site. "Delivered at" the site is only an argument for a destination contract (4-7(b)); "delivered to" isn't enough.
Treated as a shipment contract.
Shipment contract.
topic: IX · Shipment & destination contracts; shipping terms (§§ 2-504, 2-319 to 2-322) — Drafting a destination contract

q: After a clear repudiation, an aggrieved buyer waits four months for the seller to change its mind while the market price climbs. Effect?
o: Nothing; it may wait until the original delivery date.
It can't recover damages it could have avoided by acting sooner.
It has waived the repudiation.
The seller's repudiation is automatically retracted.
It may recover the higher damages caused by waiting.
oe: Only a commercially reasonable time.

Correct. Comment 1 to § 2-610: waiting beyond a commercially reasonable time bars damages that should have been avoided. Under the traditional rule, the non-repudiating party had to keep performing; § 2-610 is the modern approach.
Not waived; damages are limited.
No.
Not avoidable ones.
topic: XV · Insecurity, repudiation & retraction (§§ 2-609 to 2-611) — Waiting too long

q: Which offered evidence could the parol evidence rule bar?
o: Evidence that the seller lied to induce the contract.
A prior oral promise adding a term to a complete and exclusive writing.
A modification agreed after signing.
Evidence that the writing wasn't to take effect until financing came through.
Evidence offered only to interpret an ambiguous term.
oe: Fraud evidence isn't barred.

Correct. The PER applies only to evidence of an alleged term of the agreement. It doesn't reach a separate agreement, interpretation, a later modification, a formation defect like fraud, mistake or duress, or a condition precedent to the writing taking effect.
Later agreements aren't barred (though a NOM clause might be).
A condition precedent isn't barred.
Interpretation isn't contradiction or supplementation.
topic: XII · Parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) — When the PER bars evidence

q: Which statement about § 2-201(1) is NOT correct?
o: The record need be signed only by the party against whom enforcement is sought.
A contract within it can't be enforced by way of action or by way of defense.
It applies to a contract for the sale of goods for a price of $500 or more.
An email ending with the sender's typed name can be a signed record.
The record must state the price, or the contract is unenforceable.
oe: True. Not necessarily both parties.
True. That is the statute's language.
True.
True. "Record" includes electronic records, and a typed name adopted to authenticate is a signature (or UETA § 7 in a non-2022 state).
Correct. This is false. Only quantity is essential; a record "is not insufficient because it omits or incorrectly states a term," though the contract can't be enforced beyond the quantity shown.
topic: III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability (§§ 2-201, 2-302) — What § 2-201(1) requires

q: Absent agreement, which default rule is correct?
o: The seller may deliver in several lots at its option.
Delivery is due within 30 days of contracting.
The buyer gets 30 days of credit.
Delivery takes place at the buyer's place of business.
The buyer pays when it receives the goods, after a chance to inspect.
oe: A single lot is presumed (§ 2-307).
Within a reasonable time (§ 2-309(1)).
No credit is presumed.
The seller's place (§ 2-308(a)).
Correct. Sections 2-310(a) and 2-513(1). No credit is presumed.
topic: VIII · Tender, delivery & payment defaults (§§ 2-301, 2-307 to 2-310, 2-503, 2-507, 2-511) — Delivery and payment defaults

q: Under § 2-102(2), as amended in 2022, if the sale-of-goods aspects of a hybrid transaction do NOT predominate, Article 2:
o: does not apply at all.
applies only if the parties agree to it in a signed record.
applies to formation and the statute of frauds, but not to warranties.
applies only to provisions relating primarily to the goods aspects.
applies to the whole transaction anyway.
oe: That was the old predominant purpose result. The 2022 rule keeps the goods-related provisions.
Scope is set by § 2-102, not by agreement.
Backwards. Warranties apply; formation and § 2-201 relate to the transaction as a whole and don't.
Correct. If goods predominate, Article 2 applies (with other law possibly governing the non-goods aspects). If not, only the goods-related provisions apply.
That's the result when goods DO predominate.
topic: I · Which law governs, goods & hybrids (§§ 2-102, 2-105 to 2-107) — 2022 two-tier rule

q: Which statement about excuse is NOT correct?
o: A seller excused under § 2-615 must allocate fairly and notify its buyers.
Section 2-613 requires goods identified when the contract was made.
A seller whose costs double in a market boom is excused under § 2-615.
After a § 2-615 notice, a buyer may terminate or take its quota.
Under § 2-614(1), a commercially reasonable substitute delivery must be tendered and accepted.
oe: True.
Correct. This is false. Increased cost or a market swing alone doesn't excuse (cmt. 4).
True.
topic: XVI · Excuse (§§ 2-613 to 2-616) — Excuse rules review

q: Before using course of dealing to supply a term, which question is NOT one of the textbook's three?
o: Is the evidence admissible?
Can it be construed consistently with the express terms?
Is there enough evidence that it exists?
Was the course of dealing reduced to writing?
None of the above.
oe: One of the three.
One of the three.
One of the three.

Correct. No writing is needed. The three questions are: is there enough evidence it exists (proponent's burden), is it admissible (notice, parol evidence rule), and can it be read consistently with the express terms (else the hierarchy).
One of the other choices is correct: Was the course of dealing reduced to writing?.
topic: IV · Course of performance, dealing & usage; good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304) — Three questions for course and usage

q: A seller says, "This compressor delivers 150 psi." It never says "warrant" or "guarantee" and doesn't intend to make a warranty. Is there an express warranty?
o: No, because the seller never used "warrant" or "guarantee."
Only if the statement appears in a signed writing.
Only if the seller is a merchant that regularly sells compressors.
No, because the seller didn't intend to make a warranty.
Yes, if it's part of the basis of the bargain.
oe: Formal words aren't required.
Oral affirmations can be warranties.
Any seller can make an express warranty.
Intent isn't required.
Correct. It isn't necessary that the seller use formal words or have a specific intention to make a warranty (§ 2-313(2)).
topic: V · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — No magic words or intent

q: A homeowner sells her riding mower to a neighbor and says, "It's in my shed; come take it any time today." A tree crushes the shed that afternoon. Who bears the loss?
o: The homeowner, because the neighbor hadn't paid yet.
The neighbor, because the seller tendered.
The homeowner, because the neighbor never received it.
They split it.
The homeowner, because she still had title.
oe: Payment is irrelevant.
Correct. For a non-merchant seller, risk passes on tender (§ 2-509(3)): she held the mower at the buyer's disposition and told him so.
Receipt is the test only for merchant sellers.
No splitting.
Title is irrelevant.
topic: IX · Risk of loss, identification & bailees (§§ 2-501, 2-509, 2-510, 2-327) — Neighbor's mower

q: Which statement is correct?
o: Cancellation is for breach and keeps remedies; termination isn't.
Termination is for breach; cancellation is for any other reason.
Cancellation wipes out all remedies.
They mean the same thing.
Termination requires the other party's consent.
oe: Correct. Cancellation (§ 2-106(4)) ends the contract for breach, and the canceling party keeps its remedies for breach of the whole. Termination (§ 2-106(3)) ends it under a power from agreement or law for a reason other than breach.
Reversed.
The canceling party keeps them.
They're defined separately.
It's exercised under a power, not by mutual consent.
topic: XIV · Termination & cancellation (§§ 2-106, 2-309) — Cancellation vs. termination

q: A buyer receives defective equipment and pays to inspect it, store it pending return and arrange a replacement. Those costs are:
o: incidental damages.
consequential damages.
unrecoverable overhead.
liquidated damages.
punitive damages.
oe: Correct. Section 2-715(1): reasonable inspection, transportation, care and custody of rejected goods, and the costs of effecting cover. The types are compensatory, incidental, consequential and liquidated.
Those are losses from the buyer's needs and injuries.
They're recoverable.
Those are agreed in advance.
Not available for breach of contract.
topic: XI · Remedies & the statute of limitations (§§ 2-702 to 2-716, 2-725) — Costs of responding to breach

q: Which rule requires a "goods" merchant (one who deals in goods of that kind), not just a "practices" merchant?
o: Firm offers under § 2-205.
The merchant's confirmation exception to the SOF.
The implied warranty of merchantability.
The separate-signature rule for NOM clauses.
Additional terms joining the contract under § 2-207(2).
oe: Practices merchant.
Practices merchants ("between merchants").

Correct. Section 2-314 requires a merchant "with respect to goods of that kind," as does entrustment under § 2-403(2). Firm offers, the SOF confirmation rule, § 2-207(2) and § 2-209(2) need only practices merchants.
Practices merchants.
Practices merchants.
topic: VI · Gap fillers & merchants (§§ 2-104, 2-204(3), 2-304, 2-311) — Goods merchant rules

q: Which statement about the implied warranty of merchantability is NOT correct?
o: It covers food or drink served for value.
It requires goods to be fit for the ordinary purposes for which they are used.
It applies to used goods, but only at the level appropriate for used goods.
A seller that didn't know of the defect isn't liable.
It arises only when the seller is a merchant in goods of that kind.
oe: True: § 2-314(2)(c), the key standard.
True: cmt. 3.
Correct. This is false. Liability is strict; the seller's lack of knowledge is no defense.

q: Which is NOT one of the Orange & Rockland factors for deciding whether a demand is "unreasonably disproportionate"?
o: Whether the buyer is a merchant.
How far the demand exceeds the estimate.
Whether the seller could reasonably have foreseen the increase.
How far the market price exceeds the contract price.
The reason for the increase.
oe: Correct. The five factors: how far the demand exceeds the estimate; whether the seller could have anticipated it; how far market price exceeds contract price; whether the market rise was fortuitous; and the reason for the increase.
A factor.
A factor.
A factor.
A factor.
